content:
I’m pretty skeptical of any executive/leader that has a specific and detailed “plan” for what they would do when joining a new organization. 

Maybe it’s called “The Playbook.” 

Maybe it’s their own personal 30-60-90 day plan they’ve used at every new job for the last decade. 

Regardless of what it’s called (or even how good it is) I don’t think new execs/leaders should come in ready to roll it out. 

I think they should come in with curiosity. 

Instead of their plan, I want to hear the list of questions they would ask, the data they would review, and the processes they want to better understand. 

Then, I want to understand how they’d form a plan with that context. 

It’s easy to recite “the plan” you’ve used before. It’s never been easier to ask ChatGPT/Claude to build a plan that you can confidently present as your own. 

But people are complex, and organizations are filled with people. And plans are best made after understanding that complexity - not rolled out expecting people will just fall in line.

content:
A rep told me their account was “tapped out.” So we reassigned it. A few months later, the new AE closed a six-figure upgrade.

The first rep wasn’t doing a bad job. They knew the users, ensured adoption, and confirmed there was no fit for additional products after several demos with the existing team. 

To them, that meant the account had maxed out - so they asked for it to be replaced.

The new AE took a different approach. First, they learned how the current team was using the platform.

Then they asked:

- What problems is this company facing?
- Which ones can we help solve?
- Who owns those problems?

They found a business priority we could support, identified the team responsible, and got an intro from the existing users (who were happy to help).

Three months later, that team was fully onboarded, and we had a six-figure upsell.

I’ve seen this play out time and time again - AEs looking too narrowly at accounts, asking:
 
“How can I get the current users to spend more?”

That mindset leaves money on the table.

Start by helping your users solve the problems they bought you to solve.

Then zoom out: What other problems exist in the business that you can help with?

Use your existing success as a case study, ask for intros, and expand your impact.

Expanded revenue will follow.

Half the battle is knowing which accounts you should spend time with. 

You don’t want to neglect an account just to watch another AE close a big deal as soon as you lose it - but you also don’t want to spin your wheels for months in an account with nothing to show for the effort. 

I built a “Territory Framework” guide to help you know where to spend your time.

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal. Time really does kill deals. 

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down. 

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

“CONGRATS ON YOUR SERIES B HERE’S OUR PRODUCT”

As soon as someone updates their LinkedIn, the AI Spam Cannons launch:

“CONGRATS ON YOUR NEW ROLE HERE’S OUR PRODUCT”

If you build your outbound triggers off of common “signals” you are adding to the noise instead of breaking through it. 

Instead, take some time to define signals that are unique to your offer/product. Use those for your “why reach out now” triggers. 

I’m not saying that funding/hiring/rev growth signals are worthless - you need that data as you think about “what accounts should we care about in our TAM?” 

But using generic data like that for a “trigger” event means your outreach is landing with the same messaging and at the same time as everyone else. 

p.s. A few categories to start thinking about what specific signals would look like for you:


- Job descriptions revealing priorities
- Product launches or pricing changes
- Expansion into new segments, geographies, or customer types
- Public customer complaints that point to the problem you solve
- Leadership language in earnings calls, podcasts, or interviews
- Website copy changes that show strategic shifts
- Support, security, compliance, or infrastructure investments

content:
A lot of poor decisions made by sellers comes from a poor understanding of “expected value.”

Expected value = a predicted value of a variable, calculated as the sum of all possible values each multiplied by the probability of its occurrence.

Example: Someone offers you $100 if a coin flip comes up 'heads'

$100 (potential value) x 50% (probability of ‘heads’) = $50 expected value

Sellers make two big decisions all the time without thinking about this concept:

- Which deals to focus on
- Which job to take

When you look at extreme examples, decision making off of ‘expected value’ seems obvious.

If you spent 8 hours wandering the streets of a major city, you have a 99.99% chance of finding a penny. 

Nearly guaranteed success - but you wouldn’t do it. Because 1 cent * 99.99% probability of success = less than a penny of expected value.

Not worth the time.

If I offered you $10,000,000,000 if you were to make one hundred 50 foot putts in a row you wouldn’t quit your job and take up golf.

Because the odds of making that many long putts in a row is worse than 1 in 97 quadrillion… which makes the expected value effectively $0. The high payout is made obsolete by the impossible odds.

But less extreme examples lead to worse decision making:

The $500,000 RFP with a 2% chance of winning.

The “founding AE” job with $3,000,000 of “equity.”

Sellers know they probably aren’t going to win that RFP. But the big number in their pipeline makes them spend hours crafting the response (that won’t even be read).

If they thought through the “expected value” and calculated $500,000 deal size x 2% win rate on RFPs = $10,000 of expected value they wouldn’t waste their time.

Instead, they’d focus on the $100,000 opportunities where they have a 30%+ chance of winning:

$100,000 x 30% chance to win = expected value of $30,000. A deal ⅕ of the size… but 3x the expected value.

The “big equity” outcome has wasted many years for many talented sellers and leaders.

Let’s look at expected value:

Series A companies have a ~3% chance at a successful exit (acquisition/IPO with meaningful multiples).

That “your equity could be worth $3,000,000 at IPO” expected value is $3,000,000 x 3% = $90,000.
​
I’m not saying don’t take your shot - but I would say “don’t sacrifice 10s of thousands a year in base/variable comp to get a $3,000,000 equity package that has an expected value of $90,000.”

“But Kyle - I just have to win one of those RFPs and I make my year! Isn’t it worth my best effort, just in case?”

“But Kyle - this startup role could end up being the next Anthropic! Isn’t it worth the risk?”

I’m just sharing the odds. Maybe you can shift them in your favor, and increase your expected value.

Or, maybe you are better off prioritizing deals/jobs where the expected value is naturally higher.

You can run your job like the lottery - or you can maximize your expected value and tie your income to the highest probability outcomes.

At a recent customer panel an exec said, “I don’t care about cost as much.” Then, she shared exactly what she wants to see in vendor proposals: 

She said, “Obviously I want a fair deal for my company, but cost isn’t the main criteria for my evaluation. Instead, I’m reviewing the proposal with the question of ‘Will this tool be a success with my team.’”

Then she shared that the best proposals include “an adoption plan” that gives her confidence her team will get enabled on the tool, roll out successfully, and recognize value quickly.

She continued to share why this is her main criteria:

“My problem statement is we have too much churn with tools.”

Companies buy a lot of software. Surprisingly often, that software ends up never being implemented. 

Even if implemented, software often ends up being under-consumed relative to what is purchased (e.g., 100 users purchased, only 30 seats used).

With all the money wasted on shelfware and underutilized contracts it’s not surprising that this executive is worried less about “how much will this cost” and worried more about “if I buy this, will the team actually make full use of it.”

A good adoption plan will vary based on what you sell and which segment of the market you cover.

If selling a complex technical product to enterprises, your adoption plan likely includes professional services, technical account managers, and customer success representatives.

If selling a less technical product to SMB/MM, your adoption plan is likely tied to digital onboarding/training.

And then anything in the middle likely has a balance of both.

Regardless of your product/segment, I recommend including an adoption plan in all of your proposals.

That way your customer:

- Sees that you are thinking beyond the contract signature
- Has confidence in your team/resources to drive adoption
- Doesn’t worry “what if I buy this and the team never uses it”

If you are already doing this, I’d love to hear from you what works.

The nuance is tied to more buyer psychology - and the balance between showing up as knowledgeable vs a know-it-all. 

Get the nuance wrong, and your prospect will tune out just as much as they would if you showed up unprepared.

When your prospect says, “we want to do this, but later,” you can ask:

“When we hear ‘yes, but later’ it’s usually for one of three reasons:

- You have more pressing problems that need to be solved first

- We are solving a prioritized problem, but you have other ways to address it that come before our solution

- You don’t have the bandwidth to implement until later

It won’t necessarily save your deal or lead to a faster win. 

But you’ll at least get clarity on the timing objection - and figure out if it’s really a “yes, but later” or just a nicer way of saying “no” and brushing you off.

For a while, I used AI for everything I could. AI made a lot of my work faster and easier. Then, I realized I was getting dumber.

I got worse at brainstorming. Why go for a walk and slowly think of ideas when an LLM can generate infinite lists of ideas?

I got worse at writing. Why stumble through multiple drafts and edit when AI can generate infinite content?

So I significantly cut my use of AI.

I want my ideas to come from my experiences. I want my writing to reflect my actual beliefs. And I want my brain to "struggle" to figure things out.

I read a post a few weeks ago that nailed the risk of AI overuse specific to sales. I'll highlight some here and then link to the full post by Derek H:

You can cook a steak in 3 minutes in a microwave.
​
It’s efficient. It’s fast. It’s "productive."
​
But you’d never serve it to your most important client.
​
In tech sales right now, we are obsessed with the microwave. We’re using AI to scale our discovery, automate our research, and optimize our outreach.
​
On paper, the productivity metrics look solid. We’re doing more than ever.
​
But there’s a catch.
​
When you get in the room or on the Zoom with a customer, they can taste the microwave.
​
They can tell when your discovery questions were pulled from a generic prompt rather than genuine curiosity. They can feel the rubber texture of a pitch built by an algorithm that doesn't understand their internal politics or the stakes of their role.
​
AI can prep the ingredients.
​
But it cannot provide the sear.​
​
​Full post here: https://lnkd.in/dpHCzzCa

I remain optimistic about the use of AI in sales. I'm heavily involved in rolling out new agentic workflows for our sales org, constantly evaluating new tools, and have championed the purchase of multiple AI solutions.

But I am concerned about the sellers that rely on AI for everything. The ones that can generate a good call plan, but don't understand it. The ones that can create a bunch of accurate account plans, but can't extract the most relevant pieces. The ones that can prompt LLMs, but can't talk to customers.

Because if the only output you can create as a seller comes from AI, you've already been replaced. 

Payroll just hasn't quite caught up yet.

AI psychosis is everywhere - the funniest example I’ve seen so far is the founders posting pictures of their Anthropic or OpenAI invoices and bragging about how much they spend.

Nope. 

If you can’t take a human and teach them exactly what they need to do to successfully execute a task that leads to the right outcome, AI won’t save you. 

AI Agents follow instructions. If the instructions are vague, AI will make stuff up using pattern recognition - not GTM best practices. 

If the instructions are specific, appropriate tool access is reachable, and the data foundation is solid, AI agents can do great work. 

So when you decide “which part of our process should we make agentic first?”

Pick the use case where you know exactly how to drive great results. 

Not the use case where you’ve failed to get momentum for months/quarters/years. 

Otherwise you’ll end up with GTM agents doing stuff that doesn’t work at scale.

And all you’ll be able to brag about is how much money you are spending on AI.

content:
Discovery calls end with “can you send me info and I’ll get back to you?” unless you break from the “normal” structure. The typical (broken) discovery goes like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and small talk

- Next ten minutes: Superficial discussion of the buyer’s day-to-day

- Next ten minutes: Seller shares high-level overview of product. 

Twenty-five minutes into a thirty minute call and almost no progress is made. The seller barely knows anything about the buyer. The buyer barely knows anything about the seller’s product. 

The final few minutes become a mad scramble for the seller to find something valuable enough to earn another call, but most discoveries end with the buyer saying, “Can you send me a case study and more information so we can review and get back to you?”

A great discovery looks like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and objective set

- Next five minutes: Point-of-view validated (or corrected) and priorities confirms

- Next ten minutes: Deep discovery of how the buyer is approaching their priorities

- Last ten minutes: Seller shares how they can help accomplish priorities and next steps for evaluation finalized

Maybe all you need is the “outline” and you can go run better discoveries. 

But maybe you need a guide that breaks it down step-by-step. 

If you want the step-by-step guide to great discovery, my discovery playbook is free today: https://lnkd.in/gT7ZMQQz

content:
I’m in my 6th year as a sales VP. These are the 5 most important lessons I’ve learned:

1) Nothing matters more than who you hire 

Hiring an AE that doesn’t work out will cost you 6+ months.

Hiring a front-line leader that doesn’t work out will cost you 12+ months.

Hiring multiple leaders and AEs that don’t work out will cost you your job. 

2) You can’t “hire slow” and win

Executive sales leadership is generally a big math problem:

“Is your productive capacity sufficient to cover your quota?” 

If you hire slow, your productive capacity will be too low. Even if you hire great talent, you’ll still fall short. The math kills you. 

So, you have to hire fast. And if you hire fast, but make mistakes? See #1. 

3) You can’t out-execute bad culture 

The best thing I heard from an AE this last year was “I can’t imagine working anywhere else - I’d miss the culture too much.” 

You can have the best systems, best training, best plan - but if your team is miserable you won’t retain top talent. 

And VPs that don’t retain top talent don’t retain their jobs. 

4) Use data for hypotheses but never decisions

The larger your org, the more tempting it is to rely on data for decisions. It takes a ton of work AND time to fly low enough to make real observations (and it’s time you usually don’t have). 

But data without context is, at best, incomplete. 

And, at worst, completely wrong. 

And VPs making decisions off of incomplete or wrong assumptions (you already see where I’m going with this) don’t keep their jobs. 

5) Exceptions kill orgs 

Every exception you make is one you have to defend. 

Want to make an exception and hire an AE at a higher level to “match their comp expectations?”

Now you have to explain to all the AEs with their same experience why the new rep was hired at a higher level. 

Want to make an exception on rules of engagement for an opportunity split? 

Now you have to explain to every other rep in a similar situation why they aren’t getting the same treatment. 

The more exceptions you make, the less people respect your systems, processes, and you. 

I’ve got a lot more lessons to learn (many I’ll learn the hard way). 

Any other sales leaders willing to share what I’ve missed?

content:
I’m not one to tear down tactics but when you lead with “our process is so good it replaces a seller” you better back it up. 

And this one 100% does not. 

This post was forwarded to me by several people that were legitimately thinking they could replace people with this process. 

The company started linking to their “guide” after getting thousands of comments requesting access so I took a look. 

Here’s their “signal based outreach” motion prompt:

"I want to run a signal-based prospecting initiative.

1. Search LinkedIn and the broader web for companies that have interacted with [Competitor Name]’s content or attended their events within the last 30 days.

2. Filter results to match my ICP: B2B SaaS, 50–500 employees, North America.

3. For the top 5 qualified companies, analyze job postings to determine whether they are hiring roles responsible for managing or replacing [Competitor’s Tool].

4. Draft a personalized outbound email for the VP of Sales at each company, referencing their specific signals and context.”


3 big issues with this prompt: 

1) Targeting companies that have interacted with competitor’s content or attended their events

Unless your prospect is angrily commenting on competitor’s posts and attending their events in protest you haven’t found signals. 

You’ve found your competitor’s superfans. 

Let's give them the benefit of the doubt though and say that some of these social media engagers/event attenders are really in evaluation mode (I'm sure some are).

What % of your actual ICP engages with a competitor’s LinkedIn content and/or has attended a competitor's event in the last 30 days?

If this is your fishing pond for signals, you're going hungry.

2) ICP definition is static and generic: B2B SaaS, 50–500 employees, North America

This… isn’t an ICP. Maybe it’s a placeholder? But people aren’t grabbing your PDF that replaces SDRs for placeholders in prompts - they are grabbing your promised “system.” 

3) Draft a personalized outbound email for the VP of Sales

I like to think the VP of Sales is very important, but why are we hardcoding a static title into a prompt? 

And anyone that has tried to write with AI knows that “draft a personalized outbound email” is NOWHERE near enough context to give you anything besides AI slop.

Speaking of slop, here’s their DM template that they claim leads to an 80% response rate: 

“Hey [Name], 

Quick question - what's your biggest challenge with [topic] right now?”

I don’t care how many of your competitor’s events your new hot lead has attended in the last 30 days. 

They aren’t responding to that message. 

I know everyone is trying hard to keep up with the AI craze. No one has it figured out. 

But before you follow the process from a viral “this replaced our sales team!” post, take a deeper look.

There’s a reason these posters that have “automated outbound” use social engagement hacks to build their pipeline instead of their “process.”

An honest pros/cons of posting on LinkedIn after a few years and growing to 85,000 followers:

Pros:

1) Recruiting

I speak to a lot of candidates that are familiar with LaunchDarkly because they’ve seen my posts. 

It’s helped us earn the attention of phenomenal talent and we are fortunate many have decided to join our team. 

2) Friends

I’ve been fortunate to meet some awesome people from LinkedIn and have built meaningful friendships. But, I’ve also met Jen Allen-Knuth. 

So I guess this one is a pro/con? 

3) Additional income streams

Sales Introverts has grown significantly more than I ever anticipated when it first started. Many of my subscribers became familiar with me from LinkedIn. 

Cons:

1) “You are big on LinkedIn” is more likely to be used as a crippling insult than as a compliment

LinkedIn “influencers” don’t have a great reputation. Much of that is earned. 

I’d much rather be known as a practitioner than a content creator, but you can’t post all the time and not be grouped in with the “creator” population. 

2) Competing for attention is exhausting

I wish I could just write thoughtful, helpful content without worrying about the “hook.” 

I wish the great content I love to read from others wasn’t buried in a sea of dishonest claims, attention-demanding selfies, and artificial controversy. 

But you have to earn attention, and that takes effort unless you go for “engagement hacks.”

Which I won’t. 

3) It’s a tough game to “win” without a big time commitment 

The people that post about posting on LinkedIn will tell you how critical it is to engage with a ton of posts every day. 

“Block off 60 minutes and comment on posts, DM strangers and ask to meet, you gotta invest the time!” 

Great advice for someone who’s life is LinkedIn. 

Not something I’m able (or want) to do. 


For now, the pros outweigh the cons - I’m happy I started posting a few years ago. 

But my ultimate goal is not to “become big on LinkedIn” - it’s to no longer need LinkedIn at all.

content:
The best sales content I’ve read in a long time comes from a buyer sharing how they buy. Today, I'm highlighting my favorite parts along with a little bit of my own commentary.

Let's dive into the highlights, and I'll link the full post at the end.

Highlight one:

“Every vendor tells me their product is revolutionary. You know what’s also revolutionary? Getting fired because your “revolutionary” product bricked the payment system during Black Friday. I’ve seen it happen. It wasn’t the vendor who lost their job.”

Key takeaway:

Sellers all sound the same. Every vendor has “innovation.” Every vendor has “industry awards.” Every vendor has “cutting-edge AI.”

But while we are blabbering on about how great we are, our prospect is wondering: “Where is this most likely to go wrong? And, if it goes wrong, how devastating would it be to me and my team?”

Highlight two:

“The vendor who won my biggest contract didn’t have the best product. They had:

• A reference from a CISO I trusted
• An implementation plan that didn’t require overtime from my burned-out team
• A CEO who personally committed to our success
• Proof they’d done this exact deployment 50 times before

Their competitor had better tech and was 30% cheaper. They also had a 12-month implementation timeline and no relevant references.

Easy decision.”

Key takeaway:

This one is scary. Imagine a forecast call where you tell your boss “my champion told me we have better tech and we are 30% cheaper.”

Sounds like an easy win.

Now, you know that your “champion” could be telling their boss: “This other vendor is more expensive and doesn’t have all the functionality. But it’s the safer bet.”

Your easy win quickly becomes a shocking loss.

Highlight three:

“You tell me features. Tell me what fires you put out and whose job you saved.

You show ROI spreadsheets. Show me CISOs who didn’t get fired after deploying your product.

You push for the enterprise deal. Let me pilot first. Let me look like a hero internally before I bet my career.”

Key takeaway:

You already know features don’t sell - you need to sell “value.” But are you selling the value your prospect cares about?

For most buyers "value" is a combination of “the safest bet to work + most likely to make me look good.”

Highlight four:

“Let’s have an honest conversation. If you keep selling products while we’re buying career insurance, we’re all wasting time.”

Key takeaway:

The job market sucks. Many people (including buyers) are in survival mode.

Are you selling an unrealistic dream? Or, are you selling “career insurance?”

If you are selling the dream, you may find yourself losing to the rep selling insurance.

You can read the full post here: https://lnkd.in/gkPTXFeC

Many sales leaders abuse metrics. They’ll obsess over data and refuse to understand context. 

While metrics DEFINITELY matter, you need to use the data effectively. 

One big mistake I see is getting too focused on individual metrics without seeing the broader picture. 

If you obsess over improving one metric, your team will hit it at the expense of others. 

For example: “We need to increase our call-to-contact rate!” 

Easiest way for an AE to increase this metric is only to call lower-level prospects. 

Call to contact rate up, meaningful conversations down. 

“We need to increase our discovery conversion rates!!” 

One way to increase discovery conversion rates is to avoid meetings with non-decision makers. 

Hello, AEs refusing to take meetings set by SDRs. 

Discovery conversion rates up, number of discoveries down. 

When you focus on one metric, ensure you aren’t trading success in one area for failure in another. 

Otherwise, you'll artificially improve metrics without impacting revenue.

As an AE, I spent months trying to get into an account at “senior” levels. No one responded.

I started reaching out to entry-level professionals. One agreed to meet.

I could have quickly disqualified them as they were clearly not the right contact. Fortunately, I still decided to run a full discovery.

They gave me insight into a C-Level goal (NPS at 60 by 2021) and a breakdown of internal systems.

Using this information, I created a business case for how we could help them achieve that goal within their current internal systems.

Sent a message to the CEO with the subject line, “NPS to 60 by 2021?” and attached my business case for how we could help. He responded immediately, and we kicked off the evaluation.

Here’s the lesson: stop thinking that initial conversations are only valuable if they convert into an opportunity.

Your first conversation with an account is probably not with your eventual buyer. If you worry only about “converting” the opportunity, you’ll leave the call without being any closer.

Shift your mindset from “how can I qualify an opportunity” to “how can I better learn the value I can add to this company,” and you’ll end up with the strongest opportunities of your career.

The key is to get “nuggets” of information in any conversation with an account - cold calls, email replies, discovery calls, etc.

After reviewing countless pipeline generation plans, I’ve developed a framework that helps AEs 2x their pipe gen. Here’s the exact template and process I use:

1. Target Account Selection

Enterprise: Focus on 1-2 key accounts
Mid-market: Target 3-5 accounts
SMB: Include 5-15 accounts

2. Strategic Contact Mapping

For each target account, identify 3-15 key prospects based on your market:

Above-the-line contacts: Directors, VPs, C-Level executives
Below-the-line contacts: Managers and individual contributors

Enterprise should focus on more per account, SMB fewer per account.

3. Pain Point Analysis

Document specific challenges your target accounts face today. This isn’t about your product features – it’s about their business problems you can solve.

4. Value Hypothesis Development

Create a clear statement of how your solution addresses their specific challenges. This becomes your north star for all account engagement.

5. Relevant Success Stories

Have customer stories ready that mirror your target account’s industry, size, or challenges. These become your social proof in conversations.

6. Setting Strategic Weekly Goals

Here’s where most reps get it wrong: They default to “set a meeting” as their only goal.

The best PG plans I see often keep the same account in focus for multiple weeks. Here’s what that progression might look like:

Week 1: “Identify current feature management solution through engineering team outreach”

Week 2: “Uncover engineering team KPIs through manager-level conversations”

Week 3: “Secure director+ meeting leveraging gathered intelligence”

How did you perform against quota in your prior role” is a painful interview question to answer if you missed. Don’t say:

“I missed quota, and it was because my territory sucked, our product is lame, and my manager hates me.”

Even if it’s true! 

Lots of companies are pretty broken. Many sales leaders are incapable of helping their teams succeed. And territory models can be brutally broken.

But missing quota + pushing the blame on external factors is rarely a winning combination in an interview. 

Fair or not, you’ll benefit from taking ownership. Maybe it sounds like this:

 “I missed quota. I did a poor job vetting the organization I was joining and made some assumptions about product/market fit that were wrong. However, here are some of the wins I experienced and what I learned:” 

I’ve hired a lot of reps over the last few years. 

Many of them coming from orgs where they (and nearly everyone else) were missing quotas. 

I know that a potentially great rep in a bad environment won’t have success. I do my best to interview in a way that allows me to find those high potential reps so I can put them in a great environment where they will. 

And reps missing quota can stand out in an interview when they take ownership, share learnings, and show the capacity of having success in a better sales organization.

content:
The most important “mental model” I’ve learned as a sales leader is “what is one of many for me, is one out of one for them.”

 Let me explain:

I average twelve 1:1s per week. 

If I’m focused and attentive in eleven of those, I have a 92% success rate in 1:1 execution. 

The problem is the impact of the one where I was distracted. For me, it was ~8% of my 1:1s. 

For the rep or leader, it was 100% of their 1:1s with their VP. 

My failure in 8% of 1:1s means I 100% failed an individual. 

I average five deal reviews per week. 

If I’m useful in four of those five, I have an 80% success rate in deal review execution. 

But I’ve failed one AE with 100% of their strategy for their most important deal. 

I’m fortunate to run an organization of ~60 people. That’s a lot of individuals with personal career aspirations. That’s a lot of deals where a win or loss has significant financial impact on the AE. 

And I owe it to every one of them to make sure every interaction is treated with the importance of “one out of one” and never “one of many.”

This feels like blasphemy after how often I’ve taught the opposite, but the “best next step” is not always a call on the calendar. A few reasons why:

- Not everyone does their best thinking/communication live on a call.

- If there are introverted sellers (awkwardly raises hand) there are certainly introverted buyers.

The next best step starts with understanding (from your buyer’s perspective):

1) What decision needs to be made next?
2) What information is needed to make a great decision?
3) What’s the medium to consume that information?

Sometimes those come together to make a live conversation the next best step.

But I’m seeing (with increasing frequency) where it’s not.

I’m seeing the line between “sales-led” and “self-service” get very blurry, which creates a lot of nuance/complication for the sales process.

It’s why I’m a big fan of Consensus - they empower buyers to learn when and how they want while keeping sellers in-the-loop with visibility into what’s most important.

content:
After 8 years in sales leadership I know VERY little. But I have developed 3 foundational principles I’ll never abandon: 

1) Real life > work 

We are not our jobs. Our titles are not our identities. Our career progress matters less than our relationships. 

I refuse to live a life I’ll regret - I won’t prioritize professional progress over health or family. 

And I’m vocal about this so my team knows I support them doing the same. 

2) I refuse to take myself too seriously 

I make jokes in zoom chat, slack, in posts/comments on LinkedIn. 

Sometimes they hit, sometimes they suck (I guess I’m a “high volume” guy). 

I’m sure there are plenty of CEOs that see my jokes and think “I would NEVER hire that guy to run my sales org - he’s not taking this seriously enough.” 

Good - we wouldn’t work well together. 

I’ll stick with leadership that loves how we can deliver numbers AND have fun along the way. 

3) You aren’t better than anyone - but you aren’t worse, either 

It’s human nature to compare (I’m often guilty of this). 

When I fall into this trap I try to remind myself: “you aren’t better than anyone, but you aren’t worse, either.” 

It’s easy to feel like a failure when you compare yourself to people “ahead of you.” 

It’s a debilitating and unproductive exercise. 

It’s easy to feel superior when you compare yourself to people “behind you.” 

That arrogance will destroy your humanity. 

I’m happiest when I run in my own lane, help others along their lane, and don’t worry about “who is ahead.” 

And I bet you would be too. 

Maybe in 8 more years I’ll have learned enough to say “here’s what works in sales leadership.” 

But for now, this is what I’ve got.

content:
I’m not much of a new year’s resolution guy, but I did set one transformative goal for this year that has already changed my life:

I refuse to worry about stuff that hasn’t happened yet. 

Maybe it sounds simple, but it’s something that I’ve struggled with for a long time. And I’m not alone: in a study tracking people with generalized anxiety disorder, participants logged their worries for 10 days and then tracked what actually happened over the next 30. 

91.4% of their “worry predictions” never happened. 

I haven’t tracked it myself, but thinking back over previous months I think that number is pretty close for me. 

Worrying about resources I need to be successful being decreased (they’ve only increased).

Worrying about losing deals we needed (we’ve lost some, won a lot, and made up for the ones we did lose). 

Worrying about getting sick right before/during a big trip (I’ve had a great run of good health). 

Worrying that “this is the quarter when it all falls apart” (we’ve crushed every quarter so far)

I have wasted so much time, energy, and emotional capital worrying about crap that never happened. I have suffered the consequences of events that were only imagined. 

And this is the year it stops. 

It’s actually been pretty simple: when the worry gets into my mind I literally say, “This hasn’t happened. I’m not going to worry about it.” 

And then I turn my attention to 1) what is real and 2) what I can do now to make it even less likely that what I’m worrying about happens. 

For bigger worries, I’ll write out:

What would I do if it did happen? 

Turns out it’s never that big of a deal - I can work my way through even the worst case scenario.

What can I do now to make it less likely it happens?

Taking action is a miracle drug for eliminating worry. 

And then I move on - refusing to suffer now for something that likely won’t ever happen. 

Hopefully you aren’t a chronic worrier like I’ve been. 

But if you are, hopefully this helps give you even a bit of a mental reprieve. 

Because there’s enough crap in real life without having to deal with crap in our imaginary life.

content:
I was in a skip level 1:1 the other week when I was asked, “How do you manage stress?” I shared two different “perspective shifts” I use to combat the stress I experience in my role:

1) The “Big Picture” Shift

A few years ago, my wife walked into our baby’s nursery and screamed. I ran in to find our daughter experiencing a seizure. In pure panic, we called 911 and held her while we waited for the ambulance.

As we waited for test results in the ER over several hours, there was nothing more important to me than her health. 

I could not have cared less about my career, income, investments, car, house, or any of the other “physical comforts” that we often focus on.

Fortunately, tests went well and my daughter remains in great health today.

It also exposed how poorly we prioritize mindshare:

In moments of fear of losing what’s most important, it’s easy and obvious to worry less about what’s unimportant in comparison. 

No one worries about their quota when waiting for test results in the ER.

But when what’s most important is “normal,” it’s taken for granted. And we put our stress/focus on less important things.

When I’m experiencing stress related to work, I do my best to re-center:

“As long as my family is safe and healthy, life is good. Everything else is a bonus.”

Rather than fill my mind with “what can I worry about?” I try to fill my mind with “what can I be grateful for?”

My life is so much more than SaaS agreements and quota attainment, and my stress/anxiety dissipates when my perspective shifts accordingly.


2) The “Great Problems to Have” Shift
​
In the SaaS sales world, I have a fairly stressful role. I’m responsible for several segments of sellers across all geographies. I carry a number that is a significant proportion of the entire company’s revenue/bookings. 

But whenever I start to feel stressed to the point where it impacts my happiness, I do my best to think:

“What a great problem to have.”

Lots of people would love to have the opportunity to deal with these problems. I have a good job, making a great living, working with people I love working with.

So shame on me if I let the stress of the role impact my happiness. And shame on me if I don’t recognize the privilege I have facing these “great problems.”

I’m nowhere near perfect at applying these two shifts - I still struggle with stress and anxiety at times. But the better I get at consistently applying them, the happier I am - regardless of the outcomes I’m seeing professionally.

I have no idea the circumstances you are in today as you read this post. I don’t know the state of your health and your family’s health. I don’t know if you are in a job you love or a job you hate (or looking for work). 

But I hope one (or both) of these shifts help you take on the stress of your life with more optimism and peace.

content:
If I were an AE wanting to maximize earnings over the next three years, I’d look for 3 things in potential companies to join:

1) Leaders that develop their people

Questions to ask a manager:

“Tell me about a time you identified a skill gap in a rep - how did you help them close it?”

“Have you ever had a rep follow you from one company to another?”

“How many people have you promoted in the last 12 months?”

You are looking for leaders that can describe their coaching, have built “followership,” and have a track record of promoting members of their team. 


2) Companies at growth stages - not efficiency

Questions to ask:

“How did the comp plan change this year compared to last year?”

“Did anyone blow out their comp plan recently? Approximately how much did they earn?”

Comp plans will ALWAYS change - but if they suddenly get much worse, the company is likely prioritizing profitability/efficiency over growth. 

If no one blew out their comp plan, quotas are either too high or territories are too tight. 

If someone blew out their plan and didn’t make an exciting amount of money, accelerators are too low. 


3) Product that can sell itself/is a need-to-have

Questions to ask:

“What is your gross retention rate?”

“What is your net retention rate?” 

“What’s your win rate on expansion opportunities?”

90%+ gross retention is a good sign of a “need-to-have” product.

115%+ net retention rate is a good sign of a product that can “sell itself.” It means that the average customer spending $100k this year will spend $115k next year. 

40-50%+ win rate on expansion opportunities means you’ll be able to drive meaningful attainment through customer up-sell/cross-sell - can take out a big chunk out of your annual number. 

What else would you look for in a great company to sell for?

content:
I’m in my 6th year as a sales VP. These are the 5 most important lessons I’ve learned (no wonder average tenure for a VP is <18 months): 

1) Nothing matters more than who you hire 

Hiring an AE that doesn’t work out will cost you 6+ months.

Hiring a front-line leader that doesn’t work out will cost you 12+ months.

Hiring multiple leaders and AEs that don’t work out will cost you your job. 

2) You can’t “hire slow” and win

Executive sales leadership is generally a big math problem:

“Is your productive capacity sufficient to cover your quota?” 

If you hire slow, your productive capacity will be too low. Even if you hire great talent, you’ll still fall short. The math kills you. 

So, you have to hire fast. And if you hire fast, but make mistakes? See #1. 

3) You can’t out-execute bad culture 

The best thing I heard from an AE this last year was “I can’t imagine working anywhere else - I’d miss the culture too much.” 

You can have the best systems, best training, best plan - but if your team is miserable you won’t retain top talent. 

And VPs that don’t retain top talent don’t retain their jobs. 

4) Use data for hypotheses but never decisions

The larger your org, the more tempting it is to rely on data for decisions. It takes a ton of work AND time to fly low enough to make real observations (and it’s time you usually don’t have). 

But data without context is, at best, incomplete. 

And, at worst, completely wrong. 

And VPs making decisions off of incomplete or wrong assumptions (you already see where I’m going with this) don’t keep their jobs. 

5) Exceptions kill orgs 

Every exception you make is one you have to defend. 

Want to make an exception and hire an AE at a higher level to “match their comp expectations?”

Now you have to explain to all the AEs with their same experience why the new rep was hired at a higher level. 

Want to make an exception on rules of engagement for an opportunity split? 

Now you have to explain to every other rep in a similar situation why they aren’t getting the same treatment. 

The more exceptions you make, the less people respect your systems, processes, and you. 

I’ve got a lot more lessons to learn (many I’ll learn the hard way). 

Any other sales leaders willing to share what I’ve missed?

My hot take of the day is leaders that say “don’t bring me problems without solutions” are generally failing their team.
 
If your team can self-identify all their solutions what are you even needed for? 

Just saying, “I need you to figure this out” and then taking credit when they do? 

I’m not saying that leaders need to solve all problems - their teams should be empowered to solve plenty on their own. 

I’m also not advising you to just bring unsolved problems to your manager. Being able to showcase: “Here’s the problem I had, here’s how I solved it, here are the results I experienced” can be a career accelerant. 

But sometimes problems are complex enough that the solution requires input from someone with more experience and more knowledge. 

Isn’t that a big part of what leaders are supposed to provide?

And if you tell your team “don’t bring me problems without solutions” what do you think happens when they face a problem they don’t know how to solve? 

They try to figure it out on their own (and likely fail) because they are afraid to bring it up to their leader. 

I’ll give you an example of a time a rep did this well:

They reached out and said, “I know this account can get to $300,000+ spend with us. But I have no idea how to get there. Can we review the account together?” 

What a great problem to surface to leadership. 

We brought together a team of more experienced leaders, reviewed the account, and made a plan. 

The rep executed the plan, and contracts just went out to get the account to that level of spend. 

Maybe the rep would have figured it out on their own. But, best case, it would have taken a lot longer. 

Worst case, the customer wouldn’t have realized the additional value LD could bring them and we would have missed out on a great opportunity. 

I’m curious how other leaders handle this - how do you find the balance of empowering your team to take on challenges, while also making sure they are comfortable asking for help?

content:
A rep told me their account was “tapped out.” So we reassigned it. A few months later, the new AE closed a six-figure upgrade.

The first rep wasn’t doing a bad job. They knew the users, ensured adoption, and confirmed there was no fit for additional products after several demos with the existing team. 

To them, that meant the account had maxed out - so they asked for it to be replaced.

Being the obedient VP I am, I reassigned it.

The new AE took a different approach. First, they learned how the current team was using the platform.

Then they asked:

- What problems is this company facing?
- Which ones can we help solve?
- Who owns those problems?

They found a business priority we could support, identified the team responsible, and got an intro from the existing users (who were happy to help).

Three months later, that team was fully onboarded, and we had a six-figure upsell.

I’ve seen this play out time and time again - AEs looking too narrowly at accounts, asking:
 
“How can I get the current users to spend more?”

That mindset leaves money on the table.

Start by helping your users solve the problems they bought you to solve.

Then zoom out: What other problems exist in the business that you can help with?

Use your existing success as a case study, ask for intros, and expand your impact.

Expanded revenue will follow.

Half the battle is knowing which accounts you should spend time with. 

You don’t want to neglect an account just to watch another AE close a big deal as soon as you lose it - but you also don’t want to spin your wheels for months in an account with nothing to show for the effort.

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

“Makes perfect sense you’ve already got a handle on this. Usually this means you’ve got a similar solution in place and I didn’t do a good job sharing how we are different, or you are attacking this priority through a completely different approach.

Can I ask where you fall?”

Next time you hear “this isn’t a priority” to something that you know should be a priority, give this a shot!

content:
When I joined LaunchDarkly, we were in the middle of implementing an AI SDR. A couple of months in, we scrapped the project and “uninstalled” the AI SDR because we kept seeing: 

- Emails written for prospects sent to customers 
- “Personalization” referencing irrelevant observations 
- Nearly a 0% response rate across all campaigns 

Our root cause analysis showed a few reasons for failure. Some were tied to flaws in the vendor’s model, some were tied to our implementation approach. 

But the number one issue was our data quality. 

Apparently the eval team had been “sold” on the idea that our data didn’t have to be perfect to successfully implement the AI SDR. But that was far off from the reality we experienced. 

Our customers were getting emails written for prospects because we had duplicate accounts in our CRM.

content:
The most uncomfortable call of my career (35 seconds of silence felt like 5 minutes) taught me two important lessons about negotiation. Here’s the story:

I had a great relationship with my main contacts at an account. We had worked together for over a year, and they were planning on significantly expanding their agreement with us.

Because the license was expanding, they looped in a new stakeholder that I had never met.

This individual’s only goal was to get the lowest cost possible.

We got on a call, and the tone was completely different. The new contact went on the offensive and listed their demands.

The requests were unreasonable. Since I was confident in our solution and the value of our partnership, my response was:

“We’ve been working closely with the team for several months to right-size the agreement and to ensure that the value warrants the investment. While I appreciate your goal is to get the lowest price possible, your requests aren’t reasonable, and we cannot consider them.”

Then, I shut up.

There was silence for what felt like forever (the call recording showed it was only about 35 seconds), and the contact finally said, “Ok. We’ll need to discuss internally.”

The call ended, and we received a signed contract for the proposed amount a few days later.

While uncomfortable in the moment, I learned two essential negotiation lessons:

1) Silence is ok

Be confident, communicate clearly and don’t over-explain. Then, shut up.

2) Saying “no” is ok

When you are close to a deal, it’s tempting to remove all friction by accepting all requests thrown your way.

Don’t. Be confident in your value, and say “no” when a request isn’t reasonable.

I used to think 35 seconds of silence was a long time. 

Keith Weightman shared an example with me of a call where he had TWO MINUTES of silence. 

Can anyone top that?

content:
People evaluating software want one of these three experiences (and if you force them into the wrong experience you’ll likely lose them to a competitor):

Experience #1: Talk to them about our solution

Fortunately, this is the experience the typical sales process is built to handle. 

Unfortunately, it’s usually the last experience buyers want. 


Experience #2: Try the solution

When someone is:

1) Aware they have a problem they want to solve
2)Aware your solution is built to solve that problem
3)Going to be one of the end users of the platform 

They often just want to validate themselves that it works. 

And if you force someone to take a bunch of sales calls before they can “try it themselves,” they’ll just go sign up for a trial from your competitor. 


Experience #3: See the solution 

When someone is:

1) Aware they have a problem they want to solve
2) Aware your solution is built to solve that problem
3) Not going to be one of the end users of the platform

They often just want to see for themselves how it works. 

Generic demo videos on a website somewhat help here, but are often high-level, and miss showing a use case or outcome that a prospect cares about.

Ideally, the quick demo hits on exactly what your prospect cares about most. 

It’s why I’m a big fan of Consensus - they help you deliver “custom” and relevant demos to your prospects - even if you haven’t spoken to them yet. 

My advice to all sales and marketing teams:

Review your top-of-funnel (both inbound and outbound) looking specifically for how to identify which “evaluation experience” your prospects are looking for. 

Then, evaluate how quickly you are able to deliver the right experience. 

Because if it’s painful for your prospects to get the evaluation experience they are looking for, they’ll go evaluate something else.

My friend Anthony Natoli asked a great question: Why do senior sales leaders prefer to promote internal AEs to leadership vs hire externally? 

As a leader that does prefer to bet on internal candidates, I’ll share why:

But ultimately it's all about probabilities:

Can I find an AE externally with no leadership experience and develop them into a great leader that’s useful to their team at my company? Absolutely. 

Is that as likely to work as promoting someone internally (assuming they are actually showing the successful traits needed)? Not even close. 

So I’ll first look to promote internally before hiring externally because the probability of it working out is much higher. 

I’m not saying that sales leaders shouldn’t sometimes make “bets” - but if a VP of Sales makes a bunch of lower-probability bets for hiring, they’ll quickly become a former VP of sales.

One of our AEs was having success with their cold call opener, but they were shut down shortly after. 

Here's what worked and what we changed:

His opener (which was working): 

"This is (name) with LaunchDarkly. Just to be transparent, this is a cold call. I was wondering if I could have 20 seconds to tell you why I’m calling. And if it’s irrelevant, you can throw your phone across the room.”

Good mix of direct, transparency, and humor. Combined with great tone and it's working.

The challenges he’s seeing come from what he says next:

"We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off..."

We've already lost the prospect because we started with what we do. 

Most of our ICP already does something similar to what we offer. So, when they hear this pitch, they think, "Yep, already got a solution for that, not interested."

When you lead with what you do your pitch will only resonate with people that are actively shopping for your solution. At any given time that represents roughly 3% of your market.

Not great odds.

When you lead with problems you solve, your pitch will resonate with people that are actively facing that problem. 

If you work for a company with a legitimate product, this should be a much higher percentage (at least 40%+).

For LaunchDarkly, it might sound like:

"I'm reaching out because I noticed your team's focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity. 

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are facing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release. 

Curious if that's been a conversation with your team at all?"


We all know problems > product in selling, but sometimes we forget how it applies to prospecting. 

Lead with problems, and you are more likely to have more meaningful conversations in your cold calls and book more qualified meetings.

7 observations from a guy leading a global sales org in a brutal economy:

1) The list of “essential” technologies gets shorter every quarter.

Every potential purchase is questioned with:

“Do we need to do this now?” Or, “Can we get this done almost as well with a current tool?”

If you don’t have great answers to these questions, your tech won’t make the “essential” list. 



2) Cold outreach only works if you combine problem, person, and timing.

High volume automation doesn’t work because you won’t nail the message. 

Low volume doesn’t work because you won’t have the surface area needed to hit the combo. 

Top reps are doing quality outreach with higher volume than used to be needed. They’ve adapted. 



3) Rep desperation is at a high, which is matched by increased buyer skepticism.

Reps are afraid of getting fired if they don’t sell. Buyers are afraid of getting fired if they make a bad purchase. 

If you don’t understand that skepticism you have no shot at overcoming it. 


4) Buyers don’t want to take a risk to “make a splash.” They want to keep their jobs.

See point three - buyers aren’t putting their reputation on the line for a risky purchase. De-risk the deal through effective PoCs, demonstrate value through BVAs, or mark it lost. 


5) No one’s buying because you “might” be able to help them. Prove it, or move on.

The days of “buy a few tools, we’ll renew the ones that work best” are behind us. More buyers expect proven value before signature - the best sellers know how to prove it quickly. 


6) It’s never been easier to personalize outreach, so it’s never been harder to stand out.

The ultimate trap of AI: the better it gets, the less it stands out. When every email in an inbox is personalized, relevant, and timely, “good” gets ignored. 


7) Top reps are still having massive success. Everything is “figure-it-out-able.”

While some reps feel like it’s an insurmountable struggle, others are cashing in the biggest commission checks of their career. There’s still money to be made.

content:
Discovery calls end with “can you send me info and I’ll get back to you?” unless you break from the “normal” structure. The typical (broken) discovery goes like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and small talk

- Next ten minutes: Superficial discussion of the buyer’s day-to-day

- Next ten minutes: Seller shares high-level overview of product. 

Twenty-five minutes into a thirty minute call and almost no progress is made. The seller barely knows anything about the buyer. The buyer barely knows anything about the seller’s product. 

The final few minutes become a mad scramble for the seller to find something valuable enough to earn another call, but most discoveries end with the buyer saying, “Can you send me a case study and more information so we can review and get back to you?”

A great discovery looks like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and objective set

- Next five minutes: Point-of-view validated (or corrected) and priorities confirms

- Next ten minutes: Deep discovery of how the buyer is approaching their priorities

- Last ten minutes: Seller shares how they can help accomplish priorities and next steps for evaluation finalized

Maybe all you need is the “outline” and you can go run better discoveries. 

But maybe you need a guide that breaks it down step-by-step. 

If you want the step-by-step guide to great discovery, my discovery playbook is free today: https://lnkd.in/gT7ZMQQz

One of our AEs had massive success with their cold call opener, but they were shut down shortly after. Here's what’s working and what we are changing:

First, his opener led to 75%+ of prospects letting him pitch. Here's what he's using:

"This is (name) with LaunchDarkly. Just to be transparent, this is a cold call. I was wondering if I could have 20 seconds to tell you why I’m calling. And if it’s irrelevant, you can throw your phone across the room.”

Good mix of direct, transparency, and humor. Combined with great tone and it's working.

The challenges he saw came from what he said next:

"We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off..."

We lost the prospect’s interest because we started with what we do. 

Most of our ICP already does something similar to what we offer. So, when they hear this pitch, they think, "Yep, already got a solution for that, not interested."

When you lead with what you do your pitch will only resonate with people that are actively shopping for your solution. At any given time that represents roughly 3% of your market.

Not great odds.

When you lead with problems you solve, your pitch will resonate with people that are actively facing that problem. If you work for a company with a legitimate product, this should be a much higher percentage (at least 40%+).

For LaunchDarkly, it might sound like:

"I'm reaching out because I noticed your team's focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity. 

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are facing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release. 

Curious if that's been a conversation with your team at all?"


We all know problems > product in selling, but sometimes we forget how it applies to prospecting. 

Lead with problems, and you are more likely to have more meaningful conversations in your cold calls and book more qualified meetings.

Phone remains our best channel for pipeline generation - these 3 tactics drive our success: 

Tactic  One: “Bucket Your Buyers”

Most companies sell to a few different personas.

All companies sell to different levels of those personas.

If your list “scrambles” them altogether, you are putting yourself into constant context switching.

Instead, keep similar personas grouped together so you can get in the flow with value drivers, customer stories, and use cases.


Tactic Two: Dig for Gold

We don’t make all calls with the intent to set a meeting.

Sometimes, we are just looking for a “nugget” we can use to set a meeting with an above-the-line contact.

When we get “gold nuggets” like project names, executive KPIs, or even just current tooling challenges we use them to nail our calls to “decision makers” where we want to spend more time.


Tactic Three: Problems, Not Product

Our messaging used to be all about us:

“We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off…”

Now, we lead with problems we solve:

“I’m reaching out because I noticed your team’s focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity.

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are sharing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release.”

content:
The best sales content I’ve read in a long time comes from a buyer sharing how they buy. Today, I'm highlighting my favorite parts along with a little bit of my own commentary.

Let's dive into the highlights, and I'll link the full post at the end.

Highlight one:

“Every vendor tells me their product is revolutionary. You know what’s also revolutionary? Getting fired because your “revolutionary” product bricked the payment system during Black Friday. I’ve seen it happen. It wasn’t the vendor who lost their job.”

Key takeaway:

Sellers all sound the same. Every vendor has “innovation.” Every vendor has “industry awards.” Every vendor has “cutting-edge AI.”

But while we are blabbering on about how great we are, our prospect is wondering: “Where is this most likely to go wrong? And, if it goes wrong, how devastating would it be to me and my team?”

Highlight two:

“The vendor who won my biggest contract didn’t have the best product. They had:

• A reference from a CISO I trusted
• An implementation plan that didn’t require overtime from my burned-out team
• A CEO who personally committed to our success
• Proof they’d done this exact deployment 50 times before

Their competitor had better tech and was 30% cheaper. They also had a 12-month implementation timeline and no relevant references.

Easy decision.”

Key takeaway:

This one is scary. Imagine a forecast call where you tell your boss “my champion told me we have better tech and we are 30% cheaper.”

Sounds like an easy win.

Now, you know that your “champion” could be telling their boss: “This other vendor is more expensive and doesn’t have all the functionality. But it’s the safer bet.”

Your easy win quickly becomes a shocking loss.

Highlight three:

“You tell me features. Tell me what fires you put out and whose job you saved.

You show ROI spreadsheets. Show me CISOs who didn’t get fired after deploying your product.

You push for the enterprise deal. Let me pilot first. Let me look like a hero internally before I bet my career.”

Key takeaway:

You already know features don’t sell - you need to sell “value.” But are you selling the value your prospect cares about?

For most buyers "value" is a combination of “the safest bet to work + most likely to make me look good.”

Highlight four:

“Let’s have an honest conversation. If you keep selling products while we’re buying career insurance, we’re all wasting time.”

Key takeaway:

The job market sucks. Many people (including buyers) are in survival mode.

Are you selling an unrealistic dream? Or, are you selling “career insurance?”

If you are selling the dream, you may find yourself losing to the rep selling insurance.

content:
Read a post about a guy that was in the office at 10pm on his birthday. “He has two young boys at home. Most people would have been out the door hours ago. Instead, he’s here, merging new code into production.”

I’m not saying this was right or wrong. There’s a time and a season for different types of “sprints.”

The subject of this post probably more than made up for the late night with dedicated time with his two kids, and all parents make difficult trade-offs with work and family. 

We should NEVER shame/criticize someone for working instead of being with family - we don’t have the context to make that judgment. 

But I do think social media glorifies “hustle culture” way more than it should, so I wanted to share another perspective:

The other day, I scrolled through my digital journal. Went back a few years. 

The last few years have been really good for me professionally. Lots of great quarters (that took a lot of late nights). 

Lots of great teams built (that took a lot of travel). 

But none of that made my journal. 

No entries about late nights working on deals. 

No entries about back-to-back-to-back travel. 

Nothing about “celebrating a huge quarter with the team!” 

Instead, the journal is full of:

- Nighttime stories with kids
- Daddy/daughter dances 
- Family campfires 

This is a sensitive topic for a lot of working parents. Please don’t take it the wrong way - there are ALWAYS tradeoffs and sacrifices. Very few people have the economic luxury of being able to spend all possible time with family - we have bills to pay and people to provide for. 

I’ve had the phone calls while traveling where I hear my kid crying, “I want dad come home.”

I’ve had the dinners when I tell my kids I’m traveling next week and they say, “No, again? Why?”

I wish life was just clean and easy and we always knew exactly what to do, when, and could always be there for people that need us. It’s not. 

But I do think we can do a better job of glorifying the journal moments instead of the hustle moments. 

Because the only way the hustle ends up worth it is if it sets us up for many more journal moments.

And the only way the hustle is sustainable is if we can have journal moments along the way.

Jen Allen-Knuth said something brilliant (I know, I was shocked as well) when she mocked poorly planned AI approaches with the phrase: “Our efficiency > their experience!!!”

I’m seeing this a lot right now where companies are 100% trading “efficiency” at the cost of their buyer’s experience. 

Companies are planning how they can:

- Automate prospecting to save THEIR company time

- Cut out human interactions with buyers to save THEIR company money

Without spending nearly enough time/effort asking “how can we make buying better for the buyer?” 

Don’t get me wrong - I’m not anti-scale. 

I’m definitely not anti-AI. 

I just think we need to draw the line. 

RevOps and sales leaders SHOULD obsess with scale/AI/automation:

“How do we leverage systems to quickly get sellers the right leads, in the right accounts, understanding which signals should drive their outreach?” 

AEs SHOULD obsess with scale/AI/automation:

“How do I leverage systems to quickly get account point-of-views, build business cases, build account maps, etc.”

It’s insane what we can do with the above now compared to just a couple of years ago. It’s really exciting. 

But after all that effort to get the right person, at the right time, with the right context in front of sellers PLEASE don’t blow it by scaling the “last mile” where human to human connection is possible. 

Once it’s time to start a human conversation, don’t ask “how do we scale this?”

Instead, ask, “How do we execute plays that can’t be scaled?” 

It might be a handwritten note. It might be a custom gift. Maybe it’s executive to executive outreach. Maybe it’s a video you record yourself. 

There are lots of ways that you can “stand out” from the AI-automation that’s clogging every executive's inbox. 

And not one of those ways can be “scaled.”

I’m fanatical about pipeline generation and I think the phone is the best way to generate pipeline. But I still think “org-wide call targets” are stupid for 3 simple reasons:

1) Some reps have high connect rates, some are lower 

2) Some reps set meetings with 20% of prospects they talk to, some are lower

3) Some reps convert most of their meetings to opportunities, some convert fewer

So how would I set a call target relevant to everyone?

Set it too high, and the high-converting reps are annoyed AND their conversion likely decreases, making them less efficient. 

So I don’t set org-wide call targets. Instead, we set org-wide outcome targets (e.g., opportunities created), and then use data to inform individual input goals to reach out those outcomes.

- Initial meetings set

- Discovery meetings converting to opportunities

content:
Bad data nearly cost me my job less than 2 years into my career. 

Well, technically, my poor response to a territory deployment built on bad data nearly cost me my job. But that’s a less fun “hook” to a post. 

Here’s the story:

We were growing fast and we needed to completely redesign territories. The approach of “reps grab whatever accounts they want” wasn’t going to work anymore. 

SalesOps built a solid scoring algorithm. It had core criteria to score accounts:

- Industry
- Revenue
- Employee count

They pulled all of our customer data to see what “great fit” looks like, and could predict potential spend nearly perfectly when the algorithm was applied to current customers. 

The approach/weighting/algorithm was well designed and well tested. 

The next step was to create geographic territories, based on zip codes. They’d take all the accounts in a zip code, score them, and then sum up all the accounts to give the zip code a score. 

The logic was sound: if we know the score of a zip code, we know how much revenue to expect from that area. Then, we just need to give enough zip codes to each rep to make sure the total score is enough to support their quota. 

My territory ended up as  suburban Grand Rapids, Michigan. All the zip codes in the area that weren’t in the metro/city. 

When I dug in, I immediately found a massive issue: I had accounts that were scored high that actually sucked. 

The problem wasn’t the algorithm used to score the data. It wasn’t the zip code based approach. 

The problem was the data powering the model. 

I’d look at accounts that our data said had 750 employees and $300 million revenue. Reality was they had 14 employees and not enough revenue to build a working website. 

Out of my 2,000+ accounts, maybe 20 were actually a good fit for what we sold. 

So I threw a fit and nearly got fired (ended up suspended without pay for a day - bless up merciful sales leaders!) 

But that’s not the point of the story. The point of the story is that the great algorithm and strong strategy failed because the underlying data wasn’t accurate. 

And now, with AI, companies are able to make really bad decisions EVEN FASTER because their fancy AI tooling and strategy is powered with incomplete or inaccurate data.

My #1 priority when joining LaunchDarkly was to improve pipeline generation. Three tactics we used to improve by 142%:

Tip One: “Bucket Your Buyers”

Most companies sell to a few different personas. 

All companies sell to different levels of those personas. 

If your list “scrambles” them altogether, you are putting yourself into constant context switching. 

Instead, keep similar personas grouped together so you can get in the flow with value drivers, customer stories, and use cases. 

 
Tip Two: Dig for Gold 

We don’t make all calls with the intent to set a meeting. Sometimes, we are just looking for a “nugget” we can use to set a meeting with an above-the-line contact. 

When we get “gold nuggets” like project names, executive KPIs, or even just current tooling challenges we use them to nail our calls to “decision makers” where we want to spend more time. 


Tip Three: Problems, Not Product

Our messaging used to be all about us: 

"We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off..."

Now, we lead with problems we solve:

"I'm reaching out because I noticed your team's focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity. 

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are sharing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release.”

What’s more likely:

Your prospects are facing the problems you solve? 

Or

Your prospects are actively shopping for what you do?

Message accordingly, and conversion will increase.

content:
“No one worries about their quota when waiting for test results in the ER.”

I was in a skip level 1:1 the other week when I was asked, “How do you manage stress?” I shared two different “perspective shifts” I use to combat the stress I experience in my role:

1) The “Big Picture” Shift

A few years ago, my wife walked into our baby’s nursery and screamed. I ran in to find our daughter experiencing a seizure. In pure panic, we called 911 and held her while we waited for the ambulance.

As we waited for test results in the ER over several hours, there was nothing more important to me than her health. I could not have cared less about my career, income, investments, car, house, or any of the other “physical comforts” that we often focus on.

Fortunately, tests went well and my daughter remains in great health today.

It also exposed how poorly we prioritize mindshare:

In moments of fear of losing what’s most important, it’s easy and obvious to worry less about what’s unimportant in comparison. 

No one worries about their quota when waiting for test results in the ER.

But when what’s most important is “normal,” it’s taken for granted. And we put our stress/focus on less important things.

When I’m experiencing stress related to work, I do my best to re-center:

“As long as my family is safe and healthy, life is good. Everything else is a bonus.”

Rather than fill my mind with “what can I worry about?” I try to fill my mind with “what can I be grateful for?”

My life is so much more than SaaS agreements and quota attainment, and my stress/anxiety dissipates when my perspective shifts accordingly.


2) The “Great Problems to Have” Shift
​
In the SaaS sales world, I have a fairly stressful role. I’m responsible for several segments of sellers across all geographies. I carry a number that is a significant proportion of the entire company’s revenue/bookings. But whenever I start to feel stressed to the point where it impacts my happiness, I do my best to think:

“What a great problem to have.”

Lots of people would love to have the opportunity to deal with these problems. I have an awesome job, making a great living, working with people I love working with.

So shame on me if I let the stress of the role impact my happiness. And shame on me if I don’t recognize the privilege I have facing these “great problems.”

I’m nowhere near perfect at applying these two shifts - I still struggle with stress and anxiety at times. But the better I get at consistently applying them, the happier I am - regardless of the outcomes I’m seeing professionally.

I have no idea the circumstances you are in today as you read this post. I don’t know the state of your health and your family’s health. I don’t know if you are in a job you love or a job you hate (or looking for work). 

But I hope one (or both) of these shifts help you take on the stress of your life with more optimism and peace.
