A few years ago, all revenue was good revenue. Now, revenue leaders think about revenue through several different layers:

- Will it renew or am I buying churn?
- Will it expand or am I overpaying to acquire?
- Will it close quickly enough to keep reasonable payback periods for sales?

As if sales weren’t hard enough already.

To ensure success across all layers, I focus on two metrics for territory management:

1) Total addressable market (TAM)

TAM tells me the long-term potential of an account. Since my organization usually follows a land and expand motion, it’s critical we close initial deals in accounts where meaningful expansion can follow.

TAM is the easier of the two metrics to pull from data. At LaunchDarkly, I look at the number of developers and applications to infer potential spend.

2) Propensity

Propensity tells me how likely a company is to purchase. Like most companies, I don’t have a massive sales organization that can chase down all high TAM accounts. Since coverage is limited, I don’t want to chase high TAM accounts that are unlikely to purchase while high TAM accounts that are likely to purchase sit uncovered.

Some of my favorite signals to calculate propensity:

- Funding
- Current tech stack
- Hiring engineers with relevant skills
- Product usage (our free product or trials of our paid products)
- Mentions on community platforms, social platforms, and forums

This approach is why we love using Clay to inform our territory management. They pull signals across first, second, and third-party sources to help us narrow our focus on the accounts where we are most likely to add value.

Which helps us make sure the revenue we close is good revenue.

Candidates I interview often ask me about the section of my LinkedIn profile (pictured) where I outline my early struggles as a seller. They ask: “What was the biggest change you made?”

(they also ask about the one-day suspension but that’s another story for another post)

The biggest “tactic” change was shifting my perspective to think more like a buyer.

Less: How do I get to the next stage of the sales process?

More: What does the prospect need to get to the next stage of their evaluation process?

I approached every interaction with a prospect thinking through three key questions:

1) What decision do they need to make next to successfully evaluate how to solve their problem?

Common decisions include:

Do I have enough evidence this vendor can solve my problem to agree to a demo?

Do I have enough confidence in this seller to introduce them to my boss?

Have I seen enough value to spend time building an internal business case?


2) What information can I provide to help them make that decision?

When I was struggling, I looked at each customer interaction as "what information do I need from the customer to move forward?"

Shifting to "What information do they need from me?" made sure my customer calls were filled with conversation my buyer cared about.

Which made them much more willing to open up with the information I needed.


3) How can I package that information to make it easy for my prospect to consume?

It's really hard to buy. Making an effort to "remove the burden" wherever possible for my buyers helped deals move along faster.

Here's an example of how these three come together when entering a proof-of-concept stage:

1) Decision prospect needs to make: "Is it worth my time to run a proof-of-concept with this vendor?"

2) Information they need to make that decision:

- What would need to be tested
- Who would need to be involved
- Success criteria for features tested
- Business outcomes expected if features work

3) Packaging to make it easier: Proactively build out a proof-of-concept template with our recommendations of the above. That way the prospect can build off of a foundation rather than start from scratch.

This approach may even be MORE important today, because buyers increasingly want control, independence, and self-service.

They don’t want to patiently sit through 10 meetings so you can check off each stage of your sales process.

This is why I’m a big fan of platforms like Consensus. They allow sellers to package up the information your prospect needs in highly engaging formats that drive internal collaboration and, well, consensus.

content:
One of the least “fair” sales realities is that average sellers in great environments usually earn more than great sellers in average environments. Here are 3 ways to identify a great environment (starting with 2 critical metrics):

1) Gross Retention Rate

Gross retention rate is how well you preserve your existing renewal base. Basic example: If a company has 10 customers spending $10,000 on average, they have a renewal baseline of $100,000. 

If one customer that spends $10,000 doesn’t renew, their gross retention is $90,000, or 90%.

90%+ is good. 95%+ is great. 

2) Net Retention Rate

Net retention measures how much your customer revenue base grows each year. After you take out the lost renewals, and add in the renewals + expansion, is your customer base growing or shrinking?

110% is good. 115%+ is great. 120%+ is best-in-class. 

3) Quality of Sales Org

There are a lot of tools to identify the quality of a sales org (Glassdoor, RepVue), etc.

These are great places to start your research, but I know of sales orgs with great reviews where the team is miserable, and sales orgs where scores are “meh” but people are happy and crushing their comp plans.

So validate what you are seeing with the people that know best: current AEs at the company you are evaluating. Try and talk to at least three, otherwise you may talk to an outlier.

Finding a company with great metrics is a start.

Finding great metrics and an incredible sales org will make your career.

I botched one of the most “well-prepped” discovery calls of my career. 

The meeting was with the CMO of a large law firm - the ideal target for our new brand tracking solution. Before the call, I did tons of research on his firm, the market, and relevant trends. 

But he shut me down before I had a chance to share my “expertise.” And it was completely my fault. 

He didn’t know I had done my research. He had no idea I was prepared. He assumed I was like most salespeople:

- Didn’t understand him/his role/his priorities
- Would try to push my product
- Wouldn’t listen to him

Everything went wrong with my first (and last) question:

“Can you tell me about your role?” 

Looking back, this question was unnecessary. I knew a lot about his role from my research. But he didn’t know I knew, and my question made it sound like I was clueless.

His response (in a very irritated tone) was:

“Kyle - you asked me for this call. Why don’t you just tell me what you do.” 

Blerg. 

I stumbled over my value prop, trying to make it as specific as possible based on the research I had done. But the CMO had already mentally checked out, because he had already determined that I was “just like all the other salespeople.” 

And most salespeople don’t make good use of an executive’s time. 

That painful lesson completely changed how I ran my discovery calls. I learned that sellers are guilty until proven innocent, and I had to show up strong in the first few minutes of the call to earn a buyer’s attention. 

Since then, I’ve improved my discovery framework. No more irritated buyers, no more wasted opportunities.

Say: “You mentioned monitoring your releases over the weekend. Here’s how LaunchDarkly gives your weekends back by guarding the metrics you care about while you spend time with the people you care about.”

Instead of:

“You asked about highlighting the most likely accounts to buy, here’s where we stack rank your territory…”

Say: “You mentioned 20% of your pipeline sits with accounts where you aren’t likely to win.

Here’s how we’ll flag accounts actively looking for solutions like yours - so you can reach out to them before they inbound to your competition.”

You could show nearly the same demo as your competitor. If they explain features while you translate value, your prospect will perceive that your product is higher quality. 

And if you are explaining features while they translate value, you’ll lose. 

I’ll give you a quick homework assignment (if you want to actually get better at this):

Write out the top 10 most frequent features you talk about/show in demos.

For each one, list:

- Problems it solves for your customers
- Value it provides (in their language)
- A customer story that proves the above

Then, next time you talk about those features, use that list to translate “what it does” to “why it matters.”

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal. Time really does kill deals. 

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down. 

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

What "reality" would you add?

Got a note from someone: “I just lost a deal because I multi-threaded to a CEO and went above my champion. He said I betrayed his trust and had a hidden agenda.”

Brutal.

Then he made a great point: Everyone talks about how to multi-thread. No one talks about what not to do.

So here’s my attempt at what not to do in multi-threading:

1) Don’t go over the top of senior execs

Execs know how to get things done. Going over their head can make them feel like you don’t trust their judgment - or worse, like you’re trying to make them look junior internally.

Don’t work around senior execs - work with them.

2) Don’t surprise your champion

You want more people involved. You don’t want your champion surprised that more people are getting involved.

Make them aware of who you’re talking to, why, and how it benefits them.

They should hear it from you - not from a Slack message like, “Uh… do you know Kyle from LaunchDarkly? He wants to talk to me and says he’s working with you.”

3) Don’t neglect your contacts

Junior employees often have real influence. I’ve seen deals fall apart because a seller got access to power and left the original champion behind.

Not only is that rude - it’s risky.

Even the most talented reps will fail if they work the wrong accounts. Here are my three rules to help you get territory management right:

1) Ongoing, not static

Reps should have smaller territories so they can focus attention. 

Then, when AEs uncover details that make an assigned account a poor fit, replace it with another high-potential account. 

If a territory is too big, AEs will be pulled thin.

If it's too static, AEs will spin their wheels in poor-fit accounts. 

I've found focused but evolving territories most effective for all but strategic account segments. 

2) Accounts belong to the company, not the rep

High-potential accounts with unengaged reps are a massive waste of territory. If a rep doesn't give an account the attention it deserves, leaders should move it to a rep who will. 

I've seen "stagnant" accounts turn into six-figure wins by moving an account to a rep willing to do the work. 

3) Balance propensity and TAM

A territory full of potential whales is a slog - reps may work for quarters without closing a deal and getting paid.

A territory full of small transactions is a drain - reps will be on a hamster wheel, unable to focus on significant revenue opportunities. 

Great territory build requires understanding what drives TAM for your product (hint: it's not just revenue and the number of employees) and understanding propensity to buy via mentions, signals, multi-threading, etc., across different sources. 

Get this right, and your job becomes much easier. 

Get it wrong, and revenue targets become nearly impossible.

content:
I’ve run many deal reviews over the last few weeks. Three of the deals were “stuck.” My advice for “unsticking” each was the same:

“Make the next step easier for the prospect.”

Sellers have to remember:

99% of your prospect’s job is not related to buying your product.

100% of your job is helping them buy your product.

So you should do all you can to make every step as easy as possible for your prospect.

A common time deals get “stuck” is right before a trial or a proof-of-concept.

The most common reason deals get stuck at this stage is sellers wait for the prospect to finalize the trial/POC criteria.

Think about all the work this creates for your prospect:

- Schedule internal meetings to discuss requirements
- Document requirements, and determine outcomes
- Circulate document internally to get feedback/sign-off from anyone that missed the meeting(s)

Add in vacations/busy schedules and these few steps could easily take weeks.

A better route is making the next steps easier for your prospect - here's how we did it for our “stuck” deal:

1) Built our recommended PoC requirements and outcomes

I told the AE to review the discovery and demo transcripts to make sure we cover customer mentioned required capabilities and tie to customer stated metrics.

Then, I told them to add in additional required capabilities we know they’ll need to be successful, along with the outcomes they drive.

Ideally, at least a few of these would be required capabilities we know our competition struggles to provide.

2) Position us as experts + make prospect’s job easier

Once our recommended proof-of-concept approach was built, we sent to the prospect with a note:

“We’re looking forward to kicking off your proof-of-concept. We’ve done a ton of these so we built out an initial template you can use as you build out your requirements - we made sure to include everything you mentioned as being essential in prior conversations + what we’ve seen necessary for customers with similar goals.

Feel free to add/remove from this starting point, but hopefully this saves you some time.

How’s your calendar next week to discuss this template + any necessary revisions?”

Sure enough, this approach got the prospect engaged again.

Take 30 minutes this week to review “stuck” deals in your pipeline. For each deal, write out:

- What is the next step the prospect has to take?
- What part of it can you do for them?

And I bet you see a few “stuck” deals get moving again as you make it easier for your prospects to evaluate your solution.

1. Target Account Selection

Enterprise: Focus on 1-2 key accounts
Mid-market: Target 3-5 accounts
SMB: Include 5-15 accounts

Below-the-line contacts: Managers and individual contributors

Document specific challenges your target accounts face today. This isn’t about your product features – it’s about their business problems you can solve.

5. Relevant Success Stories

Have customer stories ready that mirror your target account’s industry, size, or challenges. These become your social proof in conversations.

Week 1: “Identify current feature management solution through engineering team outreach”

“Just show me a demo” is a tricky request to handle for many sellers. Here’s my (potentially controversial) advice for most* sellers:

When you are on a discovery call, and someone says “I really need to see a demo,” you should be ready to show your product. 

Lovers of legacy sales process and sales consultants may come at me for this: 

“When I was selling Oracle we wouldn’t show a demo until we’d had AT LEAST 15 calls and the CFO signed off on the business case!” 

Ok. 

Times have changed - buyers can get tons of info about providers and products without talking to a salesperson. They can probably even get a demo without talking to a salesperson by going to your website, YouTube, etc. 

So if your “go-to” move when a buyer finally decides to talk to you is to intentionally withhold information, you may not like the results. 

Yes, you may be able to successfully push back:

“If I were to show you a demo right now, it would likely be irrelevant and boring for you. Let’s use this time to better understand what you are looking to accomplish, and then we can schedule a demonstration.”

This can work (I’ve definitely used this myself AND taught it), but I think for many products there’s a better way. 

Especially in an environment where prospects are less patient than ever. 

I think it’s possible to give the prospect exactly what they are asking for, while allowing you to:

1) Run successful discovery on the first call
2) Give your prospect context that drives engagement
3) Scheduling time with a broader audience for deeper discovery

content:
“We’ll get back to you after we have our internal discussions” is a turning point in most deals. Most reps respond poorly, and it's the first step towards losing the deal. Here are two common (but poor) responses:

1) “Sounds great - excited to hear from you!” 

Gives up complete control to the buyer and you’ll end up sending several “any updates?” emails that feel gross to send and are annoying to read. 

2) “I’d be a terrible sales rep if we didn’t put something on the calendar - especially since leadership will be asking. How about we throw something on and we can always cancel if we need to?” 

My issues with this common approach: 

1) It’s all about you 

2) It seems weak - “I just want this in case my boss asks” 

3) It shows you care more about checking the box with scheduling a meeting than actually having the meeting - "we can always cancel"


A better response opens up more discovery and allows you to suggest value-additive next steps:

“Makes sense - we’ve covered a lot, and we need to get the broader team up to speed. 

Who will you be meeting with?” 

“What do you imagine Mary, John, and Jake will be most excited about? Most concerned?”

“To make these conversations easier, I’ll build a quick summary for each of the people you’ll talk to, and I’ll tailor it to be specific to what they’ll care about. 

Do you have 30 minutes Friday to review what I put together?” 


The key to this play working is how well you build that “quick summary” for the internal teams. 

If it’s a generic recycled version of what your champion already has, you aren’t progressing the deal. 

Instead, you need the summary to translate prior conversations into what the new stakeholders care about. 

You could spend a few hours building these summaries to give your champion what they need to sell internally.

content:
The most uncomfortable call of my career (35 seconds of silence felt like 5 minutes) taught me two important lessons about negotiation. Here’s the story:

I had a great relationship with my main contacts at an account. We had worked together for over a year, and they were planning on significantly expanding their agreement with us.

Because the license was expanding, they looped in a new stakeholder that I had never met.

This individual’s only goal was to get the lowest cost possible.

We got on a call, and the tone was completely different. The new contact went on the offensive and listed their demands.

The requests were unreasonable. Since I was confident in our solution and the value of our partnership, my response was:

“We’ve been working closely with the team for several months to right-size the agreement and to ensure that the value warrants the investment. While I appreciate your goal is to get the lowest price possible, your requests aren’t reasonable, and we cannot consider them.”

Then, I shut up.

There was silence for what felt like forever (the call recording showed it was only about 35 seconds), and the contact finally said, “Ok. We’ll need to discuss internally.”

The call ended, and we received a signed contract for the proposed amount a few days later.

While uncomfortable in the moment, I learned two essential negotiation lessons:

1) Silence is ok

Be confident, communicate clearly and don’t over-explain. Then, shut up.

2) Saying “no” is ok

When you are close to a deal, it’s tempting to remove all friction by accepting all requests thrown your way.

Don’t. Be confident in your value, and say “no” when a request isn’t reasonable.

Have you had any calls with "awkward" silence? How'd it turn out?

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

 “I missed quota, and it was because my territory sucked, our product is lame, and my manager hates me” then I’m definitely going to pass.

 “I missed quota. I did a poor job vetting the organization I was joining and made some assumptions about product/market fit that were wrong. However, here are some of the wins I experienced and what I learned:” 

Then I’ll definitely keep listening. 

A great rep in a bad environment won’t have success. I do my best to interview in a way that allows me to find those great reps so I can put them in a great environment where they will. 

If you’ve had a bad run recently, take ownership of the situation. Then, I’m rooting for you to take what you’ve learned and apply it in a better situation, and get the wins you deserve.

I’ve been the executive sponsor for two software purchases this year. I had the same decision criteria for both:

- Does this address one of my top 3 problems/priorities?

- Will my teams benefit from the tool/enjoy using it?

Take a few minutes to review your key deals for the rest of this year. Ask yourself:

If not, ask them on the next call: “I got so excited about how we could potentially impact [positive business outcome] that I didn’t take the time to make sure that was actually a priority for you.

Positive business outcomes don’t win deals. 

Positively impacting priorities do.

If no, make a plan to show how your solution will make the life of the “users” easier - executives don’t want to buy a tool their team ends up hating.

content:
We’ll get back to you after we have our internal discussions” is a turning point in most deals. Let’s look at terrible, bad, and good ways to respond:

Terrible:

“Sounds great - excited to hear from you!” 

Gives up complete control to the buyer and you’ll end up sending several “any updates?” emails that feel gross to send and are annoying to read. 


Better than nothing:

“I’d be a terrible sales rep if we didn’t put something on the calendar - especially since leadership will be asking. How about we throw something on and we can always cancel if we need to?” 

My issues with this common approach:

1) It’s all about you 

2) It seems weak - “I just want this in case my boss asks”

3) It shows you care more about checking the box with scheduling a meeting than actually having the meeting - "we can always cancel"


Good:

“Makes sense - we’ve covered a lot, and we need to get the broader team up to speed. 

Who will you be meeting with?”

“What do you imagine Mary, John, and Jake will be most excited about? Most concerned?”

“To make these conversations easier, I’ll build a quick summary for each of the people you’ll talk to, and I’ll tailor it to be specific to what they’ll care about. 

Do you have 30 minutes Friday to review what I put together?” 

This approach:

1) Adds value to the customer
2) Helps you maintain control of the deal
3) Gives you a reason to meet that actually makes sense

Bonus - if they respond with:

“No, let’s just connect over email” then you know you don’t have a deal - they weren’t going to have those conversations after all. 

They were just brushing you off. 

At least you know where you stand and won't waste time chasing.

content:
If I were an AE wanting to maximize earnings over the next three years, I’d look for 3 things in potential companies to join:

1) Leaders that develop their people

Questions to ask a manager:

“Tell me about a time you identified a skill gap in a rep - how did you help them close it?”

“Have you ever had a rep follow you from one company to another?”

“How many people have you promoted in the last 12 months?”

You are looking for leaders that can describe their coaching, have built “followership,” and have a track record of promoting members of their team. 


2) Companies at growth stages - not efficiency

Questions to ask:

“How did the comp plan change this year compared to last year?”

“Did anyone blow out their comp plan recently? Approximately how much did they earn?”

If comp plans are getting worse, the company is likely prioritizing profitability/efficiency over growth. 

If no one blew out their comp plan, quotas are either too high or territories are too tight. 

If someone blew out their plan and didn’t make an exciting amount of money, accelerators are too low. 


3) Product that can sell itself/is a need-to-have

Questions to ask:

“What is your gross retention rate?”

“What is your net retention rate?” 

“What’s your win rate on expansion opportunities?”

90%+ gross retention is a good sign of a “need-to-have” product (means 90/100 companies renew).

115%+ net retention rate is a good sign of a product that can “sell itself.” It means that the average customer spending $100k this year will spend $115k next year. 

40-50%+ win rate on expansion opportunities means you’ll be able to drive meaningful attainment through customer up-sell/cross-sell - can take out a big chunk out of your annual number. 

What else would you look for in a great company to sell for?

Walking away from bad deals, bad companies, and bad managers will speed up your deals and accelerate your career.

2) Clear writing

Your writing can be in the room with your buyers when you aren’t. Great writing wins deals, poor writing loses them.

3) Natural curiosity

A well trained but robotic rep will lose to a raw but curious rep most of the time.

4) Embracing silence

In a profession where everyone talks there’s a lot of power in shutting up.

5) Emotional story-telling

Decisions are made emotionally and validated with logic. Deliver critical facts with emotion to ensure they stick.

6) Challenge your customer’s opinions

They know more about their space. You know more about yours. Don’t be afraid to push back when they are wrong. 

7) Sprinting away from a bad manager/leader

When your manager is incapable of teaching you anything, you’ve outgrown your role and theirs. Time to go.

content:
My most unhappy periods in my career have been when I let my ego control my emotions.

Ego leads to comparison - and we all know the quote “comparison is the thief of joy.”

The problem with comparison is you are always way more successful than someone… and less successful than others.

Depending on the comparison you make, you’ll end up either arrogant or depressed.

Neither of those emotions lead to happiness.

I remember being an AE1. I compared myself to more senior reps - it seemed the AE3s had it made. They had a much higher salary, most of them drove nicer cars, it seemed to be the ideal role.

As an AE3, I looked at the OTE of an AE5 and thought, “That’s so much money - if I get there, I’m going to buy a new car, and life will be great!”

For the first several years of my career, happiness, success, and fulfillment were always just one or two promotions away.

Every time I reached the level I had previously identified as a “peak,” I decided I still needed more.

What a garbage way to live.

In my defense, I wasn’t guilty of a unique perspective. The “one promotion away” mentality is a common mindset.

The first company I worked for was acquired for $8 billion. A lot of people made a lot of money. And a lot of those people felt like they should have made more.

The people that made $500,000 compared themselves to those that made $1,000,000. “That’s so much money, and I’m just as valuable as them.”

The people that made around $1,000,000 compared themselves to the ones that made multiple millions.

The ones that made multiple millions compared themselves to the ones that made 10s of millions.

The same people that were being looked at by others as “making so much money” were looking at the ones that made more.

It reminds me of the results of a study where high net worth individuals were asked “How much is enough?”

Individuals with $3 million said $6 million was enough. At $6 million, the answer was $12 million. No matter the level, “enough” was always twice as much as they had.

Regardless of current level of success, many people are running an endless race they’ll never win.

No matter how much success, money, and accolades they earn, they’ll never have enough. All these people are running an endless race they’ll never win.

I forget who taught me this, but I’ll never forget it:

“If you aren’t happy in your current role, you won’t be happy in the next.”

If you are miserable as a mid-market AE, that enterprise promotion isn’t going to change your life.

Your struggles with anxiety, stress, and pressure as a sales manager won’t disappear when you promote to director.

And if you aren’t finding fulfillment and joy as a VP, a CRO title isn’t going to fix a thing.

Don’t worry about always getting more. Instead, find gratitude and joy in what you already have.

Otherwise, you’ll never have enough.

Even the most experienced sellers make these 3 mistakes that are more likely to make your prospect roll their eyes than agree to a next meeting: 

1) Asking questions you should know the answer to

“How does your company make money?”

“So, can you tell me about your role?”

Buyers don’t care about the 30,000-foot view. They just want to know if you can help them.

“We help you save money!”

“We help you make money!”

Yes, these are value statements. No, they don’t capture attention. Every business claims the same.

Skip the generic value statements and get right to 1) How you are different, 2) Why it matters, and 3) How you can prove it.

My #1 priority when joining LaunchDarkly was to improve pipeline generation. Three tactics we used to improve by 142%:

Tip One: “Bucket Your Buyers”

Most companies sell to a few different personas. 

All companies sell to different levels of those personas. 

If your list “scrambles” them altogether, you are putting yourself into constant context switching.

We don’t make all calls with the intent to set a meeting. Sometimes, we are just looking for a “nugget” we can use to set a meeting with an above-the-line contact. 

When we get “gold nuggets” like project names, executive KPIs, or even just current tooling challenges we use them to nail our calls to “decision makers” where we want to spend more time.

Our messaging used to be all about us:

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are sharing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release.”

content:
One of the least “fair” sales realities is that average sellers in great environments usually earn more than great sellers in average environments. Here are 3 ways to identify a great environment (starting with 2 critical metrics):

1) Gross Retention Rate

Gross retention rate is how well you preserve your existing renewal base. Basic example: If a company has 10 customers spending $10,000 on average, they have a renewal baseline of $100,000. 

If one customer that spends $10,000 doesn’t renew, their gross retention is $90,000, or 90%.

90%+ is good. 95%+ is great. 

2) Net Retention Rate

Net retention measures how much your customer revenue base grows each year. After you take out the lost renewals, and add in the renewals + expansion, is your customer base growing or shrinking?

110% is good. 115%+ is great. 120%+ is best-in-class. 

3) Quality of Sales Org

There are a lot of tools to identify the quality of a sales org (Glassdoor, RepVue), etc.

These are great places to start your research, but I know of sales orgs with great reviews where the team is miserable, and sales orgs where scores are “meh” but people are happy and crushing their comp plans.

So validate what you are seeing with the people that know best: current AEs at the company you are evaluating. Try and talk to at least three, otherwise you may talk to an outlier.

Finding a company with great metrics is a start.

Finding great metrics and an incredible sales org will make your career. 

I put together a list of questions you can ask to make sure you are looking at a great sales org. The questions assess:

- Product strength
- Executive team support

- Compensation plan quality and upside

content:
Poor territory management sinks even the best sales reps. Here are my three rules to help you get territory management right:

1) Ongoing, not static

Reps should have smaller territories so they can focus attention. 

Then, when AEs uncover details that make an assigned account a poor fit, replace it with another high-potential account. 

If a territory is too big, AEs will be pulled thin.

If it's too static, AEs will spin their wheels in poor-fit accounts. 

I've found focused but evolving territories most effective for all but strategic account segments. 

2) Accounts belong to the company, not the rep

High-potential accounts with unengaged reps are a massive waste of territory. If a rep doesn't give an account the attention it deserves, leaders should move it to a rep who will. 

I've seen "stagnant" accounts turn into six-figure wins by moving an account to a rep willing to do the work. 

3) Balance propensity and TAM

A territory full of potential whales is a slog - reps may work for quarters without closing a deal and getting paid.

A territory full of small transactions is a drain - reps will be on a hamster wheel, unable to focus on significant revenue opportunities. 

Great territory build requires understanding what drives TAM for your product (hint: it's not just revenue and the number of employees) and understanding propensity to buy via mentions, signals, multi-threading, etc., across different sources. 

Get this right, and your job becomes much easier. 

Get it wrong, and revenue targets become nearly impossible.

One of our AEs had massive success with their cold call opener, but they were shut down shortly after. Here's what’s working and what we are changing:

First, his opener led to 75%+ of prospects letting him pitch. Here's what he's using:

"This is (name) with LaunchDarkly. Just to be transparent, this is a cold call. I was wondering if I could have 20 seconds to tell you why I’m calling. And if it’s irrelevant, you can throw your phone across the room.”

Good mix of direct, transparency, and humor. Combined with great tone and it's working.

The challenges he saw came from what he said next:

"We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off..."

We lost the prospect’s interest because we started with what we do. 

Most of our ICP already does something similar to what we offer. So, when they hear this pitch, they think, "Yep, already got a solution for that, not interested."

When you lead with what you do your pitch will only resonate with people that are actively shopping for your solution. At any given time that represents roughly 3% of your market.

Not great odds.

When you lead with problems you solve, your pitch will resonate with people that are actively facing that problem. If you work for a company with a legitimate product, this should be a much higher percentage (at least 40%+).

For LaunchDarkly, it might sound like:

"I'm reaching out because I noticed your team's focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity. 

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are facing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release. 

Curious if that's been a conversation with your team at all?"


We all know problems > product in selling, but sometimes we forget how it applies to prospecting. 

Lead with problems, and you are more likely to have more meaningful conversations in your cold calls and book more qualified meetings.

I botched one of the most “well-prepped” discovery calls of my career. 

The meeting was with the CMO of a large law firm - the ideal target for our new brand tracking solution. Before the call, I did tons of research on his firm, the market, and relevant trends. 

But he shut me down before I had a chance to share my “expertise.” And it was completely my fault. 

He didn’t know I had done my research. He had no idea I was prepared. He assumed I was like most salespeople:

- Didn’t understand him/his role/his priorities
- Would try to push my product
- Wouldn’t listen to him

Everything went wrong with my first (and last) question:

“Can you tell me about your role?” 

Looking back, this question was unnecessary. I knew a lot about his role from my research. But he didn’t know I knew, and my question made it sound like I was clueless.

His response (in a very irritated tone) was:

“Kyle - you asked me for this call. Why don’t you just tell me what you do.” 

Blerg. 

I stumbled over my value prop, trying to make it as specific as possible based on the research I had done. But the CMO had already mentally checked out, because he had already determined that I was “just like all the other salespeople.” 

And most salespeople don’t make good use of an executive’s time. 

That painful lesson completely changed how I ran my discovery calls. I learned that sellers are guilty until proven innocent, and I had to show up strong in the first few minutes of the call to earn a buyer’s attention.

content:
Customers confident in their buying decisions are 2.6x more likely to buy more (Gartner). But sellers still do these 5 things that erode confidence:

1) Offering proactive discounts

When you show pricing for the first time and include a discount, you are telling your prospect “Yeah, I don’t think it’s worth the price, either.” 

2) Getting defensive/worried when competition is mentioned 

Competition in your deal is a GREAT sign - it means your prospect is committed enough to solving the problem that they are willing to evaluate multiple solutions. 

Getting defensive tells your prospect you are worried they are looking at alternatives. 

And what does it say about the strength of your solution if you get worried they are evaluating others?


3) Interrupting silence

The most interesting “sound bites” I’ve heard on calls often come after tough questions and silence. Most AEs never get these sound bites because they fill the silence rather than sit in it. 

4) Manipulative urgency 

“Expiring discounts” usually do more harm than good. Time-bound incentives should be mapped to timing valuable to both seller and buyer - not just a desperate AE or sales leader. 

5) Never saying “I don’t know”

Your prospect doesn’t expect you to know everything. They know you don’t. So when you confidently answer all questions, they know you are making it up some of the time. And that kills trust all of the time. 

“I don’t know, but I’ll find out” beats false confidence every time. 

What else have you seen damage your prospect’s confidence?

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal.

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down.

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

What "reality" would you add?

If I started at a company and knew nothing about my buyers I’d use these three ChatGPT prompts to:

- Identify who to target
- Understand what they care about
- Instantly get serviceable messaging

Here they are:

Prompt One (identify target personas):

“I sell [insert use case] technology to companies. These are the outcomes we provide:

1) [Outcome one]
2) [Outcome two]
3) [Outcome three]
4) [Outcome four]

What departments within companies should I target for my sales outreach?”


Prompt Two (what personas care about, what they are doing, how we help):

“For each of those departments, please summarize below points. Return the data in tabular format, with the below points as column headers. Each department will have its own row. Here are the points to summarize:

1) What individuals in each department care about as it relates to business outcomes
2) How individuals in each department spend their time to achieve business outcomes
3) What individuals in each department often struggle with to achieve those business outcomes 4) How the solution I sell may be able to help individuals in each department”


Prompt Three (example messaging):

“Now, let's write four prospecting emails: one for each department. Here's the outline to follow when writing each email:

1st sentence needs to evoke emotion from the recipient by describing a painful problem they are currently facing that our solution can solve.

2nd sentence needs to describe how they are likely trying to solve that problem and why it may be insufficient.

3rd sentence needs to describe how our solution could solve the problem presented in sentence 1 better than how they are trying to solve it as described in sentence 2.

4th sentence needs to ask if they are interested to learn more about how we could help.

Each email needs to be fewer than 150 words and written at a 5th grade reading level.”

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

“Makes perfect sense you’ve already got a handle on this. Usually this means you’ve got a similar solution in place and I didn’t do a good job sharing how we are different, or you are attacking this priority through a completely different approach.

Can I ask where you fall?”

Next time you hear “this isn’t a priority” to something that you know should be a priority, give this a shot!

content:
Most sales books are full of fluff or painfully outdated. But I’ve got one “must-read” recommendation - and here are 3 takeaways you need to know now:

1) The steps you take to sell your product are not the steps your prospects take to buy it

If you have a 3 month sales process, you probably meet with the customer 6-12 times over that period, and exchange a decent number of emails. 

But most of the work to evaluate your solution is happening without you. It’s happening in 1:1s between your champion and their boss. 

It’s happening in internal slack threads. It’s happening in team meetings where people debate pros/cons of different solutions. 

While you are sitting by your laptop hoping for a response to your “can I get an update on progress” emails, your buyers are evaluating without you. 


2) You communicate with both facts and feelings in the sales process - and feelings matter more

Feelings are sticky - you’ve probably heard the phrase “people don’t remember what you tell them but they remember how you make them feel.” 

And all feelings aren’t equal - the most important emotion to drive in sales is confidence. When buyers are confident, close rates are 2.6x times higher!! 


3) Match your buyer’s language, format, design as much as possible 

Nearly every company gets this wrong. Everything sales and marketing sends to the customer is 100% branded for their own company. Their logos, their quotes, their stories, their product. 

Great books lead to great takeaways. If you haven’t yet read “Selling With” by Nate Nasralla you are rapidly falling behind the modern buying experience. 

For a deeper breakdown, take a few minutes to watch the video!

content:
“We’ll get back to you after we have our internal discussions” is a turning point in most deals. Most reps respond poorly, and it's the first step towards losing the deal. Here are two common (but poor) responses:

1) “Sounds great - excited to hear from you!” 

Gives up complete control to the buyer and you’ll end up sending several “any updates?” emails that feel gross to send and are annoying to read. 

2) “I’d be a terrible sales rep if we didn’t put something on the calendar - especially since leadership will be asking. How about we throw something on and we can always cancel if we need to?” 

My issues with this common approach: 

1) It’s all about you 

2) It seems weak - “I just want this in case my boss asks” 

3) It shows you care more about checking the box with scheduling a meeting than actually having the meeting - "we can always cancel"


A better response opens up more discovery and allows you to suggest value-additive next steps:

“Makes sense - we’ve covered a lot, and we need to get the broader team up to speed. 

Who will you be meeting with?” 

“What do you imagine Mary, John, and Jake will be most excited about? Most concerned?”

“To make these conversations easier, I’ll build a quick summary for each of the people you’ll talk to, and I’ll tailor it to be specific to what they’ll care about. 

Do you have 30 minutes Friday to review what I put together?” 


The key to this play working is how well you build that “quick summary” for the internal teams. 

If it’s a generic recycled version of what your champion already has, you aren’t progressing the deal. 

Instead, you need the summary to translate prior conversations into what the new stakeholders care about. 

You could spend a few hours building these summaries to give your champion what they need to sell internally.

content:
“Just show me a demo” is a tricky request to handle for many sellers. Here’s my (potentially controversial) advice for most* sellers:

When you are on a discovery call, and someone says “I really need to see a demo,” you should be ready to show your product. 

Lovers of legacy sales process and sales consultants may come at me for this: 

“When I was selling Oracle we wouldn’t show a demo until we’d had AT LEAST 15 calls and the CFO signed off on the business case!” 

Ok. 

Times have changed - buyers can get tons of info about providers and products without talking to a salesperson. They can probably even get a demo without talking to a salesperson by going to your website, YouTube, etc. 

So if your “go-to” move when a buyer finally decides to talk to you is to intentionally withhold information, you may not like the results. 

Yes, you may be able to successfully push back:

“If I were to show you a demo right now, it would likely be irrelevant and boring for you. Let’s use this time to better understand what you are looking to accomplish, and then we can schedule a demonstration.”

This can work (I’ve definitely used this myself AND taught it), but I think for many products there’s a better way. Especially in an environment where prospects are less patient than ever. 

I think it’s possible to give the prospect exactly what they are asking for, while allowing you to:

1) Run successful discovery on the first call
2) Give your prospect context that drives engagement
3) Scheduling time with a broader audience for deeper discovery

Monday morning, I’m sharing with 17k+ newsletter subscribers exactly how to handle “just show me a demo.”

I’ll give you the talk track that:

- Balances showing product with deep discovery
- Sets expectations that a “custom” demo will require more conversation
- Earns the right to ask for more people to join a subsequent call your prospect will be excited to schedule 

You can join this newsletter (at no cost) at salesintroverts.com 

*I said most because some products just can’t be shown on a first call. But 95% of the time I hear “my product is too complex,” the AE really just needs to spend more time learning the product rather than expecting their SE to run 97% of the sales process for them.

90%+ of the 1,000+ candidates I’ve interviewed in my career tell me they are hitting quota. 

I threw the rough math into my trusty AI tool, and it tells me the odds of this happening are essentially zero. 

It makes sense that AEs might exaggerate quota attainment in the interview process. But it’s a shame, because while missing quota won’t disqualify you from a role, lying about it will. 

Missing quota isn’t a disqualifier because the industry has been challenging. Many companies are broken. And some sales leaders are completely incapable of helping their teams succeed. 

Here’s where it gets tricky:

It may not be your fault that you missed quota. But you still need to take ownership. 

If I hear:

 “I missed quota, and it was because my territory sucked, our product is lame, and my manager hates me” then I’m definitely going to pass. 

If I hear:

 “I missed quota. I did a poor job vetting the organization I was joining and made some assumptions about product/market fit that were wrong. However, here are some of the wins I experienced and what I learned:” 

Then I’ll definitely keep listening. 

A great rep in a bad environment won’t have success. I do my best to interview in a way that allows me to find those great reps so I can put them in a great environment where they will. 

If you’ve had a bad run recently, take ownership of the situation. Then, I’m rooting for you to take what you’ve learned and apply it in a better situation, and get the wins you deserve.

After reviewing countless PG plans, I’ve developed a framework that consistently drives results. Here’s the exact template and AI-powered process I use to create winning PG plans in minutes instead of hours:

Your pipeline generation plan needs six core components to be effective:

1. Target Account Selection

Enterprise: Focus on 1-2 key accounts
Mid-market: Target 3-5 accounts
SMB: Include 5-15 accounts

2. Strategic Contact Mapping

For each target account, identify 3-15 key prospects based on your market:

Above-the-line contacts: Directors, VPs, C-Level executives
Below-the-line contacts: Managers and individual contributors

Enterprise should focus on more per account, SMB fewer per account.

3. Pain Point Analysis

Document specific challenges your target accounts face today. This isn’t about your product features – it’s about their business problems you can solve.

4. Value Hypothesis Development

Create a clear statement of how your solution addresses their specific challenges. This becomes your north star for all account engagement.

5. Relevant Success Stories

Have customer stories ready that mirror your target account’s industry, size, or challenges. These become your social proof in conversations.

Week 1: “Identify current feature management solution through engineering team outreach”

Week 2: “Uncover engineering team KPIs through manager-level conversations”

Buyer skepticism makes your discovery calls “feel” uncomfortable. There are 2 concerns you have to resolve (and there are 2 easy ways to do it). Here are the concerns: 

- Does this rep know anything about me?

- Are they going to push me to buy, even if it’s not a fit?


Two ways to remove this tension:

1) Ask questions that show you understand your buyer

Instead of:

“Tell me about your role.”

Try:

“Many [insert role] we are working with are focused on improving [key priority]. How are you approaching this opportunity?”


2) Empower the “no”

Instead of:

“Thanks for taking the time to help me understand your business today. Let’s find 30 minutes to dive deeper into how we might be able to help.”

Try:

“Based on our conversation today, we may be able to help you improve [outcome] by improving how you approach [use case].

If we were to continue the conversation, we’d be sharing in more depth our approach to driving [outcome] through [how you improve their current state].

Last thing we want to do is waste either of our time pursuing a non-priority. Is [outcome] enough of a priority to warrant further discussion?”

Fair or not, buyers enter sales conversations with skepticism.

content:
When I was an AE1, I thought the AE3s had it made. With a much higher salary and bigger accounts, it seemed the ideal role.

As an AE3, I looked at the OTE of an AE5 and thought, “That’s so much money - if I get there, I’m going to buy a new car, and life will be great!”

For the first several years of my career, happiness, success, and fulfillment were always just one or two promotions away.

What a garbage way to live.

In my defense, I wasn’t guilty of a unique perspective. The “one promotion away” mentality is a common mindset.

I remember seeing a study where high-net-worth individuals were asked, “How much is enough?”

At $3 million, the answer was $6 million. At $6 million, the answer was $12 million. No matter the level, “enough” was always twice as much as they had. All these people running an endless race they’ll never win.

I forget who taught me this, but I’ll never forget it:

“If you aren’t happy in your current role, you won’t be happy in the next.”

If you are miserable as a mid-market AE, that enterprise promotion isn’t going to change your life.

Your struggles with anxiety, stress, and pressure as a sales manager won’t disappear when you promote to director.

And if you aren’t finding fulfillment and joy as a VP, a CRO title isn’t going to fix a thing.

Don’t worry about always getting more. Instead, find gratitude and joy in what you already have.

Otherwise, you’ll never have enough.

content:
I discourage my team from putting multiple options in proposals. It comes across like, “We aren’t sure what’s best for you, why don’t you decide?” I usually hate these metaphors but I’ll give it a go:

Imagine your doctor runs a full diagnosis of an issue. Then, once they have all the details, they say:

“Alright, we’ve got 5 options that you can choose from. Idk which one is best - why don’t you review and let me know?”

Not exactly a confidence boosting experience. 

You are the expert for your solution. Your buyer has spent a lot of time sharing their problems/goals with you. 

If you don’t know the best way for them to use your solution, how can you expect them to decide? 

I’m not saying to never give options - we often provide single year and multi-year agreements for review. 

And sometimes there are multiple “good” fit solutions at different price points the buyer wants to see. 

But wherever possible, minimize the number of options you show. Fewer options = higher confidence you understand what they need. 

And coming across with low confidence is the last emotion you want to show when sharing price.

content:
“We’ll get back to you after we have our internal discussions” is a turning point in most deals. Let’s look at bad, better than nothing, and good ways to respond:

Bad:

“Sounds great - excited to hear from you!” 

Gives up complete control to the buyer and you’ll end up sending several “any updates?” emails that feel gross to send and are annoying to read. 


Better than nothing:

“I’d be a terrible sales rep if we didn’t put something on the calendar - especially since leadership will be asking. How about we throw something on and we can always cancel if we need to?” 

My issues with this common approach:

1) It’s all about you 
2) It seems weak - “I just want this in case my boss asks”
3) It shows you care more about checking the box with scheduling a meeting than actually having the meeting - "we can always cancel"

Use as a last resort. 


Good:

“Makes sense - we’ve covered a lot, and we need to get the broader team up to speed. 

Who will you be meeting with?”

“What do you imagine Mary, John, and Jake will be most excited about? Most concerned?”

“To make these conversations easier, I’ll build a quick summary for each of the people you’ll talk to, and I’ll tailor it to be specific to what they’ll care about. 

Do you have 30 minutes Friday to review what I put together?” 

This approach:

1) Adds value to the customer
2) Helps you maintain control of the deal
3) Gives you a reason to meet that actually makes sense

Bonus - if they respond with:

“No, let’s just connect over email” then you know you don’t have a deal - they weren’t going to have those conversations after all. They were just brushing you off. 

At least you know where you stand and won't waste time chasing.

Got a note from someone: “I just lost a deal because I multi-threaded to a CEO and went above my champion. He said I betrayed his trust and had a hidden agenda.”

Brutal.

Then he made a great point: Everyone talks about how to multi-thread. No one talks about what not to do.

So here’s my attempt at what not to do in multi-threading:

1) Don’t go over the top of senior execs

Execs know how to get things done. Going over their head can make them feel like you don’t trust their judgment - or worse, like you’re trying to make them look junior internally.

Don’t work around senior execs - work with them.

2) Don’t surprise your champion

You want more people involved. You don’t want your champion surprised that more people are getting involved.

Make them aware of who you’re talking to, why, and how it benefits them.

They should hear it from you - not from a Slack message like, “Uh… do you know Kyle from LaunchDarkly? He wants to talk to me and says he’s working with you.”

3) Don’t neglect your contacts

Junior employees often have real influence. I’ve seen deals fall apart because a seller got access to power and left the original champion behind.

Not only is that rude - it’s risky.

What would you add to the list of “what not to do in multi-threading?”

content:
A few weeks ago I told a seller to stop asking about business impact. I asked them to focus on the technical requirements instead. Sounds weird, but I’ll explain:

Important context to begin - I was acting as a buyer and had looped in my team to help with the evaluation. Let’s look at my decision criteria as the executive sponsor on the deal:

1) Is my current state poor enough to make a change?

2) Do I need a change in strategy, a change in providers, or both? 

3) Is there enough business value to justify the investment in a more expensive tool?

4) If we purchase a new solution, will my teams be excited to use and adopt the tool? 

Then, let’s look at what I decided before even speaking with vendors:

- Current state is broken to the point that we have to make a change.

- We need a slight shift in strategy, and an improved tool would compound the impact of the change in strategy. 

We had a call with the rep at the vendor we selected to evaluate (he did a great job throughout the process btw) and discussed the business value elements. 

Based on the demo I saw, I was convinced this tool would drive the necessary business value to justify championing the spend.

But business value isn’t realized without successful adoption: I still needed to be confident my teams would love the solution. 

So, we set up another demo, and I brought in reps from my team. 

That’s when the rep started doing business impact discovery with my team that would be end users of the solution. And that’s when I interrupted him and pointed him back to the technical criteria. 

He had already won the deal based on business value. But he had not yet won the support of my reps. And I’m not going to implement a solution for them to use without their buy-in. 

Kudos to the rep - he pivoted the conversation and dug more into their technical requirements. That allowed him to show a feature-heavy demo that got them excited, followed by a successful POC. 

I’m sharing this because sellers are always told to “sell value.” 

This is accurate - but “value” is different based on the audience. 

For me, value was tied to rep productivity and engagement. 

For my reps, value was simply “does this make my job easier?” 

So yes, always sell value. But make sure you are selling the right value to the right audience to keep your deals moving along.

content:
I’ve read a lot of sales books. Most are full of fluff or painfully outdated. But I’ve got one “must-read” recommendation - and here are 3 takeaways you need to know now:

1) The steps you take to sell your product are not the steps your prospects take to buy it

If you have a 3 month sales process, you probably meet with the customer 6-12 times over that period, and exchange a decent number of emails. 

But most of the work to evaluate your solution is happening without you. It’s happening in 1:1s between your champion and their boss. 

It’s happening in internal slack threads. It’s happening in team meetings where people debate pros/cons of different solutions. 

While you are sitting by your laptop hoping for a response to your “can I get an update on progress” emails, your buyers are evaluating without you. 


2) You communicate with both facts and feelings in the sales process - and feelings matter more

Feelings are sticky - you’ve probably heard the phrase “people don’t remember what you tell them but they remember how you make them feel.” 

And all feelings aren’t equal - the most important emotion to drive in sales is confidence. When buyers are confident, close rates are 2.6x times higher!! 


3) Match your buyer’s language, format, design as much as possible 

Nearly every company gets this wrong. Everything sales and marketing sends to the customer is 100% branded for their own company. Their logos, their quotes, their stories, their product. 

A killer quote from the book exposes this problem: 

“If a company’s brand is all over the materials they send me, the chances that I forward it to my team are next to none. Because it’ll look like a massive billboard.” 

Companies don’t make large purchases because you emailed over a billboard version of a PDF.

Companies make large purchases because they see how you fit with them and solve their problems. 


Great books lead to great takeaways. If you haven’t yet read “Selling With” by Nate Nasralla you are rapidly falling behind the modern buying experience. 

So go fix that :)

It was scary for me to take full ownership. If I went “all in” and still failed, I’d have no one else to blame.

Better to go all in, fall flat on my face, and know I gave it everything than live with the regret that I never really tried.

That decision changed the trajectory of my career, and I’m forever grateful to the leader that called out my crap and told me to “run in your lane.”

content:
Too many AEs treat expansion like: “Hey, you are using our product - want to buy more seats/usage?” But the best expansion plays aren’t just about volume. It’s about solving more problems.

Here’s the expansion framework I use:

1) Make sure they’ve solved the first problem they bought you for

I’m not even thinking about expansion until I know we are delivering what they need from their initial purchase. No one wants to pay you more if they are still sorting out what they get from the first purchase. 


2) Find out what other problems they are looking to solve 

These problems might be faced by the team you are already working with. They might be sitting with other teams within the company. 


3) Demonstrate how you can solve the additional problems

This sales motion looks a lot like a new logo pursuit. The main difference is you have the perfect case study/proof point to build trust: 

“Here’s how your company is already having success with our solutions.”

Next time you inherit a customer account, get right into “what problems are we helping you solve today, and how can we do it better?” 

Obsess over making them successful with solving those problems. 

And then you’ve earned the right to ask to solve more problems.

content:
A few years ago, I interviewed for a sales leadership role after finishing as the #1 AE.
In the final round, my SVP said:

 “You clearly know how to sell. But your style is so specific to you I’m not sure you can teach it to others.”

It was a fair challenge. 

Fortunately, he placed a bet on me so I got the role. But I quickly realized he was right: I could sell, but I couldn’t teach others effectively.

My challenge was I didn’t follow a textbook sales process. I had built my own system over time - intuitively.

So I started documenting everything:

content:
If I were an AE wanting to maximize earnings over the next three years, I’d look for 3 things in potential companies to join:

1) Leaders that develop their people

Questions to ask a manager:

“Tell me about a time you identified a skill gap in a rep - how did you help them close it?”

“Have you ever had a rep follow you from one company to another?”

“How many people have you promoted in the last 12 months?”

You are looking for leaders that can describe their coaching, have built “followership,” and have a track record of promoting members of their team. 


2) Companies at growth stages - not efficiency

Questions to ask:

“How did the comp plan change this year compared to last year?”

“Did anyone blow out their comp plan recently? Approximately how much did they earn?”

If comp plans are getting worse, the company is likely prioritizing profitability/efficiency over growth. 

If no one blew out their comp plan, quotas are either too high or territories are too tight. 

If someone blew out their plan and didn’t make an exciting amount of money, accelerators are too low. 


3) Product that can sell itself/is a need-to-have

Questions to ask:

“What is your gross retention rate?”

“What is your net retention rate?” 

“What’s your win rate on expansion opportunities?”

90%+ gross retention is a good sign of a “need-to-have” product (means 90/100 companies renew).

115%+ net retention rate is a good sign of a product that can “sell itself.” It means that the average customer spending $100k this year will spend $115k next year. 

40-50%+ win rate on expansion opportunities means you’ll be able to drive meaningful attainment through customer up-sell/cross-sell - can take out a big chunk out of your annual number. 

What else would you look for in a great company to sell for?

content:
Your champion isn’t blocking you from their boss because they don’t like you. It’s not because they don’t think your solution could be a good fit. It’s because they don’t trust you yet. 

When you ask for an exec introduction, you’re asking them to bet their credibility. If your meeting flops, it doesn’t just waste an exec’s time - it makes them look bad.

The first step should be obvious but I’ll type it out anyway - you start to build trust with your champion by showing up prepared to all meetings and adding value throughout the sales cycle. 

If you aren’t doing that, there’s no way to ask for the introduction that will work. 

Assuming you are building that trust, here’s to ask for the intro:

1) Be specific - say exactly who you want to meet and why it matters.

Not, “My VP wants us to talk to one of your execs because they have decision making power and idk maybe some money too.” 


2) Reduce the risk - offer to send a short exec-ready doc before the meeting.

Extra insurance that the meeting will be well-prepared and a good use of time. 


3) Clarify expectations - explain what you’ll need from everyone on the call.

Execs don’t attend calls where they don’t have an important role to play. 

And no, putting a “face to the name” is not an important reason for an exec to join a sales call. 

Here’s how it might sound:

“Chris, sounds like we’ve got strong alignment here. But before we move forward, we’d want to get buy-in from your head of infrastructure. 

We’ll prep a 1-pager summarizing conversations so far so it’s a quick read. 

On the call, we’d just need their take on how our plan fits long-term. 

Otherwise, we run the risk of scoping an implementation that doesn’t align with exec goals, which is a bad outcome for us both.”

Make it easy for them to say yes -  and harder to say no.

1) Bucket your buyers

Stop switching between different titles and industries. Group similar prospects together so you can nail your talk track.
​
2) Dig for gold nuggets

The best calls to executives start with insights you learned from others in their org. Every conversation is a chance to learn something valuable.
​
3) Master storytelling

Instead of "we save customers 40% of their time," try: "One client used to stay until 7pm updating spreadsheets. Now they leave at 5 and have dinner with their kids."
​
4) Stop obsessing over openers

Your prospect only cares about three things:

- Who you are
- Why you're calling
- What you want

5) Have a real reason to call

The best reason? You know from research that you can solve one of their biggest problems.

content:
One of my reps told me their account was “tapped out.” So we reassigned it. Three months later, the new AE closed a six-figure upgrade.

The first rep wasn’t doing a bad job. They knew the users, ensured adoption, and confirmed there was no fit for additional products after several demos with the existing team. 

To them, that meant the account had maxed out - so they asked for it to be replaced.

Being the obedient VP I am, I reassigned it.

The new AE took a different approach. First, they learned how the current team was using the platform.

Then they asked:

- What problems is this company facing?
- Which ones can we help solve?
- Who owns those problems?

They found a business priority we could support, identified the team responsible, and got an intro from the existing users (who were happy to help).

Three months later, that team was fully onboarded, and we had a six-figure upsell.
I’ve seen this play out time and time again - AEs looking too narrowly at accounts, asking:
 
“How can I get the current users to spend more?”

That mindset leaves money on the table.

Start by helping your users solve the problems they bought you to solve.

Then zoom out: What other problems exist in the business that you can help with?

Use your existing success as a case study, ask for intros, and expand your impact.

Expanded revenue will follow.

content:
Vague next steps don’t win deals. 

Instead of, “Let’s schedule a demo”

Try:

“We’d love to show you how we help drive [priority outcomes] through [required capabilities] - I think you’ll especially like [key differentiator]. What else would you want us to cover?”


Instead of, “Let’s set you up with a trial”

Try: 

“We’ll get you in the platform so you can see [required capability]. It seems we’ll know it’s successful if you experience [goal after state], any other criteria you’d use to determine success?” 


Getting specific next steps means you have to do great discovery before moving on in your sales cycle. 

If you can’t define specific next steps, you’ll leave your prospect in stage one while you move the opportunity to stage two. 

And prospects stuck in stage one while you think the opportunity is stage two is the first step towards closed/lost.

content:
Asking prospects to quantify their pain early in a sales cycle can be painfully salesy. 

“How bad does it hurt?” sounds a lot like, “How much money will you give me if I can make this go away?”

I understand why we ask: we want to know if the problem is big enough to solve. We all know that no pain means no deal. 

Here’s a less… abrasive question to ask: 

“If you are anything like most [titles] I talk to, you are juggling a lot of problems/priorities. Is this one big enough to address now, or does it need to go on the backburner for a bit as you address other challenges first?”

Before you worry about quantifying a problem, make sure you’ve found a problem worth solving. 

Then, your buyer will support the effort to quantify the problem as you build a mutual business case.

content:
One of our AEs is having massive success with their cold call opener, but they are shut down shortly after. 

Here's what’s working and what we are changing:

First, his opener is crushing with 75%+ of prospects letting him pitch. Here's what he's using:

"This is (name) with LaunchDarkly. Just to be transparent, this is a cold call. I was wondering if I could have 20 seconds to tell you why I’m calling. And if it’s irrelevant, you can throw your phone across the room.”

Good mix of direct, transparency, and humor. Combined with great tone and it's working.

The challenges he’s seeing come from what he says next:

"We are a feature flagging platform that allows developers to separate deploy from release, toggle features on or off..."

We've already lost the prospect because we started with what we do. 

Most of our ICP already does something similar to what we offer. So, when they hear this pitch, they think, "Yep, already got a solution for that, not interested."

When you lead with what you do your pitch will only resonate with people that are actively shopping for your solution. At any given time that represents roughly 3% of your market.

Not great odds.

When you lead with problems you solve, your pitch will resonate with people that are actively facing that problem. If you work for a company with a legitimate product, this should be a much higher percentage (at least 40%+).

For LaunchDarkly, it might sound like:

"I'm reaching out because I noticed your team's focus on AI-driven development to increase velocity. 

A lot of engineering leaders we talk to are facing the challenging trade-off between speed and risk: more code with less time for testing means more potential for things to go wrong at release. 

Curious if that's been a conversation with your team at all?"


We all know problems > product in selling, but sometimes we forget how it applies to prospecting. 

Lead with problems, and you are more likely to have more meaningful conversations in your cold calls and book more qualified meetings.
