I’ve studied enough discovery calls to know exactly what sellers do that makes the light leave their buyer’s eyes.

 Here are three mistakes you may be making that are killing your chance to convert your disco meetings to opportunities: 

1) Asking questions you should know the answer to

“How does your company make money?”

“So, can you tell me about your role?”

“What are some of the goals you are working on?”

Your buyer enters the conversation worried you don’t know them well enough to help them. These questions prove them right, and make it easy for them to check out. 



2) Offer a “high-level overview”

Buyers don’t care about the 30,000-foot view. They just want to know if you can help them.

Leave the high-level overview to your website. The longer it takes you to define exactly how you can help your buyer, the less they will pay attention.


3) Generic value statements

“We help you save money!”

“We help you make money!”

“We help you reduce risk!”

Yes, these are value statements. No, they don’t capture attention. Every business claims the same.

Skip the generic value statements and get right to 1) How you are different, 2) Why it matters, and 3) How you can prove it.

Maybe you know exactly how to do this, and your discovery conversations are fluid, impactful, and always converting. 

Or maybe you could use some help mastering this process.

content:
7 observations from a guy leading a global sales org in a brutal economy:

1) The list of “essential” technologies gets shorter every quarter.

Every potential purchase is questioned with:

“Do we need to do this now?” Or, “Can we get this done almost as well with a current tool?”

If you don’t have great answers to these questions, your tech won’t make the “essential” list. 



2) Cold outreach only works if you combine problem, person, and timing.

High volume automation doesn’t work because you won’t nail the message. 

Low volume doesn’t work because you won’t have the surface area needed to hit the combo. 

Top reps are doing quality outreach with higher volume than used to be needed. They’ve adapted. 



3) Rep desperation is at a high, which is matched by increased buyer skepticism.

Reps are afraid of getting fired if they don’t sell. Buyers are afraid of getting fired if they make a bad purchase. 

If you don’t understand that skepticism you have no shot at overcoming it. 


4) Buyers don’t want to take a risk to “make a splash.” They want to keep their jobs.

See point three - buyers aren’t putting their reputation on the line for a risky purchase. De-risk the deal through effective PoCs, demonstrate value through BVAs, or mark it lost. 


5) No one’s buying because you “might” be able to help them. Prove it, or move on.

The days of “buy a few tools, we’ll renew the ones that work best” are behind us. More buyers expect proven value before signature - the best sellers know how to prove it quickly. 


6) It’s never been easier to personalize outreach, so it’s never been harder to stand out.

The ultimate trap of AI: the better it gets, the less it stands out. When every email in an inbox is personalized, relevant, and timely, “good” gets ignored. 


7) Top reps are still having massive success. Everything is “figure-it-out-able.”

While some reps feel like it’s an insurmountable struggle, others are cashing in the biggest commission checks of their career. There’s still money to be made.

content:
The typical (broken) discovery goes like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and small talk

- Next ten minutes: Superficial discussion of the buyer’s day-to-day

- Next ten minutes: Seller shares high-level overview of product. 

Twenty-five minutes into a thirty minute call and almost no progress is made. The seller barely knows anything about the buyer. The buyer barely knows anything about the seller’s product. 

The final few minutes become a mad scramble for the seller to find something valuable enough to earn another call, but most discoveries end with the buyer saying, “Can you send me a case study and more information so we can review and get back to you?”

A great discovery looks like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and objective set

- Next five minutes: Point-of-view validated (or corrected) and priorities confirms

- Next ten minutes: Deep discovery of how the buyer is approaching their priorities

- Last ten minutes: Seller shares how they can help accomplish priorities and next steps for evaluation finalized

When a prospect says they are surprised by how expensive your product is, consider this response:

“I’m surprised that you are surprised, and worry that I haven’t done a good job tying our solution to the value we see for your business. 

Before we go into that, though - when you say it’s expensive, it’s expensive compared to what?” 

“This is way too expensive” can mean a lot:

- It’s more than they budgeted
- It’s more than the competitor they know won’t work
- It’s fine, but they think they can get a better deal if you get nervous

Do take time to understand the objection, take the conversation back to value, and find a mutually beneficial path forward.

content:
A decade into my sales career, and I still get just as nervous for big presentations as I did as a new AE.

The difference is that now I have a proven preparation method that guarantees a smooth, confident delivery.

Here’s how I prepare to ensure I perform at my best:
​
​Two days before:​
​
- Review prep materials/research to determine what is top of mind for attendees

The goal is to identify the top outcome they want to drive and the biggest pain they want to solve.

​​
- Identify my one takeaway that ties back to my audience’s “top of mind"

If the audience only remembers one point, what do I need it to be?
​
​

- Build a talk track to emphasize my primary takeaway

They'll forget what they hear while remembering what they feel. I build my talk track around the question, " What do I want them to feel that is associated with my main takeaway?"

​​
​One day before:​
​
- Practice until mostly smooth, with minimal reliance on notes

The timing here is extremely intentional: sleep reinforces learning. One night’s rest between practice and presentation allows my brain to cement the flow.


If I'm 80% polished the day before, simply sleeping and waking up gets me to 95%.

Brain science is cool.


Day of:​
​
- One more walkthrough, with emphasis on tonality (where I want to pause for emphasis, etc.)

At this point, I've mastered the material. I know what I want to say. I just need to polish how I want to say it.

Then, I enter the call with the confidence that stems from preparation.

​
Regardless of your experience or comfort presenting, you should never outgrow the need to practice and prepare.

Next time you have a big presentation, try this framework. I bet you'll deliver a more confident and impactful message.

content:
The worst part of sales is being ghosted. Absolutely drives me crazy. You can’t help wonder:

“Why can’t they just give a quick update?”

“It takes a few seconds to say they aren’t interested anymore… just let me know!”

After being a “buyer” for some time, and also the recipient of MANY pitches, I’ve learned why people ghost. Responding with bad news opens up a can of worms:

If a buyer takes the time to say “no,” most salespeople ask, “Why?” Then, if they explain why, we’ll try to overcome their objections.

Buyers don’t want this back and forth. It just draws out the process of delivering bad news…

and most people don’t like to share bad news. It’s much more comfortable to stay silent than share a negative update.

Here’s my stupid simple tip to minimize ghosting: don’t sell like a seller.

Selling like a seller might mean you:


- Argue against objections
- Push unnatural timelines
- Act like the buyer owes you 
- Force a buyer to follow your rigid process
- Withhold information (like demos or pricing) 

Stop selling like a seller, and I bet you’ll be ghosted less. Start with NOT doing the above, and you are on your way.

content:
As an AE, I spent months trying to get into an account at “senior” levels. No one responded.

I started reaching out to entry-level professionals. One agreed to meet.

I could have quickly disqualified them as they were clearly not the right contact. Fortunately, I still decided to run a full discovery.

They gave me insight into a C-Level goal (NPS at 60) and a breakdown of internal systems.

Using this information, I created a business case for how we could help them achieve that goal within their current internal systems.

Sent a message to the CEO with the subject line, “NPS to 60?” and attached my business case for how we could help. He responded immediately, and we kicked off the evaluation.

Here’s the lesson: stop thinking that initial conversations are only valuable if they convert into an opportunity.

Your first conversation with an account is probably not with your eventual buyer. If you worry only about “converting” the opportunity, you’ll leave the call without being any closer.

Shift your mindset from “how can I qualify an opportunity” to “how can I better learn the value I can add to this company,” and you’ll end up with the strongest opportunities of your career.

content:
Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about database maintenance. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to maintain the database. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal.

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down.

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

What’d I miss?

The meeting was with the CMO of a large law firm - the ideal target for our new brand tracking solution. To prep for the call, I did tons of research on his firm, the market, and relevant trends. 

But he shut me down before I had a chance to share my “expertise.” And it was completely my fault. 

He didn’t know I had done my research. He had no idea I was prepared. He assumed I was like most salespeople:

- Didn’t understand him/his role/his priorities
- Would try to push my product
- Wouldn’t listen to him

Everything went wrong with my first (and last) question:

“Can you tell me about your role?” 

Looking back, this question was unnecessary. I knew a lot about his role from my research. But he didn’t know I knew, and my question made it sound like I was clueless.

His response (in a very irritated tone) was:

“Kyle - you asked me for this call. Why don’t you just tell me what you do.” 

Blerg. 

I stumbled over my value prop, trying to make it as specific as possible based on the research I had done. But the CMO had already mentally checked out, because he had already determined that I was “just like all the other salespeople.” 

And most salespeople don’t make good use of an executive’s time. 

That painful lesson completely changed how I ran my discovery calls. I learned that sellers are guilty until proven innocent, and I had to show up strong in the first few minutes of the call to earn a buyer’s attention.

My career lowlight was being suspended for a day without pay (was close to being fired).

Here's how a bad territory (and a bad reaction) changed my career:

We launched a new territory model to support company growth. The model was based on scored zip codes.

I got suburban Grand Rapids, MI. Not the city of Grand Rapids… the stuff near the city. 

Nothing against the fine people of suburban Grand Rapids, but my territory sucked. To make matters worse, my friend sitting beside me was assigned to Metro New York.

I spent my days trying to get contact information for companies that were not even on LinkedIn.

My friend often had multiple inbounds in a single day.

Frustrated, I threw a fit about how the zip code territory was flawed to senior leaders and my peers.

Leadership didn’t love that. Some wanted to fire me.

Fortunately, my boss fought for me. Instead of being terminated, I was suspended for a day without pay to fix my attitude (bless up).

Eventually, the territory model was adjusted, and everyone lived happily ever after.

Here are a few lessons:

1) Propose solutions instead of throwing fits.

2) Bring data, not emotion.

3) Vent up - not across. If you are frustrated, talk to your manager. Don’t bring negativity to your peers.

4) Everyone at your company is doing the best they can. Be forgiving of others' errors, and you’ll find people more forgiving of yours.

10 unsolicited pieces of career advice from a guy that’s seen acquisitions, IPOs, and works for a best-in-class tech company:

1) Your career won’t grow faster than your company.

6) Your company’s goal is to retain you at the lowest possible cost to the business. If you feel you are worth more, ask for more.

7) If you can’t find a company to pay you what you think you are worth then you have either a value problem or a messaging problem.

Several years ago, an exec met with our leadership team. He shared an anecdote from an investor that I’ll never forget (it completely changed my approach to my career).

The investor had told him: “Everyone is winning right now, and it’s not sustainable. Usually, if we invest in ten companies, we lose money on seven. We break even on two, and we make our money on one. 

Right now, everyone is winning. We are going ten for ten. But it won’t last.”

Those were fun years. Compensation for tech sellers rapidly increased, quota attainment numbers were high, and a lot of people made tons of money. 

The following message from the executive has stuck with me: 

“Let’s get it while the getting is good.”

We couldn’t control how long the macro-economic environment would stay hot for tech. But we could take advantage of every good moment through relentless execution. 

And we did - we were acquired for $8 billion, and then spun off for a successful IPO. Two meaningful exits early in my career was a very fortunate start. 

Now we find ourselves in a very different economic environment. It’s nowhere near as favorable as it was in the “zero-interest era.” But I’m not going to hit you with the usual “quota attainment is down, deals taking longer” spiel. 

Instead, I’m going to challenge you to think of some reasons why you currently have it good. 

If you’ve got a place to live, people that care about you, and decent health, then you’ve got a lot of good. 

If you’ve got access to the internet, ways to learn, and a desire to get better, you’ve got it good. 

I’ve learned that “Let’s get it while the getting is good” is less about your circumstances and more about what you do with them. 

So let’s get it.

content:
I’ve spent hours reading LinkedIn posts about how not to do outbound so you don’t have to. Here are 10 things you should NEVER do in outbound sales: 

1) Don’t personalize

You call it research, they call it stalking. If your outreach shows you know ANYTHING about them, you are creepy. Maybe don’t even include their name - try “Dear sir or madame” to be safe. 

2) Don’t skip personalization

You’ll never stand out if the buyer doesn’t know your email is just for them. Research EVERYTHING about them - where they live, went to school, favorite foods, etc. Then, make sure your email includes everything you know about them and how their elementary school mascot reminds you of your product’s value prop. 

3) Don’t follow-up

No response IS a response. If you reached out once and they didn’t answer, any additional follow-ups should lead to your email being suspended. Or maybe jail. 

4) Don’t don’t follow up

You gotta be persistent! Buyers are busy and appreciate it when you keep them top of mind. After all, studies done by sequencing tools show that 97% of meetings are set after the 728th touch. So, buy that sequencer, and get to sequencing. 

5) Don’t write long emails

Ain’t nobody got time for that.

6) Don’t write short emails

Don’t be lazy - make sure the buyer knows why you’re reaching out and how you can help!

7) Don’t reach out on weekdays

Execs are in meetings non-stop during the week. Don’t make their inbox busier than it already is!

8) Don’t reach out on weekends

After a long week of work, why would you think someone wants more work coming their way on a weekend?

9)  Don’t cold call

It’s 2024. Everyone hates cold calls.

10) Don’t forget the phone

It’s 2024, the only channel that’s not saturated is the phone. 


I hope this is helpful. Successful outbound is simple - you just need to find a way to follow all of these rules at once, and you’ll have great success.

Seven things I wish I could tell myself on my first day of sales:

1) The success of your career isn’t determined in the first few years. Calm down, deep breaths, get good.

2) You’ll hear “Ok, we’ll sign today” many times. Don’t panic when they don’t. “We’ll sign today” is buyer code for “We’ll sign in 3 weeks when you’ve lost your mind from anxiety and have given up hope.”

3) You’ll win deals you should’ve lost and lose deals you should’ve won. Sometimes it just be like that though.

4) The nicer the procurement person is when you first meet them, the more brutal they will be in negotiations. Don’t fall for it - buckle up.

5) “You are such a good sales rep” is not a real compliment unless it comes with a signed agreement. It’s just a nice buyer that wants to let you down easy.

6) Your potential for success is not limited by others having success, so cheer others on.

7) If you are miserable at work don’t “wait it out.” There will always be a reason to stay (a deal closing, stock vesting, etc.) but life is too short to stay in a job you hate. 

What would you add?

content:
One of our SDRs went from hitting ~60% of quota to 120%+ with the simple change of “bucketing” their prospects. 

Before making the change, they were uploading all of their prospects into a call list and cranking out dials. 

High volume, tons of conversations, very few conversions. 

They’d call a VP of engineering, then a product manager, then an engineering IC, all across different industries. 

They were making it nearly impossible for themselves to be “audible ready” for conversations because they were creating their own massive context switching problem. 

The change we made was simple: they started bucketing their prospects into lists based on level and title. 

Then, they spent entire call blocks on the same level and title, making it incredibly easy to nail the talk track when someone answered. 

Their conversion jumped, along with their quota attainment and commission checks. 

How do you organize your call list? Do you “bucket” your prospects?

content:
I’m either a statistical impossibility or living a lie. 

I’ve interviewed several hundred candidates for sales jobs in my career. The vast majority tell me they are hitting quota. 

I threw the rough math into my trusty AI tool, and it tells me the odds of this happening are essentially zero. 

It makes sense that AEs might exaggerate quota attainment in the interview process. But it’s a shame, because while missing quota won’t disqualify you from a role, lying about it will. 

Missing quota by itself isn’t a disqualifier because the industry has been challenging. Many companies are broken. And some sales leaders are completely incapable of helping their teams succeed. 

Here’s where it gets tricky:

It may not be your fault that you missed quota. But you still need to take ownership. 

If I hear:

 “I missed quota, and it was because my territory sucked, our product is lame, and my manager hates me” then I’m definitely going to pass. 

If I hear:

 “I missed quota. I did a poor job vetting the organization I was joining and made some assumptions about product/market fit that were wrong. However, here are some of the wins I experienced and what I learned:” 

Then I’ll definitely keep listening. 

A great rep in a bad environment won’t have success. I do my best to interview in a way that allows me to find those great reps so I can put them in a great environment where they will. 

If you’ve had a bad run recently, take ownership of the situation. Then, I’m rooting for you to take what you’ve learned and apply it in a better situation, and get the wins you deserve.

content:
If I could only teach three principles to help sales teams sell more, I’d hammer home these points:

1) If you are still searching for pain in your second discovery call, you’ve lost.

Great initial discovery uncovers the biggest problems your buyer needs to solve, and why they haven’t yet been solved.

If your second discovery is still trying to find a big problem you aren’t going to get a third call.


2) Negative consequences are not a description of what’s going wrong. They are a definition of why what’s going wrong matters.

- “We are spending too much money”
- “Employees are wasting their time”
- “We have data silos”

So what?

Every company has areas where they spend too much money, employees waste time, and have data silos.

Keep asking, “so what?” until everyone agrees the problem is big enough to solve now.


3) When required capabilities are only defined by the customer, the lowest cost solution will win.

When customers form their shopping list, they default to widely available capabilities.

Widely available capabilities are met by all of your competitors.

Either influence the required capabilities in your favor, or make sure you are the cheapest proposal.

Otherwise, closed/lost.

What would you add?

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

“Makes perfect sense you’ve already got a handle on this. Usually this means you’ve got a similar solution in place and I didn’t do a good job sharing how we are different, or you are attacking this priority through a completely different approach.

Can I ask where you fall?”

Next time you hear “this isn’t a priority” to something that you know should be a priority, give this a shot!

content:
I’m not saying cold email is dead, but if it’s your only channel you are in trouble. 

Even if you hit the “primary inbox,” many execs are filtering you out. 

All that time researching and perfecting a timely, relevant, personalized message and you’ll get left unread. 

Obviously this isn’t only an email problem. Some execs will never answer their phone. Some never check LinkedIn. You don’t know their communication preferences when you reach out. 

My advice is to follow these rules:

1) Multi-channel every prospect (email, LinkedIn, call)

Use all channels, but do more with LinkedIn and calls than email. 

Most sellers have a ratio of 10 emails / 2 calls / 1 LinkedIn messages across their sequences. 

I recommend 2 emails / 8 calls / 3 LinkedIn messages. 

Don’t go crazy getting the ratio exact. But, if you are doing way more emails than anything else, you are not playing the odds. 


2) No wasted touches (e.g., automated generic emails, calls with no VM left)

It’s easy to feel busy loading prospects into automated, multi-touch sequences. 

It’s easy to rip through a bunch of dials to a stale list, knowing no one is going to answer. 

It’s hard to make every touch intentional, relevant, and valuable. 

Which one do you think is going to break through the noise?

3) Do what AI can’t 

Less: “Saw you went to Ohio State - how about that championship game? Btw, we offer the first proprietary…” 

More: “I spoke with Alice and learned the team is working towards [outcome] but running into [pain]. We helped [customer] achieve outcome by [customer story].”

AI tools have already replaced average outreach. 

So you need to obsess with beating average. 

Or you will be left behind.

Next time you are stressed about quota I want you to remember the SaaS sellers of 1582. 

Many countries decided to adopt the Gregorian calendar, which required removing 10 days in October. October 4th, 1582 was followed by October 15th.

My most popular framework is my “Good Day Framework.”

Done right, it will give you complete predictability for what you need to do each day to hit quota. 

After a few months of using the “Good Day Framework” you should know exactly how many points per day you need to have success.

Here are the data points you need (preferably over at least a three-month period):

- Total points earned
- Total opportunities created
- Average deal size
- Win rate

Now, some very easy math to figure out exactly how to hit quota:

1) Average points needed to create an opportunity

How to calculate: Total points earned / Total opportunities created

Example seller: 510 points earned in a quarter / 22 opportunities created = 23.2 points required to create one opportunity.

2) Opportunities needed to hit quota

How to calculate: Quota / average deal size / win rate

Example seller: $150k quota / $27k avg deal size / 30% win rate = 18.5 opportunities needed to hit quota.

3) Points needed to hit quota

How to calculate: Opportunities needed to hit quota x Average points needed to create an opportunity

Example seller: 18.5 opportunities needed x 23.2 avg points = 429.2 points needed

4) Daily points needed

How to calculate: Points needed to hit quota / working days in a quarter (account for holidays and PTO)

Example seller: 429.2 points needed / 55 working days in a quarter = 7.8 points each day.


Start tracking with the “Good Day Framework” today, and soon you’ll have a very strong idea of what you need to do every single day to hit (and exceed) quota.

I’ve sat on hundreds of discovery calls in my career - many feel uncomfortable until a key shift occurs.

The tension comes from buyer skepticism:

- Does this rep know anything about me?

- Are they going to push me to buy, even if it’s not a fit?

Two ways to remove this tension:

1) Ask questions that show you understand your buyer

Instead of:

“Tell me about your role.”

Try:

“Many [insert role] we are working with are focused on improving [key priority]. How are you approaching this opportunity?”


2) Empower the “no”

Instead of:

“Thanks for taking the time to help me understand your business today. Let’s find 30 minutes to dive deeper into how we might be able to help.”

Try:

“Based on our conversation today, we may be able to help you improve [outcome] by improving how you approach [use case].

If we were to continue the conversation, we’d be sharing in more depth our approach to driving [outcome] through [how you improve their current state].

Last thing we want to do is waste either of our time pursuing a non-priority. Is [outcome] enough of a priority to warrant further discussion?”

Fair or not, buyers enter sales conversations with skepticism.

Try these tactics to reduce that skepticism, and you’ll find your discovery calls turning into conversations.

content:
In a recent coaching session, I told a rep to be “more curious than credible.”

The gap I observed is common: they skipped over parts of discovery because they didn’t understand what the customer was talking about. They were worried they would lose credibility if they admitted confusion. 

As sellers, we want to be trusted consultants. We want to be subject matter experts. But until you’ve been at a company for years, and selling to a persona for years, you’ll fall short of that level of credibility. 

So, close the gap with curiosity:

“You mentioned [topic], I have to admit that’s a new one for me. Can you share more of what you mean?”

“Thank you for sharing all of that detail. I followed most of it, but I’m a little unclear on [topic]. Can we go deeper there?” 

Worst case, you trade a little bit of credibility for real understanding. 

More likely, your curiosity increases both understanding and credibility. 

Either way, I think it’s a win.

- Identify who to target

“I sell [insert use case] technology to companies. These are the outcomes we provide:

1) [Outcome one]
2) [Outcome two]
3) [Outcome three]
4) [Outcome four]

What departments within companies should I target for my sales outreach?”

“For each of those departments, please summarize below points. Return the data in tabular format, with the below points as column headers. Each department will have its own row. Here are the points to summarize:

1) What individuals in each department care about as it relates to business outcomes
2) How individuals in each department spend their time to achieve business outcomes
3) What individuals in each department often struggle with to achieve those business outcomes 4) How the solution I sell may be able to help individuals in each department”


Prompt Three (example messaging):

“Now, let's write four prospecting emails: one for each department. Here's the outline to follow when writing each email:

1st sentence needs to evoke emotion from the recipient by describing a painful problem they are currently facing that our solution can solve.

2nd sentence needs to describe how they are likely trying to solve that problem and why it may be insufficient.

3rd sentence needs to describe how our solution could solve the problem presented in sentence 1 better than how they are trying to solve it as described in sentence 2.

4th sentence needs to ask if they are interested to learn more about how we could help.

Each email needs to be fewer than 150 words and written at a 5th grade reading level.”

4) Changing jobs every 18 months will increase your short-term earnings. Staying long enough to actually get good will increase your career earnings.

5) Obsess over finding something you can be the “best” at. If you don’t have a superpower, you are a commodity.

6) Your company’s goal is to retain you at the lowest possible cost to the business. If you feel you are worth more, ask for more.

7) If you can’t find a company to pay you what you think you are worth then you have either a value problem or a messaging problem.

8) There are no short-cuts but there are accelerators.

9) No matter your career path, learn to sell.

10) No matter your career path, learn to write.

content:
I dressed up in a nice shirt and tie for my final sales leadership interview with a member of our executive team. The office was very casual, so I looked out of place, but “dressing up” felt the right approach to show my excitement for the role.

A few minutes before the interview, his assistant told me we’d have to reschedule.

I dressed up again the next day. I felt a little bit silly and received a few comments, but it was an important day in my career.

A few minutes before the interview, his assistant told me we needed to reschedule again.

I dressed up for a third time. I remember waiting near my desk right before we met - I could see him in a conference room.

He was sitting casually, laughing, and scrolling on his phone, so I was surprised when I got the Gchat from his EA saying, “He’s caught up and can’t meet today.”
Maybe he really was caught up. Or, maybe he didn’t want to “waste” his time interviewing a junior potential leader.

Regardless of the reason, the interview never happened. I moved into the role without having the conversation.

I’ll never forget how crappy it felt to be so excited/nervous for a meeting with an exec only to see it move twice and then cancel. I felt pretty unimportant - not only did the meeting never happen, but he never bothered acknowledging the situation.

I’ve made tons of mistakes as a leader. I’ll make plenty more. I’m sure many people could write stories about mistakes I’ve made.

But I hope to never act “too important” for SDRs, AEs, and aspiring leaders in my organization for two reasons:

1) It’s a silly way to live (no one in the real world cares what your title/level is)

2) You can’t build a winning culture if execs don’t invest in more junior employees

This story reminds me of one of my favorite quotes:

“You aren’t better than anyone else, but you aren’t worse, either.”

So this week, don’t act like you are better than anyone.

And certainly, don’t feel like you are any worse.

A consequence of a global leadership role is increased travel. Over the last several weeks, I’ve spent time in London, Boston, San Francisco, and Las Vegas.

I’d summarize, but that won’t do it justice, so I’ll copy/paste from Chelsea Castle:

“Make it worth it.

This is a phrase my husband and I often say to each other.

When leaving my family for an event or work, make the time away worth it.

When either of us is doing something for ourselves — instead of spending time together (our absolute top priority in life) — make it worth it.

When I'm taking my family across the country so they can be with me while I'm at a work event, make it worth it.

Whenever I've evaluated a new job, the question has always been: does this align with my values and priorities? When it takes me away from my family, is it worth it?

This phrase has permeated all aspects of my life and has become a guiding principle.

That doughnut? Make it worth it. 😜

That 20-minute walk when you need to check something off your work to-do list? Make it worth it.

Every blog post, video, or [insert tactic here] you spend time and energy on? Make it worth it.

Life is full of choices and trade-offs. When we're constantly doing X instead of Y, the best we can do is ensure those choices lead to a fulfilling and meaningful outcome.

Those moments are all you've got. Make it matter.”


Thank you, Chelsea, for writing exactly what I needed to read that night. We won’t always spend our time exactly how we want, but we can make it matter. 

And when we are lucky to be spending time doing what we want, we can do more to make it matter. 

Here’s to making the rest of this year matter.

I’ve never set an org-wide call target. Here’s why:

Some reps have high connect rates, some are lower.

content:
Whenever an AE is struggling to set meetings, I run a three-step diagnosis:

1) Are you calling the right accounts?

Here are a few questions I ask to check territory management strategy:

Are the accounts you are working investing in areas tied to your solution?

For example, at LaunchDarkly, we look for companies that are hiring developers.

If they are hiring developers, they are more likely to be investing in solutions that support releasing software fast without the risk. 


Are there multiple landing spots for your product?

For example, at Qualtrics I focused on accounts that needed to understand brand, customer, and product experience. Three different use cases = three shots to win business at the account.

Do you understand the accounts you are calling?

Massive budget and multiple use cases won’t help you land an account if you can’t speak their language.

Simple question to ask yourself: “If I was in a room with their executive team, could I have a conversation about their business, in their language, without being completely out of place?”

Good accounts that you understand are better targets than great accounts that you don’t understand.


2) Are you calling the right contacts?


Two questions to ask about the contacts in your sequences:

- Would this person personally benefit from our solution?

- Is this person at all responsible for solving the business pain our solution solves?

No personal benefit = no reason for them to respond.

No connection to business pain = no reason for you to want them to respond.


3) Messaging

Two points I’m looking for in effective messaging:

- Emotional relevance

What is the email/phone call your buyer never wants to get from their boss? If your email shows them a way to avoid that dreaded call, it’s emotionally relevant.

- Specificity

Could you use the same messaging with another prospect? Or, worse, could your competitor send your same email to your buyer?

If the answer to either of those questions is “yes,” your messaging isn’t specific enough.

Meetings are tough to come by right now. But it’s hard to go wrong if you use the right messaging, with the right people, within the right accounts.

content:
Asking prospects to quantify their pain early in a sales cycle can be painfully salesy. 

“How bad does it hurt?” sounds a lot like, “How much money will you give me if I can make this go away?”

I understand why we ask: we want to know if the problem is big enough to solve. We all know that no pain means no deal. 

Here’s a less… abrasive question to ask: 

“How else have you tried to solve this problem?”

Or, if you made the prospect aware of a pain they hadn’t previously considered:

“Now that this is on your radar, is it significant enough to solve? Or is it one of those many ‘pesky’ problems that you can live with?” 

Before you worry about quantifying a problem, make sure you’ve found a problem worth solving. 

Then, your buyer will support the effort to quantify the problem as you build a mutual business case.

content:
Seven things I wish I could tell myself on my first day of sales:

1) The success of your career isn’t determined in the first few years. Calm down, deep breaths, get good.

2) You’ll hear “Ok, we’ll sign today” many times. Don’t panic when they don’t. “We’ll sign today” is buyer code for “We’ll sign in 3 weeks when you’ve lost your mind from anxiety and have given up hope.”

3) You’ll win deals you should’ve lost and lose deals you should’ve won. Sometimes it just be like that though.

4) The nicer the procurement person is when you first meet them, the more brutal they will be in negotiations. Don’t fall for it - buckle up.

5) “You are such a good sales rep” is not a real compliment unless it comes with a signed agreement. It’s just a nice buyer that wants to let you down easy.

6) Your potential for success is not limited by others having success, so cheer others on.

7) If you are miserable at work don’t “wait it out.” There will always be a reason to stay (a deal closing, stock vesting, etc.) but life is too short to stay in a job you hate. 

What would you add?

A big issue with sales content is how often someone sees something work once and declares it as “the way.”

Just because something works once, in your bubble, doesn’t mean it scales. 

But people write like their one-time success is a proven, repeatable approach. 

Then, people try to adopt it but fail, because it was either a fluke for the author or it was a unique circumstance.

Saw a post the other day that recommended building tons of rapport (10 minutes worth on a 30 minute first call!!)

Works great for a founder talking to warm connections. Really good advice for that audience and valuable takeaways. 

But imagine an AE going into a first call with a VP of Engineering thinking “Gotta make sure to spend at least 10 minutes on rapport so we can become friends.”

Disaster.

When consuming content, don’t assume that because it worked for someone else that it will work for you.

content:
When I was an AE1, I thought the AE3s had it made. With a much higher salary and bigger accounts, it seemed the ideal role.

As an AE3, I looked at the OTE of an AE5 and thought, “That’s so much money - if I get there, I’m going to buy a new car, and life will be great!”

For the first several years of my career, happiness, success, and fulfillment were always just one or two promotions away.

What a garbage way to live.

In my defense, I wasn’t guilty of a unique perspective. The “one promotion away” mentality is a common mindset.

I remember seeing a study where high-net-worth individuals were asked, “How much is enough?”

At $3 million, the answer was $6 million. At $6 million, the answer was $12 million. No matter the level, “enough” was always twice as much as they had. All these people running an endless race they’ll never win.

I forget who taught me this, but I’ll never forget it:

“If you aren’t happy in your current role, you won’t be happy in the next.”

If you are miserable as a mid-market AE, that enterprise promotion isn’t going to change your life.

Your struggles with anxiety, stress, and pressure as a sales manager won’t disappear when you promote to director.

And if you aren’t finding fulfillment and joy as a VP, a CRO title isn’t going to fix a thing.

Don’t worry about always getting more. Instead, find gratitude and joy in what you already have.

Otherwise, you’ll never have enough.

There are no shortcuts in sales, but I think there are seven sales superpowers.

Here are the seven superpowers I wish I would have developed earlier:

1) Saying no

Walking away from bad deals, bad companies, and bad managers will speed up your deals and accelerate your career.

2) Clear writing

Your writing can be in the room with your buyers when you aren’t. Great writing wins deals, poor writing loses them.

3) Natural curiosity

A well trained but robotic rep will lose to a raw but curious rep most of the time.

4) Embracing silence

In a profession where everyone talks there’s a lot of power in shutting up.

5) Emotional story-telling

Decisions are made emotionally and validated with logic. Deliver critical facts with emotion to ensure they stick.

6) Challenge your customer’s opinions

They know more about their space. You know more about yours. Don’t be afraid to push back when they are wrong. 

7) Sprinting away from a bad manager/leader

When your manager is incapable of teaching you anything, you’ve outgrown your role and theirs. Time to go.

content:
After I was “sold” on a solution, it took over nine months to earn approval for use within my organization.

First, I needed approval to access an internal tool that was used to request approval to evaluate a new vendor. 

Only took a couple of weeks and we got that approved!

Then, I had to collect supporting documents and fill out extensive questionnaires to compile:

- Risks
- Benefits
- Roll-out plan

All of this work wasn’t to get a purchase approved. This work was just to get approval for our security and legal teams to review the vendor for initial compliance. 

Those processes were… not fast.

Months later, I was assigned a project manager to help onboard the solution… which kicked off another few months of conversations.

Throughout this process, there were many “exit points” where I could have just dropped the project and resumed focus on my core job.

I didn’t abandon it for two reasons:

- I was confident the solution would make my org better

- I was motivated to make an impact 

Selling is hard. Buying might be harder.

So sellers should:

1) Make sure you’re heping your champion get personal wins, or they won’t be motivated to push through when they hit internal resistance

2) Remove the burden from the buyer wherever possible by making legal, security, and business case reviews as low of a lift as you can 

Otherwise, you’ll be asking your buyer for updates on a deal they’ve given up on.

content:
Soft costs (e.g., ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!’) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about building feature flags. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to build internal tooling. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore.

If I buy this software,  I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

While the rep is claiming cost savings, the exec sees a cost increase. 

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

Three attributes I’m looking for on your resume that give me confidence to hire you:

1) Trajectory

I’m looking for career progression. Promotions or moving to better companies are both indicators of a successful seller.

“Better companies” is subjective, based on the role you want. For some roles, going from a less technical product to a more technical product could be better. For others, going from a tiny startup to a more structured company could be progression. For another, the reverse could be true.

2) Stats

Specificity matters. If I don’t see details about your performance, I assume you didn’t think it was worth sharing.

Comparative is also helpful. If 87% of quota was the highest attainment out of 30 reps, that’s more impressive than a seller that hit 100% but was middle of the pack.

3) Story

Careers aren’t linear. No one is always having success. Not all companies you join were a good decision.

Short stays at companies aren’t a disqualifier. I understand layoffs have been common, and I know some companies just suck. 

Where things went wrong, share what you learned and how you moved forward.

What attributes did I miss?

content:
I got my first taste of end-of-quarter pressure when a teammate had a large deal scheduled to close on the final day.

All signs showed a clear path to closing - legal was done, budgets had been approved, and all parties were aligned on the close date.

Then, the champion asked for a call. The rep, their manager, and head of sales all joined from the same conference room.

The update sucked: “We’ll get a deal done today, but the $500,000 is out of the question. We can do something in the neighborhood of $100,000.

Obviously, this destroyed the rep and team's forecast and heavily damaged the company’s call - we weren’t that big yet, and this deal was a big chunk of our expected revenue.

I’ll never forget how the two leaders responded:

One put his head in his hands, rocked back and forth, and talked about how big of a disaster this was.

The other jumped up and said, “Lemonade, baby, lemonade.”

Both were (and are!) great leaders. But only one response inspired confidence in the team’s ability to take the bad news and make the most of it.

That customer ended up closing a quarter-making seven-figure deal just a few months later. 

Lemons became lemonade.

No matter your sales success, you’ll still face some very bad days. Deals slipped, deals lost, promotions missed, jobs lost, the list of negatives in sales is… extensive.

And unless you are superhuman, you won’t always face each challenge with a smile.

But try to think, “lemonade, baby, lemonade,” whenever you face bad news. 

You'll still have bad moments, but this perspective of positivity will make all the difference in how quickly you recover.

A very simple discovery question I heard on a recent call and why I loved it:

“What are you looking to get out of a platform like this for your own use?” 

I love it because nothing gets someone engaged/interested like talking about what they, as an individual, want. 

No, it’s not “business impact.” No, it’s not going to convince an economic buyer. 

But, in discovery, your first priority is winning another call. And you win the next call by making an individual confident you can help them. 

Then, you win moving to a demo/POC by making them confident you can help their team. 

Finally, you win the deal by making them confident you can help their business. 

Before each call, figure out what “win” your buyer is looking to get. Deliver that win, and you’ll see your deals progress faster and more consistently.

I got myself into terrible shape early in my career. I didn't exercise, ate poorly, slept poorly, and was under high stress - the whole combo.

After putting on about seventy pounds, I decided I wanted to live differently. So, I hired a coach. The coach taught me how to train effectively and how to structure nutrition plans.

content:
Saying, “yep, that makes sense,” is killing your discovery.

Here’s my favorite coaching method to help reps fix:

When reviewing calls, if I hear a rep say, “that makes sense,” I’ll pause the recording and ask, “did that actually make sense to you?”

9 times out of 10 they’ll laugh and say “no.” It was just more comfortable to move on rather than admitting confusion.

Think about how this feels as a buyer:

1) They just walked you through a complicated problem.

2) They know they didn’t explain it clearly because it’s difficult to put into words.

And they get hit with a, “yep - that makes sense!” in response?

How are they going to believe you have a solution for them if they can’t even believe you understand their problem?

Good sellers have no problem asking for clarification.

Great sellers refuse to move on in a conversation until they are on the same page as their buyer.

Next time you are tempted to say, “that makes sense,” try, “I’m not sure I’m following. Can you explain…” and you’ll have a more meaningful conversation.

Here's the story:

We needed a new territory model to support company growth. The new model was based on scored zip codes.

I got suburban Grand Rapids, MI. Not the city of Grand Rapids… the stuff near the city. 

Nothing against the fine people of suburban Grand Rapids, but my territory sucked. To make matters worse, my friend sitting beside me was assigned to Metro New York.

I spent my days trying to get contact information for companies that were not even on LinkedIn.

My friend often had multiple inbounds in a single day.

Frustrated, I threw a fit about how the zip code territory was flawed to senior leaders and my peers.

Leadership didn’t love that. Some wanted to fire me.

Fortunately, my boss fought for me. Instead of being terminated, I was suspended for a day without pay to fix my attitude (bless up).

Eventually, the territory model was adjusted, and everyone lived happily ever after.

Here are a few lessons:

1) Propose solutions instead of throwing fits.

2) Bring data, not emotion.

3) Vent up - not across. If you are frustrated, talk to your manager. Don’t bring negativity to your peers.

4) Everyone at your company is doing the best they can. Be forgiving of others' errors, and you’ll find people more forgiving of yours.

p.s. I still haven’t been to Grand Rapids, but I absolutely love Michigan now, so I think we are on good terms.

However, Minnesota and I remain sworn enemies. That’s a story for another day.

content:
The most awkward call of my career (35 seconds of silence felt like 5 minutes) taught me two important lessons about negotiation.

Here’s the story:

I had great champions at an account. After a successful first year,  they planned to significantly expand their agreement with us.

The new scope required bringing in a new stakeholder that I had never met, and their goal was to get the lowest cost possible.

We got on a call, and the tone was completely different. The new contact went on the offensive and listed their demands.

The requests were unreasonable. Since I was confident in our solution and the value of our partnership, my response was:

“We’ve been working closely with the team for several months to right-size the agreement and to ensure that the value warrants the investment. While I appreciate your goal is to get the lowest price possible, your requests aren’t reasonable, and we cannot consider them.”

Then, I shut up.

There was silence for what felt like forever (the call recording showed it was only about 35 seconds), and the contact finally said, “Ok. We’ll need to discuss internally.”

The call ended, and we received a signed contract for the proposed amount a few days later.

While uncomfortable in the moment, I learned two essential negotiation lessons:

1) Silence is ok

Be confident, communicate clearly and don’t over-explain. Then, shut up.

2) Saying “no” is ok

When you are close to a deal, it’s tempting to remove all friction by accepting all requests thrown your way.

Don’t. Be confident in your value, and say “no” when a request isn’t reasonable.

Any other tips for negotiation?

content:
One of the first things I was taught as an AE was the importance of multi-threading.

But when I tried to do it I failed. I got frustrated: why would my champion block me?

This post will teach you what took me lots of failure to learn.

First, understand when you ask for introductions, you aren’t just asking them to send a quick email.

You are asking them to bet their credibility on you.

If they connect you with a coworker that doesn’t end up finding value in meeting with you, it reflects poorly on them.

It’s a big deal at the executive level: no one wants an executive annoyed at them because they wasted their time with a bad sales call!

Here’s my framework for successfully multi-threading with your champion:

1) Build their confidence by always adding value when you meet with them

2) Have a specific reason for your request to meet with new stakeholders

3) Detail what will be expected from all attendees (not just an agenda - specifically what role each attendee will play)

4) Share your plan to make sure it’s a successful meeting


Here’s what the request could look like:

“Linda, it’s been great working with you to identify how LaunchDarkly could help your dev team improve efficiency.

Last thing we’d want to do is begin implementation without a clear picture of how our work would impact the broader engineering org - we want to optimize for the long-term.

Typically the CTO is the best person to speak to long-term architecture goals. We’d love to bring Angela onto the next call to bring her up to speed on our planned implementation to see where she would recommend adjustments.

We won’t waste her time: we’ll prepare an executive summary she can review before the call so we can make the most of the conversation.

The main feedback we’ll want from her is related to the milestones we’ve discussed - now is the right time to change those definitions or timing.

To ensure the call is successful, we’ll also include an executive from our solution architect team - that way, any questions she has can be addressed during the call.”


Following this approach will increase your champion’s confidence in you, earn an audience with others, and ensure you are ready to make those conversations effective.

content:
A few weeks ago, I was asked to present at our All Leadership company meeting on my favorite topic: "Nail the Basics."

I love this topic because I’ve built my career on the basics. Sometimes, that disappoints people. 

When they ask me, "What's working for your teams?" They hope to hear something "new and exciting" or "complex and advanced."

But nothing beats basic when you execute well.

I think we should hate complexity. Complexity is harder to learn, harder to implement, and harder to track.

When programs are complex, there are too many points of failure, so it’s impossible to know what’s working and what’s broken.

On the other hand, when focus areas are simple, you can easily diagnose what’s broken (so you can replace), and what’s working (so you can build on that foundation).

Once you have a strong, basic foundation, you can build on areas where you are seeing a return. Because the foundation is strong, you can expect greater returns from that emphasis.

Basics also give the opportunity for mastery. This mastery gives opportunities for you to be flexible in how you implement.

My favorite example of this is the best sellers that seem to have their own process. It looks like they are playing an entirely different game as they close the largest deals and crush quota year over year.

But I've found that they rarely have their own process. They’ve just mastered the basics so incredibly well that they can flex the process and immediately pivot based on customer input.

I'll keep teaching the basics. Maybe because it's all I know, or maybe because I know it works.

Vague next steps don’t win deals. 

Instead of, “Let’s schedule a demo”

Try:

“We’d love to show you how we help drive [priority outcomes] through [required capabilities] - I think you’ll especially like [key differentiator]. What else would you want us to cover?”


Instead of, “Let’s set you up with a trial”

Try: 

“We’ll get you in the platform so you can see [required capability]. It seems we’ll know it’s successful if you experience [goal after state], any other criteria you’d use to determine success?” 


Getting specific next steps means you have to do great discovery before moving on in your sales cycle. 

If you can’t define specific next steps, you’ll leave your prospect in stage one while you move the opportunity to stage two. 

And prospects stuck in stage one while you think the opportunity is stage two is the first step towards closed/lost.

My initial focus when joining LaunchDarkly was turning around our outbound motion. In my first full quarter, we’ve seen a 170%+ increase in outbound pipeline generated. 

Today I’m highlighting our PG leader, Marissa Mengert, and sharing what’s working for her:


1) Targeted Prospecting

It starts with deep research - crafting a clear hypothesis on how a specific organization can benefit from our solution. Understanding buyer personas and aligning their needs with what we offer is key.

2) Balancing Personalized Outreach

Personalization goes beyond surface-level changes. She tailors her messaging to top prospects, focusing on their pain points and what really matters in their day-to-day. Whether it’s email, phone, or social media, she ensures each touchpoint is relevant and specific.

3) Consistent Follow-Up

Persistence is non-negotiable. It often takes 3-8 touches to get a response, but that’s where the magic happens. Consistent, thoughtful follow-ups keep you in the game.

4) Clear (and Brief) Value Proposition

She keeps her value proposition to three sentences: what we offer, the problem we solve, and proof that we deliver.

5) Multi-Channel Engagement

Utilizing various channels (email, calls, social media) not only increases response rates but also meets prospects on the platforms they prefer and builds familiarity over time.

6) Diligent Preparation

She starts every week with a template that outlines which current customers and prospects she’ll be reaching out to, with tailored messaging ready to go. She also makes sure to log off every Friday knowing exactly who she is outbounding to the following week.

I’ll leave you with her mindset: 

“The 50th "no" in a row can be tough, but with a well-prepared plan, it’s easy to stay focused. Success in sales is about execution - and the best way to execute is to prepare diligently, every single time.”

content:
Five common interview questions and what a great answer looks like:

1) “What would your manager say is your biggest weakness?”

This one is all about EQ. Do you recognize your gaps?

A bad answer is a humble brag: “My biggest weakness is I work so hard sometimes I forget to unplug.”

A great answer identifies:

- A real gap
- How you are closing the gap
- The progress you have made


2) “What achievement are you most proud of?”

This question measures talent, effort, and grit.

My favorite answers have often been outside of work accomplishments (1st generation college grad, working through school to graduate debt free, etc.)

A great answer showcases your ability to accomplish special outcomes even in adverse environments.


3) “How would you describe the value of the products we sell?”

This question measures two areas:

- Your research/understanding of the job
- Your ability to sell value instead of features

A great answer includes the value of the solution for different personas. For example, the value of LaunchDarkly for engineers, VP of Eng, and CTOs.

A poor answer is a description of what the product is or what the product does.

“LaunchDarkly makes sure you rollback release issues before your customers notice them” is a better answer than “LaunchDarkly is an easy-to-use feature flagging tool.”


4) “Tell me about a time you failed. What went wrong?”

A great answer includes something that actually went wrong, a willingness to take ownership, and how you worked to fix the situation.

A bad answer puts the blame entirely on someone else and/or no attempt at resolution.


5) “What questions do you have?”

Possibly the most important question of the interview. How you ask questions in the interview tells me a lot about how you run discovery.

Great questions are ones that you would not be able to learn on your own and show that you did your research.

I’m not gonna give all the answers to the “test,” but I hope this is helpful to those of you interviewing!

content:
The typical (broken) discovery goes like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and small talk

- Next ten minutes: Superficial discussion of the buyer’s day-to-day

- Next ten minutes: Seller shares high-level overview of product. 

Twenty-five minutes into a thirty minute call and almost no progress is made. The seller barely knows anything about the buyer. The buyer barely knows anything about the seller’s product. 

The final few minutes become a mad scramble for the seller to find something valuable enough to earn another call, but most discoveries end with the buyer saying, “Can you send me a case study and more information so we can review and get back to you?”

A great discovery looks like this:

- First five minutes: Intros and objective set

- Next five minutes: Point-of-view validated (or corrected) and priorities confirms

- Next ten minutes: Deep discovery of how the buyer is approaching their priorities

- Last ten minutes: Seller shares how they can help accomplish priorities and next steps for evaluation finalized

I recently published a new no-cost guide to help sellers run great discovery.

The more I’ve thought about this, the more confident I am in my response:

Top performers take complete ownership of their development.

3) Learn how to do deep discovery, quickly

Most discovery calls spend 20+ minutes on superficial conversation. Great discovery calls get to priorities in the first few minutes. 

Bringing a point of view of business objectives + team objectives will help you quickly narrow to priorities.

content:
This morning, I read travel advice from a respected “influencer.” I applied it today, and it was a disaster.

Each bullet point is the advice Jen Allen-Knuth gave. My experience follows in-line:


1) “Stand Up As Soon As The Flight Lands. Immediately. Don't hesitate. There are prizes waiting outside for the first person to deplane.”

I stood up even before the flight landed to make sure I was first off. Literally stood in the doorway as flight attendants yelled at me while I waited for the door to open. 

I burst out as soon as it opened. Turns out the “prize” is a security escort and potentially losing the right to book future flights. 

Lame.


2) “Always Pack Tuna Fish & Hard-Boiled Eggs. Flights are strenuous. Protein is essential. Your seatmates will respect you for your commitment to health.”

People complained and they took away my snack. Yes, the flight was strenuous. Yes, protein is essential. I took Jen’s advice and ended up strained and hungry. 

3) “Don't Wait For The Row In Front Of You To Deplane. You paid for this flight. You deserve to go first. You are important.”

This is really good advice and all went well from my perspective. Guess even a broken clock is right twice a day.

4) “Put Your Backpacks & Small Bags In The Overhead Bins. Those announcements asking you to place those items under the seat in front of you aren't for you. You have special privileges!”

Someone put their big heavy suitcase on my snack bag and the aforementioned tuna fish/hard-boiled eggs got squished and leaked everywhere. If it was your suitcase, and you are reading this, please DM me your apology. 

 5) “Always Talk to Your Seatmates. Don't worry if they have headphones on. They're just shy. If they can't hear you, tap them on the shoulder. Everyone likes the gentle touch of a stranger.”

I traded for a middle seat to take full advantage of this. No one around me wanted to buy my ebooks. I even threw in some discounts and no movement. When I asked, “What if I offered the gentle touch of a stranger?” I was threatened. This advice from Jen seems unsafe. 

Anyhow, just a reminder to be careful who you listen to on this platform. Even people with large followings might give terrible advice.

I remember my friends waiting for me after hours, and celebrating with me that 1) I didn’t finish at $0, and 2) I wasn’t on a PIP.

Sometimes it’s the little things. 

Following that quarter, I doubled down on effort: No one had higher prospecting activity than me.

I doubled down on development: I consumed content from Gong’s research, read the Challenger Sale, and built myself trainings to reinforce those learnings.

I doubled down on ownership: Success or failure was up to me, and I was going to have to accept responsibility for either outcome.

Following that quarter, I only missed once more as an AE (finished at 91% in a quarter two years later).

The trainings I built for myself evolved into trainings I shared with my team.

Trainings I shared with my team became standard for our entire sales org.

Then, I took the best of my learnings from five consecutive President’s Clubs and packaged them into Frameworks that have helped over 4,000 sellers sell more and promote faster.

content:
One of my favorite leader development exercises is “Start, Stop, Continue.”

I meet with the AEs, without their leader present, and we discuss what they want their manager to start, stop, and continue doing.

I’ve run dozens of these. Here are the most impactful “stops” and “continues” I hear:

Stop:

1) Holding “check-the-box” meetings

AEs can’t stand pointless or extended meetings. If there isn’t a meaningful agenda for a recurring meeting (like team meetings) cut it short or cut it out.

2) Accountability to worthless metrics

AEs tolerate metrics that matter. AEs hate reporting on and being held accountable to metrics that don’t impact their success.

3) Sugarcoating the suck

AEs know when company changes aren’t in their favor. Managers lose trust and credibility when they sugarcoat those changes and try to make them seem like a good thing.

Sometimes changes are necessary but unfavorable. Call it what it is and rally the team around reality instead of fluff.


Continue:

1) Caring personally

I love it when AEs tell me they know their manager cares about them as a person. A lot of leadership mistakes are forgiven when they trust your intent.

2) Developing/coaching

Reps are hungry for improvement and love to work with leaders that help them get better.

3) Fostering peer learning environment

Great managers know they don’t have to teach everything. Instead, they create an environment where everyone shares best practices in meetings, slack channels, and one-off mentorship conversations.

I’ve been lucky to work with great leaders throughout my entire career. I hope the feedback shared by their teams is as helpful for you as it’s been for me!

“People hate being sold, but... please follow a rigid sales process that makes people feel like they are being sold."

Yikes.

IMO, this is the biggest misalignment in sales.

Don’t get me wrong: I love sales process. Companies need to teach sales process, and AEs need to master sales process.

But the key to becoming a top performer is to be so good at sales process that you can adapt it to win. 

Here's one simple tweak to get you started:

Stop thinking, "How do I get my buyer to the next step in the sales process?"

Start thinking, "What does my buyer need from me to get to the next stage in their buying process?"

Sure, this may mean you give pricing before discovery. Could mean you show a bit of a demo on the first call.

Great sales process + buyer-centric flexibility is hard to beat.

Supporting your buyer on their journey may lead to "breaking" all sorts of rules.

But I'd rather break some rules and win instead of following the rules and lose.

Three mistakes leaders make that kill morale:

1) Criticism without context

Few things are more discouraging than a leader ripping apart someone’s performance without understanding their business.

If you are too detached to know the details, you are too far removed to give detailed criticism.

2) Leaving people thinking, “I suck,” instead of, “Yeah, I can do better!”

Leaders should not only be cheerleaders. Part of the job is to highlight gaps to drive improvement.

But if you leave your team thinking, “Dang, I suck,” they’ll get crushed by teams thinking, “Yeah, I can do better!”

3) Driving accountability while never taking accountability

Every leader makes mistakes. If you rarely (or never) say, “Sorry, I screwed up,” in front of your team, then you are failing at holding yourself accountable.

And few things lose a team’s buy-in faster than seeing a leader who pushes accountability for everyone else while taking none themselves.

Most leaders (myself included) have been guilty of all these. The key is identifying when you fall into these traps and moving forward as an improved leader.

Several years ago, one of the founders of Qualtrics met with the entire sales leadership team. He shared an anecdote from one of our investors. 

He shared: “Everyone is winning right now, and it’s not sustainable. Historically, if we invest in ten companies, we lose money on seven. We break even on two, and we make our money on one.

The following message from the executive has stuck with me: 

“Let’s get it while the getting is good.”

We couldn’t control how long the macro-economic environment would stay hot for tech. But we could take advantage of every good moment through relentless execution. 

The current economic environment isn’t as favorable as it was in the “zero-interest” era. But I’m not going to hit you with the usual “quota attainment is down, deals taking longer” spiel. 

Instead, I’m going to challenge you to think of some reasons why you currently have it good. 

If you’ve got a place to live, people that care about you, and decent health, then you’ve got a lot of good. 

If you’ve got access to the internet, ways to learn, and a desire to get better, you’ve got it good. 

So let’s get it.

content:
Three ways to immediately lose your buyer’s attention:

1) Ask questions you should know the answer to

“How does your company make money?”

“So, what do you do for [company?]”

Your buyer enters the conversation worried you don’t know them well enough to help them.

Questions like these validate that worry and kill your chance at meaningful conversation.


2) Offer a “high-level overview”

Buyers don’t care about the 30,000-foot view. They just want to know if you can help them.

Leave the high-level overview to your website. The longer it takes you to define exactly how you can help your buyer, the less they will pay attention.

3) Generic value statements

“We help you save money!”

“We help you make money!”

“We help you reduce risk!”

Yes, these are value statements. No, they don’t capture attention. Every business claims the same.

Skip the generic value statements and get right to 1) How you are different, 2) Why it matters, and 3) How you can prove it.

Quickly entering a meaningful conversation requires entering with a strong point of view on both the account and the individual.

content:
After reading hundreds of angry LinkedIn posts about outbound approaches, I’ve compiled a list of things sellers should never do:

1) Don’t personalize

Buyers hate being stalked. If your outreach shows you know anything about them, you are creepy.

2) Don’t skip personalization

Buyers hate being one of many on your “list.” You need to research and personalize to stand out from the crowd.

3) Don’t follow-up

If you emailed once and they didn’t answer, then that’s your response. If they were interested, they’d let you know!

4) Don’t don’t follow up

You gotta be persistent! Buyers are busy and appreciate it when you keep them top of mind.

5) Don’t write long emails

Ain’t nobody got time for that.

6) Don’t write short emails

Don’t be lazy - make sure the buyer knows why you’re reaching out and how you can help!

7) Don’t mention competitors

You’ll really make someone mad if you mention you are helping their competitors.

8) Don’t exclude competitors

How will they know you can help if you aren’t working with someone similar? Nothing is more relevant than a competitor’s use case.

9) Don’t reach out on weekdays

Execs are in meetings non-stop during the week. Don’t make their inbox busier than it already is!

10) Don’t reach out on weekends

After a long week of work, why would you think someone wants more work coming their way on a weekend?

11) Don’t cold call

It’s 2024. Everyone hates cold calls.

12) Don’t forget the phone

It’s 2024, the only channel that’s not saturated is the phone. 

I hope this is helpful. Successful outbound is simple - you just need to find a way to follow all of these rules at once, and you’ll have great success.

content:
I remember losing a deal to “status quo” that should have been an easy win.

Nearly everyone loved us. We had a much better product at a similar price point.

Here’s what I missed:

I didn’t understand the political aspect of replacing a solution someone had previously purchased.

One of the key stakeholders had been the champion for the competitive solution. They were responsible for the purchase, and moving to a new solution so soon would be evidence that they had made a bad decision.

I lost because they had enough influence to protect their reputation by blocking our replacement solution.

When replacing an incumbent, be mindful of the politics. Who looks “wrong” if you take out a competitor?

Then, work to paint them in a positive light.

Instead of “You chose the wrong solution, it’s time for the right one.”

Try, “You chose the right solution at the time. Here’s why we have the right solution now.”

Remember: the more you make people look good, the more they’ll root for you to win.

content:
I spent my first two years as an AE making these 5 mistakes. Rarely made quota, no chance at promotion.

Learning to solve them helped me sell more.

Teaching how to solve them has helped thousands of others sell more.

Here they are:

1) Setting an agenda instead of an objective

Earn the right to ask questions by helping your buyer understand what they will get out of the call is more impactful than a generic agenda.

Think: “What will they get out of this?” instead of “How will we spend the time?”


2) Asking, “tell me about your role”

Senior buyers don’t have time/patience to explain their job to you.

If you don’t even know the basics of their role, why would they trust your recommendations?

3) Pretending to understand

Buyers lose trust when you act like you understand and they know you don’t.

Instead of, “Yeah, that makes sense,” be willing to say, “I didn’t completely follow… can we go deeper into [reframe their words].

4) Overwhelming with irrelevant complexity

Showing unnecessary functionality makes your solution seem expensive, regardless of the price.

When planning your demos ask, “How would my customer use this?” for every feature you’ll show. If you don’t know, don’t show it.

5) Negotiating price before finalizing scope

Negotiating at the wrong time is a sure way to reduce your deal size.

If pressed, just say: “We’ll work with you to ensure a mutually beneficial agreement. To prevent unnecessary back and forth, let’s finalize exactly what we’re going to be providing your team and then we can hammer out the financial details.”
