content:
Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about database maintenance. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to maintain the database. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

content:
Struggling with getting next steps with an opportunity? Stop adding to your buyer's plate.

Here’s what adding to their plate looks like:

"It's been a bit since we last connected. Can we find time to discuss what's changed on your end?"

This request puts all the effort on the buyer. They’d need to find time to update you on things they already know *just in case* you can help them.

Email deleted.

Here’s what removing things from their plate looks like:

"It's been a bit since we last connected. If you are anything like similar companies, you are likely working through [priority 1, 2, 3].

I've attached a hypothesis of how we could help in those areas - if I'm not completely off base, could we find some time to discuss in more depth?"

This request shows your willingness to make their job easier. You'll stand out even if your hypothesis isn’t completely accurate.

Many people treat their inbox as a “to-do” list. When a seller adds to that list, it’s the easiest email to ignore.

Turn your outreach into a “look what I did for you - imagine how much more I could help with your input,” and you’ll see higher buyer engagement.

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal.

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down.

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

What’d I miss?

content:
A few years ago, all revenue was good revenue. 

Now, revenue leaders think about revenue through several different layers:

- Will it renew or am I buying churn?
- Will it expand or am I overpaying to acquire? 
- Will it close quickly enough to keep reasonable payback periods for sales? 

As if sales weren’t hard enough already. 

To ensure success across all layers, I focus on two metrics for territory management:

1) Total addressable market (TAM)

TAM tells me the long-term potential of an account. Since my organization usually follows a land and expand motion, it’s critical we close initial deals in accounts where meaningful expansion can follow. 

TAM is the easier of the two metrics to pull from data. At LaunchDarkly, I look at the number of developers and applications to infer potential spend. 

2) Propensity 

Propensity tells me how likely a company is to purchase. Like most companies, I don’t have a massive sales organization that can chase down all high TAM accounts. Since coverage is limited, I don’t want to chase high TAM accounts that are unlikely to purchase while high TAM accounts that are likely to purchase sit uncovered.

Some of my favorite signals to calculate propensity:

- Funding
- Current tech stack
- Hiring engineers with relevant skills 
- Product usage (our free product or trials of our paid products)
- Mentions on community platforms, social platforms, and forums

That's why I'm so bullish on platforms like Common Room. They pull signals across first, second, and third-party sources to increase the volume of prospects your team can call while maintaining (or improving!) the quality of prospects, the relevance of your message, and conversion across sales stages.

That way, you don’t have to choose between TAM or propensity. 

And all the revenue you close will be good revenue. 

I know I’ve got some people in my network that love signals - what are some of your favorites?

Recently, a vendor offering a potentially interesting service sent me a request for a meeting.

I encouraged them to research my current state (there are plenty of public resources for this) and come back with more details on how they can help me.

They responded, “Well, that’s what the call would be for.”

Here’s the problem:

Buyers only take discovery calls if they are confident you can help them. I was curious enough to respond, but I needed to be more confident that they could help before committing to a meeting.

My ask was that they take some time to develop a more researched point of view before we spoke.

Buyers don’t want to schedule discovery calls to educate you. They want to learn quickly and easily if you can help them.

If you aren’t willing to put in the work upfront to make a buyer confident you can help them, you won’t find many willing to “jump on a call” to figure it out with you.

content:
"We don’t have any budget” is not what you want to hear at the start of a demo.

In this case, it wasn’t a surprise. I had been working with a transparent buyer, and our solution wasn’t a planned expense.

30 minutes after we ended the demo, he sent me an email:

“We need to get access to this right away. I’ll figure out the budget - when can we talk commercials?”

Here’s how we went from “no money” to “we’ll find money” in one call:

1) Identified one big win for each individual on the call

I prepared for the call by understanding how each attendee would “win” with our solution.

Then, I highlighted those wins in the demo.

You get incredible momentum when 100% of demo attendees are excited about your solution and slacking their boss to let them know.
​
​2) Dragged them through the glass

We tied one of our biggest differentiators to their biggest pain.

After walking them through the functionality, we asked the question that likely won the deal:

“I’m curious - how would you create this outcome today?”

The answer was exactly what we needed:

“We couldn’t. There aren’t enough hours in the day to accomplish this with our current system.”
​
3) One more big dose of pain:

“Hmm… you had mentioned earlier that a key objective for your team was [x]. How will you hit that critical objective if you can’t accomplish what I just showed you?”

(Deep breath) “We won’t.”

If you find big enough problems, your buyer will find budget to solve them.

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

“Makes perfect sense you’ve already got a handle on this. Usually this means you’ve got a similar solution in place and I didn’t do a good job sharing how we are different, or you are attacking this priority through a completely different approach.

Can I ask where you fall?”

Next time you hear “this isn’t a priority” to something that you know should be a priority, give this a shot!

My most popular framework is my “Good Day Framework.”

Done right, it will give you complete predictability for what you need to do each day to hit quota. 

After a few months of using the “Good Day Framework” you should know exactly how many points per day you need to have success.

Here are the data points you need (preferably over at least a three-month period):

Total points earned
Total opportunities created
Average deal size
Win rate

Now, some very easy math to figure out exactly how to hit quota:

1) Average points needed to create an opportunity

How to calculate: Total points earned / Total opportunities created

Example seller: 510 points earned in a quarter / 22 opportunities created = 23.2 points required to create one opportunity.

2) Opportunities needed to hit quota

How to calculate: Quota / average deal size / win rate

Example seller: $150k quota / $27k avg deal size / 30% win rate = 18.5 opportunities needed to hit quota.

3) Points needed to hit quota

How to calculate: Opportunities needed to hit quota x Average points needed to create an opportunity

Example seller: 18.5 opportunities needed x 23.2 avg points = 429.2 points needed

4) Daily points needed

How to calculate: Points needed to hit quota / working days in a quarter (account for holidays and PTO)

Example seller: 429.2 points needed / 55 working days in a quarter = 7.8 points each day.


Start tracking with the “Good Day Framework” today, and soon you’ll have a very strong idea of what you need to do every single day to hit (and exceed) quota.

6) Abandoning discovery

Discovery is not a sales process stage - it should continue through contract signature (and beyond).

7) Negotiating price before finalizing scope

Negotiating at the wrong time is a sure way to reduce your deal size.

content:
My first visit to Chicago was for an onsite demonstration to a candy company.

Flew out at the end of December (it was freezing: negative 10 degrees).

I had arranged the last-minute trip because there was a good chance of closing the deal before the end of the year, and I needed it to hit my quota.

The demo went well. I earned consensus in the room that they would move forward. Confirmed with my champion that we could get it done before the end of the year.

Barely got out of Chicago before a massive storm hit (I remember the flight attendant yelling at us to get seated quickly because “If we don’t get out in the next 15 minutes, we aren’t getting out today!”)

My champion emailed me on the 31st. I was sitting in a parking lot when I read, “Everyone is really excited. Mark is out of the country and won’t be able to sign until the first week of January - sorry for the delay.”

That really sucked.

I had built up this cool story in my mind about how, when quota was in doubt, I jumped on a plane and made it happen.

Instead, I jumped on a plane, did everything I possibly could to hit my goal, and still fell short.

I didn’t realize it at the time (I was too upset), but this experience taught me one of the most important lessons of my career:

You can do absolutely everything right and still lose.

Since then, I’ve learned to never get upset as long as two things are true:

1) We make a good plan
2) We execute the plan well

When those are true, we win more than we lose and losing has less of a sting.

Regardless of how 2024 has started for you, go make a good plan for the rest of the year, do the best you can to execute, and I’ll bet on your success.

Years ago, our top enterprise rep taught me the first thing to do when you get an inbound is to go outbound. Here’s why:

Executive priorities lead to department goals.

Department goals lead to team projects.

Team projects lead to needing new tools.

And needing new tools lead to inbound demo requests.

His lesson was the minute you get an inbound, you know there’s likely an executive priority.

While the competition waited to talk to the project team, he was working to get intel (and mindshare) with the executive team.

If I did this today, here’s what my executive outreach would look like after getting an inbound:

“Looking forward to meeting with [name] in [department] this week.

When companies reach out to us, they are often working to solve for [insert common problems you solve].

I’d hate to waste any of our time discussing solutions that don’t map back to company priorities. Which of the above problems are top of mind for you? Anything you’d add?”

Worst case is they ignore you or respond with, “Please talk to [name], they’ll have details.”

Best case is they validate their priority and you’ve opened up a line of communication with an executive weeks (or months) before your competitor does.


p.s. This was internally called “The Marcov” approach, and is credited to Richard Marcov!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 year ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

content:
As a new AE I'd get excited when my prospect listed their requirements and we met them all.

"We can do ALL of that!" I'd think.

I'd show them the demo, commit the deal to my manager (after all, I showed them all the things), and prepare the proposal.

Then, I lost deal after deal with my prospect saying, "Your competitor also meets our requirements and they cost 40% less."

The problem with buyer requirements is they are basic.

The problem with basic is all of your competitors offer the same.

The problem with all competitors offering the same requirements is it becomes purely about price.

So, unless you sell the cheapest product, you lose.

Everything changed when I learned a technique called "trap-setting."

In it's most basic form, trap-setting is influencing your buyer's requirements to include your product's differentiators.

Done right, it disqualifies your competition because your buyer understands their success is best met through capabilities unique to your solution.

Here's how to run this play:

1) Define your differentiators

Identify your differentiators across three types:

- Unique (features only you provide)

- Comparative (features you share with the competition that you do better)

- Holistic (company advantages, e.g., more engineers which lets you innovate faster)

2) Defend your differentiators

For unique differentiators, you’ll need to defend why your company took a different approach than the competition and the value it will bring your customer.

For comparative, you must define why it’s better and matters.

For holistic, establish why these advantages would give your customer peace of mind (think: how does this de-risk our solution?)

You should introduce unique and comparative differentiators early in the sales process.

Here’s one way to introduce on a discovery call after your customer describes one of their required capabilities:

“Many customers that require [insert customer required capability] also require [insert unique or comparative differentiator].

They’ve found that without that capability they [insert negative consequence].”

Holistic differentiators are best at the end of the deal cycle. Use them to give your customer confidence they are partnering with the right company, not just purchasing the right product.

Effective trap-setting takes preparation and planning, but few things in sales are more fun than disqualifying your competition from consideration.

content:
I’ve sat on hundreds of discovery calls in my career - many feel uncomfortable until a key shift occurs.

The tension comes from buyer skepticism:

- Does this rep know anything about me?

- Are they going to push me to buy, even if it’s not a fit?

Two ways to remove this tension:

1) Ask questions that show you understand your buyer

Instead of:

“Tell me about your role.”

Try:

“Many [insert role] we are working with are focused on improving [key priority]. How are you approaching this opportunity?”


2) Empower the “no”

Instead of:

“Thanks for taking the time to help me understand your business today. Let’s find 30 minutes to dive deeper into how we might be able to help.”

Try:

“Based on our conversation today, we may be able to help you improve [outcome] by improving how you approach [use case].

If we were to continue the conversation, we’d be sharing in more depth our approach to driving [outcome] through [how you improve their current state].

Last thing we want to do is waste either of our time pursuing a non-priority. Is [outcome] enough of a priority to warrant further discussion?”

Fair or not, buyers enter sales conversations with skepticism.

Try these tactics to reduce that skepticism, and you’ll find your discovery calls turning into conversations.

content:
10 unsolicited pieces of career advice from a guy that’s seen acquisitions, IPOs, and works for a best-in-class tech company:

1) Your career won’t grow faster than your company.

2) If execs are constantly defending your product as a “need-to-have” then your product is a nice-to-have.

3) If you want a company that has great processes, join one that hasn’t changed in years. Otherwise, accept that growth means chaos.

4) Changing jobs every 18 months will increase your short-term earnings. Staying long enough to actually get good will increase your career earnings.

5) Obsess over finding something you can be the “best” at. If you don’t have a superpower, you are a commodity.

6) Your company’s goal is to retain you at the lowest possible cost to the business. If you feel you are worth more, ask for more.

7) If you can’t find a company to pay you what you think you are worth then you have either a value problem or a messaging problem.

8) There are no short-cuts but there are accelerators.

9) No matter your career path, learn to sell.

10) No matter your career path, learn to write.

It sucks to think you are winning a deal at the end of a cycle and you hear “we’re going to take a look at a few more of your competitors.”

1) Find out how the other vendors were picked to participate

Ask: “Those are some great companies with slightly different approaches.

This will give insight into the evaluation criteria of the team.


2) Uncover the gaps in your offering worrying your contact

Ask: “Sometimes companies are added to an evaluation process because you didn’t see or experience something early in the process with us.

What might we be missing that would be important to your success?”

When the evaluation process shifts, it's a great time to re-calibrate and determine where you stand.


3) Understand how their evaluation process changed after meeting with the other vendors

Ask: “Now that you’ve seen other approaches to your problem, how have your priorities changed?”

The other teams will try and set traps against you by influencing the evaluation process.

This question helps you keep up when your customer shifts.


What do you like to uncover when the competitive landscape gets bigger?

My quota in my third quarter as an AE was $50,000.

On the last day of the quarter, I was stuck at $0. It'd be pretty cool to tell you how I pulled in a big deal to save my quarter and never missed again, but that's not my story.

I also didn't end at zero. I went HARD at a $7,000 upgrade from a $3,000 pilot I had sold the previous quarter to a regional bakery.

Thanks to that bakery, I ended at 14% of quota instead of 0%.

I remember sending a Gchat to my manager: "Am I going to be put on a PIP?" His (delayed) response was that he needed to talk to me at the end of the day.

Fortunately for me, that ended up being a very positive meeting. We agreed on metrics I needed to hit the following quarter, but he shared his confidence in me.

I ended up hitting quota the following quarter. The quarter after that, I pulled in a late deal that put me far enough over quota to earn a promotion.

The quarter after my promotion, I hit 91% of quota.

Then, I never missed again as an AE.

While my results picked up, my confidence lagged. I spent a while on my first stage:

"I'm so bad I'm going to get fired."

After a few quarters of success, my second stage arrived:

"Maybe I can actually be an average rep."

It was several years before my confidence reached the level of "maybe I can accomplish something special."

I'm sharing this because many reading this are earlier in their careers.

Maybe you are worried you are about to be put on a PIP.

Maybe you are just hoping to be an average AE someday.

Or maybe you are starting to catch some momentum and thinking, "This may actually go somewhere."

My message for today is simple: where you are on your journey today has little to do with where you end up... as long as you keep moving.

As an AE, I spent months trying to get into an account at “senior” levels. No one responded.

I started reaching out to entry-level professionals. One agreed to meet.

I could have quickly disqualified them as they were clearly not the right contact. Fortunately, I still decided to run a full discovery.

They gave me insight into a C-Level goal (NPS at 60 by 2021) and a breakdown of internal systems.

Using this information, I created a business case for how we could help them achieve that goal within their current internal systems.

Sent a message to the CEO with the subject line, “NPS to 60 by 2021?” and attached my business case for how we could help. He responded immediately, and we kicked off the evaluation.

Here’s the lesson: stop thinking that initial conversations are only valuable if they convert into an opportunity.

Your first conversation with an account is probably not with your eventual buyer. If you worry only about “converting” the opportunity, you’ll leave the call without being any closer.

Shift your mindset from “how can I qualify an opportunity” to “how can I better learn the value I can add to this company,” and you’ll end up with the strongest opportunities of your career.

If you show too much of your solution, you lose because you are too expensive.

If you show too little, you lose because you don't meet buyer needs.

It's the ultimate demo dilemma. But I've got the three-step fix:

1) Don't oversell basic features

The buyer needs to know you can do it. You don't have to act "proud" of it.

2) Expose a bigger problem

Small problems get fixed with basic solutions. Basic solutions are cheap.

Either discount deeply or attach to a bigger problem.

Anything in the middle = closed/lost.


3) Tie your differentiators to the bigger problem

Bigger problem + differentiators that solve that problem = a solution worth a premium.

content:
Struggling to set meetings?

Try my three-step framework to make sure you are using the right messaging, with the right contacts, within your best accounts.

Here are the questions to answer:

1) Are you calling the right accounts?

Here’s what to make sure you are focused on the right companies:

- Potential budget

Are they investing in areas tied to your solution?

For example, at LaunchDarkly, we look for companies that are hiring developers.

Hiring developers = releasing software = spending money on releasing fast without risk. 

- Use case

Are there multiple landing spots for your product?

For example, at Qualtrics I focused on accounts that needed to understand brand, customer, and product experience. Three different use cases = three shots to win business at the account.

- Personal Familiarity

Massive budget and multiple use cases won’t help you land an account if you can’t speak their language.

Simple question to ask yourself: “If I was in a room with their executive team, could I have a conversation about their business, in their language, without being completely out of place?”

Good accounts that you understand are better targets than great accounts that you don’t understand.


2) Are you calling the right contacts?


Two questions to ask about the contacts in your sequences:

- Would this person personally benefit from our solution?

- Is this person at all responsible for solving the business pain our solution solves?

No personal benefit = no reason for them to respond.

No connection to business pain = no reason for you to want them to respond.


3) Messaging

Two points I’m looking for in effective messaging:

- Emotional relevance

What is the email/phone call your buyer never wants to get from their boss? If your email shows them a way to avoid that dreaded call, it’s emotionally relevant.

- Specificity

Could you write the same email to a different person? Or, worse, could your competitor send the same email to your buyer?

If the answer to either of those questions is “yes,” your messaging isn’t specific enough.


Meetings are tough to come by right now. But it’s hard to go wrong if you use the right messaging, with the right people, within the right accounts.

content:
“Sales math” used to be simple. Just get your conversion rates for:

Cold outreach -> initial meeting

Initial meeting -> opportunity

Opportunity -> closed won

Throw in average deal size, and you could reverse engineer exactly how many cold calls/emails you need to hit quota.

Now, the math is breaking.

Conversion rates (especially at top of funnel) have gotten so low that this “sales math” leads to impossible to reach volume metrics.

Where 200-400 activities used to generate an opportunity, we now see 1,300+.

So sales reps (and sales leaders) that made a living off of “Well, we’ll just have to do more” are left without a viable answer.

Instead, we need to get hyper-focused on conversion rates:

Less, “Make more calls” and more “Improve the quality of our call list.”

Less, “You need more meetings” and more “How are we making the most of each meeting?”

Quantity will always matter - great conversion across a tiny sample size is a losing strategy. 

But volume alone isn’t leading any company to sustainable revenue. 

I asked eleven top-performing AEs to summarize how they are having success in this “new age” of selling.

Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!’) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about building feature flags. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to build internal tooling. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

content:
If I could only teach three principles to help sales teams sell more, I’d hammer home these points:

1) If you are still searching for pain in your second discovery call, you’ve lost.

Great initial discovery uncovers the biggest problems your buyer needs to solve, and why they haven’t yet been solved.

If your second discovery is still trying to find a big problem you aren’t going to get a third call.


2) Negative consequences are not a description of what’s going wrong. They are a definition of why what’s going wrong matters.

- “We are spending too much money”
- “Employees are wasting their time”
- “We have data silos”

So what?

Every company has areas where they spend too much money, employees waste time, and have data silos.

Keep asking, “so what?” until everyone agrees the problem is big enough to solve now.


3) When required capabilities are only defined by the customer, the lowest cost solution will win.

When customers form their shopping list, they default to widely available capabilities.

Widely available capabilities are met by all of your competitors.

Either influence the required capabilities in your favor, or make sure you are the cheapest proposal.

Otherwise, closed/lost.

Which of these lessons resonate with you?

content:
Stop asking your buyer to quantify their pain as a way to identify urgency early in the deal cycle.

It’s salesy and the numbers are all made up.

Instead, ask “how else have you tried to solve this problem?”

If they haven’t been actively trying to solve the problem, you haven’t identified a real pain.***

If they have been trying (and failing) to solve the problem, you are on the right track.

Save quantifying pain for when you are building a business case with your champion.

Use the “how else have you tried to solve this problem?” question to see if it’s worth your time to build a business case.




***Like everything, there are exceptions to the “if they aren’t trying to solve it today it’s not a problem” concept. Sometimes you teach the buyer about an unforeseen future problem or expose a massive problem they aren’t aware of yet. However, this rule will frequently help you qualify if an opportunity is worth pursuing.

content:
A few years ago, I went into our end-of-year leadership planning sessions hoping to land a second-line leadership role. I had the metrics to justify a promotion, I just needed an opening. 

To kick off the session, our SVP ran the most transparent org chart exercise I’ve ever seen. He put the proposed leadership structure in front of the entire team, and highlighted all of the open roles. 

As he introduced each role, he asked anyone interested to raise their hand. If you raised your hand, you’d be entered into the interview process for the role. 

He went through around eight roles, many of them second-line opportunities. All of them were “promotions” from my level. All of my peers raised their hands for at least one of the roles, some of them entered the interview process for multiple. 

I didn’t raise my hand for any of them. While they were all promotions, none of them were the right fit for what I wanted my next step to look like. 

After the session my manager asked why I didn’t pursue any of the openings. I said, “My goal is to get into second-line leadership as soon as possible, but none of these roles seem right. I’ll keep running my team until a second-line role opens up that is a better fit.”

Interviews were conducted over the next week and the org chart was finalized. I was ready for another year running my awesome team as a front-line manager. 

Then, a few weeks later, I got a life-changing call the day before Thanksgiving:

“We’ve made some changes to our strategy for next year. How would you feel about moving to Chicago?” 

The ideal role for me had opened. Instead of promoting into a different business unit, I was able to promote members of our team to grow into a region. We had an incredible run and I enjoyed some of the best quarters of my career. 

Looking back now, waiting for the “right” job has had a much bigger impact on my career than just those couple of years:

It forced a move to Chicago that never would have happened without this “perfect” role.

Moving to Chicago opened up an opportunity at MongoDB a couple of years later. 

My experience at MongoDB opened up the opportunity to run a global sales org at LaunchDarkly. 

And it all started by saying “No thanks” to potential promotions that didn’t fit what I wanted to do with my career. 

You should always be thinking about your next career step. Just remember: a bigger job doesn’t always mean the right job. 

And if you say yes to the wrong job, you may not get the opportunity to pursue the right one.

content:
Poor territory management sinks even the best sales reps. Here are my three rules to help you get territory management right:

1) Ongoing, not static

Reps should have smaller territories so they can focus attention. 

Then, when AEs uncover details that make an assigned account a poor fit, replace it with another high-potential account. 

If a territory is too big, AEs will be pulled thin.

If it's too static, AEs will spin their wheels in poor-fit accounts. 

I've found focused but evolving territories most effective for all but strategic account segments. 

2) Accounts belong to the company, not the rep

High-potential accounts with unengaged reps are a massive waste of territory. If a rep doesn't give an account the attention it deserves, leaders should move it to a rep who will. 

I've seen "stagnant" accounts turn into six-figure wins by moving an account to a rep willing to do the work. 

3) Balance propensity and TAM

A territory full of potential whales is a slog - reps may work for quarters without closing a deal and getting paid.

A territory full of small transactions is a drain—reps will be on a hamster wheel, unable to focus on significant revenue opportunities. 

Great territory build requires understanding what drives TAM for your product (hint: it's not just revenue and the number of employees) and using tools like Common Room to uncover propensity to buy via mentions, signals, multi-threading, etc., across different sources. 

Accurate TAM projections + understanding buying propensity = balanced and scalable territory management. 

Any other territory management rules you have seen drive success?

content:
The most uncomfortable call of my career (35 seconds of silence felt like 5 minutes) taught me two important lessons about negotiation.

Here’s the story:

I had a great relationship with my main contacts at an account. We had worked together for over a year, and they were planning on significantly expanding their agreement with us.

Because the license was expanding, they looped in a new stakeholder that I had never met.

This individual’s only goal was to get the lowest cost possible.

We got on a call, and the tone was completely different. The new contact went on the offensive and listed their demands.

The requests were unreasonable. Since I was confident in our solution and the value of our partnership, my response was:

“We’ve been working closely with the team for several months to right-size the agreement and to ensure that the value warrants the investment. While I appreciate your goal is to get the lowest price possible, your requests aren’t reasonable, and we cannot consider them.”

Then, I shut up.

There was silence for what felt like forever (the call recording showed it was only about 35 seconds), and the contact finally said, “Ok. We’ll need to discuss internally.”

The call ended, and we received a signed contract for the proposed amount a few days later.

While uncomfortable in the moment, I learned two essential negotiation lessons:

1) Silence is ok

Be confident, communicate clearly and don’t over-explain. Then, shut up.

2) Saying “no” is ok

When you are close to a deal, it’s tempting to remove all friction by accepting all requests thrown your way.

Don’t. Be confident in your value, and say “no” when a request isn’t reasonable.

content:
Saying, “yep, that makes sense,” is killing your discovery.

Here’s my favorite coaching method to help reps fix:

When reviewing calls, if I hear a rep say, “that makes sense,” I’ll pause the recording and ask, “did that actually make sense to you?”

9 times out of 10 they’ll laugh and say “no.” It was just more comfortable to move on rather than admitting confusion.

Think about how this feels as a buyer:

1) They just walked you through a complicated problem.

2) They know they didn’t explain it clearly because it’s difficult to put into words.

And they get hit with a, “yep - that makes sense!” in response?

How are they going to believe you have a solution for them if they can’t even believe you understand their problem?

Good sellers have no problem asking for clarification.

Great sellers refuse to move on in a conversation until they are on the same page as their buyer.

Next time you are tempted to say, “that makes sense,” try, “I’m not sure I’m following. Can you explain…” and you’ll have a more meaningful conversation.

content:
After reading hundreds of angry LinkedIn posts about outbound approaches, I’ve compiled a list of things sellers should never do: 

1) Don’t personalize

Buyers hate being stalked. If your outreach shows you know anything about them, you are creepy. 

2) Don’t be generic 

Buyers hate being one of many on your “list.” You need to research and personalize to stand out from the crowd. 

3) Don’t follow-up

If you emailed once and they didn’t answer, then that’s your response. If they were interested, they’d let you know! 

4) Don’t don’t follow up 

You gotta be persistent! Buyers are busy and appreciate it when you keep them top of mind. 

5) Don’t write long emails 

Ain’t nobody got time for that.

6) Don’t write short emails 

Don’t be lazy - make sure the buyer knows why you’re reaching out and how you can help! 

7) Don’t mention competitors 

You’ll really make someone mad if you mention you are helping their competitors.

8) Don’t exclude competitors 

How will they know you can help if you aren’t working with someone similar? Nothing is more relevant than a competitor’s use case. 

9) Don’t reach out on weekdays

Execs are in meetings non-stop during the week. Don’t make their inbox busier than it already is! 

10) Don’t reach out on weekends 

After a long week of work, why would you think someone wants more work coming their way on a weekend?


I hope this is helpful. Successful outbound is simple - you just need to find a way to follow all of these rules at once, and you’ll have great success.

content:
One of my favorite leader development exercises is “Start, Stop, Continue.” 

I meet with the AEs, without their leader present, and we discuss what they want their manager to start, stop, and continue doing. 

I’ve run dozens of these. Here are the most impactful “stops” and “continues” I hear:

Stop:

1) Holding “check-the-box” meetings

AEs can’t stand pointless or extended meetings. If there isn’t a meaningful agenda for a recurring meeting (like team meetings) cut it short or cut it out. 

2) Accountability to worthless metrics

AEs tolerate metrics that matter. AEs hate reporting on and being held accountable to metrics that don’t impact their success. 

3) Sugarcoating the suck

AEs know when company changes aren’t in their favor. Managers lose trust and credibility when they sugarcoat those changes and try to make them seem like a good thing. 

Sometimes changes are necessary but unfavorable. Call it what it is and rally the team around reality instead of fluff. 


Continue:

1) Caring personally

I love it when AEs tell me they know their manager cares about them as a person. A lot of leadership mistakes are forgiven when they trust your intent. 

2) Developing/coaching

Reps are hungry for improvement and love to work with leaders that help them get better. 

3) Fostering peer learning environment 

Great managers know they don’t have to teach everything. Instead, they create an environment where everyone shares best practices in meetings, slack channels, and one-off mentorship conversations. 

I’ve been lucky to work with great leaders throughout my entire career. I hope the feedback shared by their teams is as helpful for you as it’s been for me!

content:
Three mistakes leaders make that kill morale: 

1) Criticism without context

Few things are more discouraging than a leader ripping apart someone’s performance without understanding their business. 

If you are too detached to know the details, you are too far removed to give detailed criticism. 

2) Leaving people thinking, “I suck,” instead of, “Yeah, I can do better!”

Leaders should not only be cheerleaders. Part of the job is to highlight gaps to drive improvement. 

But if you leave your team thinking, “Dang, I suck,” they’ll get crushed by teams thinking, “Yeah, I can do better!” 

3) Driving accountability while never taking accountability 

Every leader makes mistakes. If you rarely (or never) say, “Sorry, I screwed up,” in front of your team, then you are failing at holding yourself accountable. 

And few things lose a team’s buy-in faster than seeing a leader who pushes accountability for everyone else while taking none themselves.

Most leaders (myself included) have been guilty of all these. The key is identifying when you fall into these traps and moving forward as an improved leader.

content:
I spent my first two years as an AE making these 5 mistakes. Rarely made quota, no chance at promotion.

Learning to solve them helped me sell more. 

Teaching how to solve them has helped thousands of others sell more. 

Here they are:

1) Setting an agenda instead of an objective

Earn the right to ask questions by helping your buyer understand what they will get out of the call is more impactful than a generic agenda.

Think: “What will they get out of this?” instead of “How will we spend the time?”


2) Asking, “tell me about your role”

Senior buyers don’t have time/patience to explain their job to you.

If you don’t even know the basics of their role, why would they trust your recommendations?

3) Pretending to understand

Buyers lose trust when you act like you understand and they know you don’t.

Instead of, “Yeah, that makes sense,” be willing to say, “I didn’t completely follow… can we go deeper into [reframe their words].

4) Overwhelming with irrelevant complexity

Showing unnecessary functionality makes your solution seem expensive, regardless of the price.

When planning your demos ask, “How would my customer use this?” for every feature you’ll show. If you don’t know, don’t show it.

5) Negotiating price before finalizing scope

Negotiating at the wrong time is a sure way to reduce your deal size.

If pressed, just say: “We’ll work with you to ensure a mutually beneficial agreement. To prevent unnecessary back and forth, let’s finalize exactly what we’re going to be providing your team and then we can hammer out the financial details.”

content:
One of the first things I was taught as an AE was the importance of multi-threading.

But I wasn’t taught how. So when I tried to do it I failed.

I got frustrated: why would my champion block me?

This post will teach you what took me lots of failure to learn.

First, understand when you ask for introductions, you aren’t just asking them to send a quick email.

You are asking them to bet their credibility on you.

If they connect you with a coworker that doesn’t end up finding value in meeting with you, it reflects poorly on them.

This is magnified at the executive level: no one wants an executive annoyed at them because they wasted their time with a poor sales call!

Here’s my framework for successfully multi-threading with your champion:

1) Build their confidence by always adding value when you meet with them

2) Have a valid and specific reason for your request to meet with new stakeholders

3) Detail what will be expected from all attendees (not just an agenda - specifically what role each attendee will play)

4) Share your plan to make sure it’s a successful meeting


Here’s what the request could look like:

“Linda, it’s been great working with you to identify how LaunchDarkly could help your dev team improve efficiency.

Last thing we’d want to do is begin implementation without a clear picture of how our work would impact the broader engineering org - we want to optimize for the long-term.

Typically the CTO is the best person to speak to long-term architecture goals. We’d love to bring Angela onto the next call to bring her up to speed on our planned implementation to see where she would recommend adjustments.

We don't want to waste her time: we’ll prepare an executive summary she can review before the call so we can make the most of the conversation.

The main feedback we’ll want from her is related to the milestones we’ve discussed - now is the right time to change those definitions or timing.

To ensure the call is successful, we’ll also include an executive from our solution architect team - that way, any questions she has can be addressed during the call.”


Following this approach will increase your champion’s confidence in you, earn an audience with others, and ensure you are ready to make those conversations effective.

No one on your team is as credible to your customer as your champion.

Involve them in call preparation and assign them an active role where you make them look good.

content:
I used to view discovery meetings as pass/fail:

Pass: Right person, right problem, continued conversation with that person. 

Fail: No next steps with that prospect. 

Now, I break successful discovery into two categories:

1) Opportunity progressing discovery

2) Account progressing discovery 

Opportunity progressing discovery means right person, big problem you can solve, and next steps agreed with that individual. 

This is the best outcome, but when it’s an early discovery meeting with an account, it’s unlikely. 

The next best outcome is an account-progressing discovery.

This means you leave the conversation with more knowledge about problems the company is solving, how they are trying to solve them, and gaps in their process. 

You may not have next steps because the person you spoke with isn’t the right person, but you have a stronger point of view. 

And that point of view will get you in front of the right people where you’ll evolve from account progressing discovery to opportunity progressing discovery. 

If you view discovery as pass/fail, you’ll abandon great accounts too soon. 

If you view discovery as an ongoing process for each account, you’ll break into more of your best accounts.

content:
Only hearing good news from your buyer?

Sorry, you are probably losing the deal.

Only hearing good news usually means:

1) Your buyer knows the bad news but won’t tell you.

This is a sign that they either don’t trust you or don’t believe you can help them navigate the curveballs they are seeing.

Either way, they aren’t a champion. And no champion means no deal.


2) Your buyer is too far removed from decision-making to know the concerns.

If your buyer isn’t hearing the concerns, they aren’t influencing the decision.


Next time you have a deal that seems to be nothing but sunshine, slow down and dig for the bad news.

If you still can’t find any, you know you have work to do to earn your buyer's trust or need to go wider in the account.

Here are a couple of questions you could use:

“I know how hard it can be to get everyone on the same page - who do you think is most skeptical of the value our solution can bring?”

“What other business priorities would we be pulling attention from if we moved forward with our solution? Who on your side is pushing to solve those priorities first?”


Find the bad news early, or you'll get bad news late.

content:
Three ways to immediately lose your buyer’s attention:

1) Ask questions you should know the answer to

“How does your company make money?”

“So, what do you do for [company?]” 

Your buyer enters the conversation worried you don’t know them well enough to help them. 

Questions like these validate that worry and kill your chance at meaningful conversation. 


2) Offer a “high-level overview”

Buyers don’t care about the 30,000-foot view. They just want to know if you can help them. 

Leave the high-level overview to your website. The longer it takes you to define exactly how you can help your buyer, the less they will pay attention. 

3) Generic value statements

“We help you save money!”

“We help you make money!”

“We help you reduce risk!” 

Yes, these are value statements. No, they don’t capture attention. Every business claims the same. 

Skip the generic value statements and get right to 1) How you are different, 2) Why it matters, and 3) How you can prove it. 

Quickly entering a meaningful conversation requires entering with a strong point of view on both the account and the individual. 

It used to take hours of research to build a strong point-of-view for an account. 

Now, teams can pull every data point we care about from internal and external sources (job listings, company news, site visits, product usage, social, community channels etc) to form a stronger point-of-view in minutes that actually earns a buyer's attention.

content:
Here’s why you can’t “quantify the pain” early in a deal to drive urgency:

1) Your buyer determines urgency - you don't

Try as we might, we aren't changing our buyer's priorities. Instead, we should map to them.

2) "How much is this problem costing you?" sounds incredibly salesy

Your buyer knows you just want this number to convince them your solution is cheap in comparison to their pain. 

So they aren’t going to put a lot of thought into it. 

3) The numbers are all made up

Early in the deal cycle, quantification is inaccurate. You'll struggle to build a real ROI-based business case until you are deeper in the sales cycle.

While you can’t quantify the pain early, you can see if it’s significant with a simple tweak: 

Instead of asking, “How much is this problem costing you?” Try, “How else have you tried to solve this problem?”

If they haven’t been actively trying to solve the problem, you haven’t identified a real pain. 

You are on the right track if they have been trying (and failing) to solve the problem.

And if you are on the right track, you can quantify the pain when building the business case with your champion.

content:
A decade into my sales career, and I still get just as nervous for big presentations as I did as a new AE.

The difference is that now I have a proven preparation method that guarantees a smooth, confident delivery.

Here’s how I prepare to ensure I perform at my best:
​
​Two days before:​
​
- Review prep materials/research to determine what is top of mind for attendees

The goal is to identify the top outcome they want to drive and the biggest pain they want to solve.

​​
- Identify my one takeaway that ties back to my audience’s “top of mind"

If the audience only remembers one point, what do I need it to be?
​
​

- Build a talk track to emphasize my primary takeaway

They'll forget what they hear while remembering what they feel. I build my talk track around the question, " What do I want them to feel that is associated with my main takeaway?"

​​
​One day before:​
​
- Practice until mostly smooth, with minimal reliance on notes

The timing here is extremely intentional: sleep reinforces learning. One night’s rest between practice and presentation allows my brain to cement the flow.


If I'm 80% polished the day before, simply sleeping and waking up gets me to 95%.

Brain science is cool.


Day of:​
​
- One more walkthrough, with emphasis on tonality (where I want to pause for emphasis, etc.)

At this point, I've mastered the material. I know what I want to say. I just need to polish how I want to say it.

Then, I enter the call with the confidence that stems from preparation.

​
Regardless of your experience or comfort presenting, you should never outgrow the need to practice and prepare.

Next time you have a big presentation, try this framework. I bet you'll deliver a more confident and impactful message.

content:
My career lowlight was being suspended for a day without pay (was close to being fired).

Here's the story:

The company was growing rapidly and we needed a new territory model. The decision was made to deploy territories based on zip codes.

I got a patch of zip codes in suburban Grand Rapids, MI.

In other words, I owned any account in the Grand Rapids area that wasn’t in the city. Nothing against the fine people of suburban Grand Rapids, but my territory sucked. To make matters worse, my friend that sat next to me was assigned to Metro New York.

I spent my days trying to get contact information for companies not even on LinkedIn.

My friend often had multiple inbounds in a single day.

Frustrated, I threw a fit about how the zip code territory was flawed to senior leaders and my peers.

Leadership didn’t love that. Some wanted to fire me.

Fortunately, my boss fought for me. Instead of termination, I was suspended for a day without pay so I could fix my attitude (bless up).

Eventually, the territory model was adjusted, and everyone lived happily ever after.

Here are a few lessons:

1) When things go wrong, be patient and propose solutions instead of throwing a fit.

2) If you want to recommend organizational changes then bring data, not emotion.

3) Vent up - not across. If you are frustrated, talk to your manager. Don’t bring negativity to your peers.

4) Everyone at your company is doing the best they can. Be forgiving of others' errors, and you’ll find people being more forgiving of yours.

p.s. I still haven’t been to Grand Rapids but I absolutely love Michigan now so I think we are on good terms.

content:
My first visit to Chicago was for an onsite demonstration to a candy company.

Flew out at the end of December (it was freezing: negative 10 degrees).

I had arranged the last-minute trip because there was a good chance of closing the deal before the end of the year, and I needed it to hit my quota.

The demo went well. I earned consensus in the room that they would move forward. Confirmed with my champion that we could get it done before the end of the year.

Barely got out of Chicago before a massive storm hit (I remember the flight attendant yelling at us to get seated quickly because “If we don’t get out in the next 15 minutes, we aren’t getting out today!”)

My champion emailed me on the 31st. I was sitting in a parking lot when I read, “Everyone is really excited. Mark is out of the country and won’t be able to sign until the first week of January - sorry for the delay.”

That really sucked.

I had built up this cool story in my mind about how, when quota was in doubt, I jumped on a plane and made it happen.

Instead, I jumped on a plane, did everything I possibly could to hit my goal, and still fell short.

I didn’t realize it at the time (I was too upset), but this experience taught me one of the most important lessons of my career:

You can do absolutely everything right and still lose.

Since then, I’ve learned to never get upset as long as two things are true:

1) We make a good plan
2) We execute the plan well

When those are true, we win more than we lose and losing has less of a sting.

Regardless of how 2024 has started for you, go make a good plan for the rest of the year, do the best you can to execute, and I’ll bet on your success.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 years ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

content:
Five common interview questions and what a great answer looks like:

1) “What would your manager say is your biggest weakness?”

This one is all about EQ. Do you recognize your gaps?

A bad answer is a humble brag: “My biggest weakness is I work so hard sometimes I forget to unplug.”

A great answer identifies:

- A real gap
- How you are closing the gap
- The progress you have made


2) “What achievement are you most proud of?”

This question measures talent, effort, and grit.

My favorite answers have often been outside of work accomplishments (1st generation college grad, working through school to graduate debt free, etc.)

A great answer showcases your ability to accomplish special outcomes even in adverse environments.


3) “How would you describe the value of the products we sell?”

This question measures two areas:

- Your research/understanding of the job
- Your ability to sell value instead of features

A great answer includes the value of the solution for different personas. For example, the value of MongoDB for engineers, VP of Eng, and CTOs.

A poor answer is a description of what the product is or what the product does.

“MongoDB Atlas allows developers to spend time building differentiated products instead of maintaining their database” is a better answer than “MongoDB Atlas is a NoSQL fully-managed database solution.”


4) “Tell me about a time you failed. What went wrong?”

A great answer includes something that actually went wrong, a willingness to take ownership, and how you worked to fix the situation.

A bad answer puts the blame entirely on someone else and/or no attempt at resolution.


5) “What questions do you have?”

Possibly the most important question of the interview. How you ask questions in the interview tells me a lot about how you run discovery.

Great questions are ones that you would not be able to learn on your own and show that you did your research.

I’m not gonna give all the answers to the “test,” but I hope this is helpful to those of you interviewing!

I’ve tried to accelerate deals in many ways:

- Pain amplification (dragging them through the glass)

- Proof of concepts/proof of value

- Discounts (rarely work)

Nothing I’ve tried has ever worked as well as having a true champion sprinting through walls to get the deal done.

Here are my top 3 recommendations for developing champions:

1) Motivate

People act in self-interest. You need to tie your solution to personal wins for your champion – not just company benefits.

2) Mitigate risk

While you excitedly talk about all the things that could go right, they are thinking about what could go wrong and how that would impact them.

3) Help remember and repackage

Even your strongest champions will forget most of what you discuss. Helping them remember key points and package them for other audiences will make it easier for them to champion your solution.

Your ability to build champions will make or break your sales career. If you want a deeper dive into how to execute these three points, take 3 minutes and read this: https://lnkd.in/gURbZ_NJ

content:
I’ve sat on hundreds of discovery calls in my career - many feel uncomfortable until a key shift occurs.

The tension comes from buyer skepticism:

- Does this rep know anything about me?

- Are they going to push me to buy, even if it’s not a fit?

Two ways to remove this tension:

1) Ask questions that show you understand your buyer

Instead of:

“Tell me about your role.”

Try:

“Many [insert role] we are working with are focused on improving [key priority]. How are you approaching this opportunity?”


2) Empower the “no”

Instead of:

“Thanks for taking the time to help me understand your business today. Let’s find 30 minutes to dive deeper into how we might be able to help.”

Try:

“Based on our conversation today, we may be able to help you improve [outcome] by improving how you approach [use case].

If we were to continue the conversation, we’d be sharing in more depth our approach to driving [outcome] through [how you improve their current state].

Last thing we want to do is waste either of our time pursuing a non-priority. Is [outcome] enough of a priority to warrant further discussion?”

Fair or not, buyers enter sales conversations with skepticism.

Try these tactics to reduce that skepticism, and you’ll find your discovery calls turning into conversations.

Recently, a vendor offering a potentially interesting service sent me a request for a meeting. 

I encouraged them to research my current state (there are plenty of public resources for this) and come back with more details on how they can help me.
 
They responded, “Well, that’s what the call would be for.” 

Here’s the problem: 

Buyers only take discovery calls if they are confident you can help them. I was curious enough to respond, but I needed to be more confident that they could help before committing to a meeting. 

My ask was that they take some time to develop a more researched point of view before we spoke. 

They expected that I would take my time to educate them on stuff they could learn on their own. 

Buyers don’t want to schedule discovery calls to educate you. They want to learn quickly and easily if you can help them. 

If you aren’t willing to put in the work upfront to make a buyer confident you can help them, you won’t find many willing to “jump on a call” to figure it out with you.

I spent my first two years as an AE making these 7 mistakes. Rarely made quota, no chance at promotion.

Learning to solve them led to becoming the #1 AE.

Teaching how to solve them helped our team finish #1 in consecutive years.

Here they are:

1) Setting an agenda, instead of an objective

Earn the right to ask questions by helping your buyer understand what they will get out of the call is more impactful than a generic agenda.

2) Asking, “tell me about your role”

Senior buyers don’t have time/patience to explain their job to you.

3) Being afraid to ask for clarification

Buyers lose trust when you act like you understand and they know you don’t.

4) Only matching your buyer’s requirements

Your buyer’s requirements will be met by most solutions in your space. Simply matching leads to a decision made only on price.

5) Overwhelming with irrelevant complexity

Showing unnecessary functionality makes your solution seem expensive.

6) Abandoning discovery

Discovery is not a sales process stage - it should continue through contract signature (and beyond).

7) Negotiating price before finalizing scope

Negotiating at the wrong time is a sure way to reduce your deal size.


You don’t have to spend years learning from these mistakes like I did.

content:
Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about database maintenance. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to maintain the database. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

Years ago, our top enterprise rep taught me the first thing to do when you get an inbound is to go outbound. Here’s why:

Executive priorities lead to department goals. 

Department goals lead to team projects. 

Team projects lead to needing new tools.

And needing new tools lead to inbound demo requests. 

His lesson was the minute you get an inbound, you know there’s likely an executive priority. 

While the competition waited to talk to the project team, he was working to get intel (and mindshare) with the executive team. 

If I did this today, here’s what my executive outreach would look like after getting an inbound:

“Looking forward to meeting with [name] in [department] this week. 

When companies reach out to us, they are often working to solve for [insert common problems you solve].

I’d hate to waste any of our time discussing solutions that don’t map back to company priorities. Which of the above problems are top of mind for you? Anything you’d add?” 

Worst case is they ignore you or respond with, “Please talk to [name], they’ll have details.” 

Best case is they validate their priority and you’ve opened up a line of communication with an executive weeks (or months) before your competitor does.

content:
I have over 100,000 accounts to cover with thirty-seven AEs. I’ll assign fewer than 3,000. 

Here’s how we identify the top 3%:

1) Total Addressable Market (TAM)

We know the average number of developers it takes to build/maintain an application. We also know the average amount spent on a database for an application. 

If we have the number of developers, we can calculate the potential spend of an account. 

It’s better for my team to land a $50,000 license with a $1 million TAM account than a $100,000 license with a $150,000 TAM account. 

Focusing on TAM ensures we acquire the right customers that support long-term growth. 

2) Propensity-to-buy

Higher propensity accounts (showing buying indications) lead to faster sales cycles, which reduce the cost of sale. Lower cost of sale supports improved profitability. 

To flag high-propensity accounts, we obsess over signals that indicate a company may benefit from our solution. 

Some of my favorites:

- Funding
- Current tech stack
- Hiring engineers with relevant skills 
- Product usage (our free product or trials of our paid products)
- Mentions on community platforms, social platforms, and forums

A few years ago, all revenue was good revenue. 

Now, the pressure is on to acquire revenue quickly in high-potential accounts. Combining TAM with propensity supports my organization in achieving this goal. 

I’m grateful to partner with Common Room. They help my team flag high-propensity accounts along with the people behind them so we can have high-value conversations with high-value customers faster.

content:
I remember losing a deal to “status quo” that should have been an easy win. 

Nearly everyone loved us. We had a much better product at a similar price point. 

Here’s what I missed: 

I didn’t understand the political aspect of replacing a solution someone had previously purchased. 

One of the key stakeholders had been the champion for the competitive solution. They were responsible for the purchase, and moving to a new solution so soon would be evidence that they had made a bad decision. 

I lost because they had enough influence to protect their reputation by blocking our replacement solution. 

When replacing an incumbent, be mindful of the politics. Who looks “wrong” if you take out a competitor? 

Then, work to paint them in a positive light. 

Instead of “You chose the wrong solution, it’s time for the right one.” 

Try, “You chose the right solution at the time. Here’s why we have the right solution now.” 

Remember: the more you make people look good, the more they’ll root for you to win.

My quota in my third quarter as an AE was $50,000.

On the last day of the quarter, I was stuck at $0. It'd be pretty cool to tell you how I pulled in a big deal to save my quarter and never missed again, but that's not my story.

I also didn't end at zero. I went HARD at a $7,000 upgrade from a $3,000 pilot I had sold the previous quarter to a regional bakery.

Thanks to that bakery, I ended at 14% of quota instead of 0%.

I remember sending a Gchat to my manager: "Am I going to be put on a PIP?" His (delayed) response was that he needed to talk to me at the end of the day.

Fortunately for me, that ended up being a very positive meeting. We agreed on metrics I needed to hit the following quarter, but he shared his confidence in me.

I ended up hitting quota the following quarter. The quarter after that, I pulled in a late deal that put me far enough over quota to earn a promotion.

The quarter after my promotion, I hit 91% of quota.

Then, I never missed again as an AE.

While my results picked up, my confidence lagged. I spent a while on my first stage:

"I'm so bad I'm going to get fired."

After a few quarters of success, my second stage arrived:

"Maybe I can actually be an average rep."

It was several years before my confidence reached the level of "maybe I can accomplish something special."

I'm sharing this because many reading this are earlier in their careers.

Maybe you are worried you are about to be put on a PIP.

Maybe you are just hoping to be an average AE someday.

Or maybe you are starting to catch some momentum and thinking, "This may actually go somewhere."

My message for today is simple: where you are on your journey today has little to do with where you end up... as long as you keep moving.

“We don’t have any budget” is not what you want to hear at the start of a demo.

In this case, it wasn’t a surprise. I had been working with a transparent buyer, and our solution wasn’t a planned expense.

30 minutes after we ended the demo, he sent me an email:

“We need to get access to this right away. I’ll figure out the budget - when can we talk commercials?”

Here’s how we went from “no money” to “we’ll find money” in one call:

1) Identified one big win for each individual on the call

I prepared for the call by understanding how each attendee would “win” with our solution.

Then, I highlighted those wins in the demo.

You get incredible momentum when 100% of demo attendees are excited about your solution and slacking their boss to let them know.
​
​2) Dragged them through the glass

We tied one of our biggest differentiators to their biggest pain.

After walking them through the functionality, we asked the question that likely won the deal:

“I’m curious - how would you create this outcome today?”

The answer was exactly what we needed:

“We couldn’t. There aren’t enough hours in the day to accomplish this with our current system.”
​
3) One more big dose of pain:

“Hmm… you had mentioned earlier that a key objective for your team was [x]. How will you hit that critical objective if you can’t accomplish what I just showed you?”

(Deep breath) “We won’t.”

If you find big enough problems, your buyer will find budget to solve them.

content:
My team was working on a highly competitive RFP. Imagine our delight when our champion called after the competitor’s demo and said, “Guys, it was a disaster. They quit.”

Here’s the story of how we convinced our biggest competitor to withdraw from the RFP:

The customer was one of the fastest-growing companies in the world. We’d done a good job building champions, driving value, and earning executive buy-in.

Because this was a “must-win” logo, our competitor was trying to “buy the business” by offering everything at a shockingly low price. Their approach was so aggressive that the prospect had to consider their offer.

Part of the RFP process was a Q&A with the evaluation team. This call would have ALL the vendors on simultaneously to ensure an even playing field.

I love the competitive nature of sales. You rarely get the chance to compete in the same arena at the same time, so I was excited.

Our goal for the call was to convince the competitor that they were wasting their time bidding on this deal so we could accelerate our win and preserve value in negotiations by eliminating their lowball offer.

Here’s how we stacked the deck in our favor:

- Identified our primary differentiators compared to our main competitor

- Tied those differentiators to the outcomes the customer had prioritized

- Met with our champion to confirm they agreed those differentiators were critical


Procurement kicked off the call with us, our buying committee, and our competitor.

When it was our turn to ask questions, we used this format:

“How important is [differentiator] to ensure [program goal] is successful?

For each of these questions, our champion gave some version of “extremely important.”

At the end of the call, I made this statement:

“Based on this conversation, we’ll prepare our demonstration to go deep into how we address [differentiator 1, 2, 3]. To ensure an apples-to-apples comparison, it would likely be helpful if [competitor] could prepare the same.”

The demo round happened a few days later. Our champion called us after our competitor presented: “Guys - it was a disaster. They quit.”

We had created such an unfair evaluation environment for our competitor that they refused to demonstrate their technology.

They got on the call, tried to bash the evaluation process, and said, “When you are serious about making a good decision for your business, you can give us a call,” and withdrew their bid.

Our “demo” became an implementation call, and contracts were signed shortly after.

Champion-building and trap-setting are valuable as standalone tactics.

Combined, they create such an advantage that your competitors may literally run away.

10 unsolicited pieces of career advice from a guy that’s seen acquisitions, IPOs, and works for a best-in-class tech company:

1) Your career won’t grow faster than your company.

2) If execs are constantly defending your product as a “need-to-have” then your product is a nice-to-have.

3) If you want a company that has great processes, join one that hasn’t changed in years. Otherwise, accept that growth means chaos.

4) Changing jobs every 18 months will increase your short-term earnings. Staying long enough to actually get good will increase your career earnings.

5) Obsess over finding something you can be the “best” at. If you don’t have a superpower, you are a commodity.

6) Your company’s goal is to retain you at the lowest possible cost to the business. If you feel you are worth more, ask for more.

7) If you can’t find a company to pay you what you think you are worth then you have either a value problem or a messaging problem.

8) There are no short-cuts but there are accelerators.

9) No matter your career path, learn to sell.

10) No matter your career path, learn to write.

content:
I responded to a cold email: “This isn’t my priority. Best of luck with your outreach!”

Got hit with an objection handle: “Just to confirm - closing more deals faster isn’t a priority?”

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

Here’s what that follow-up might look like:

“Makes perfect sense you’ve already got a handle on this. Usually this means you’ve got a similar solution in place and I didn’t do a good job sharing how we are different, or you are attacking this priority through a completely different approach.

Can I ask where you fall?”

Next time you hear “this isn’t a priority” to something that you know should be a priority, give this a shot!

Struggling with getting next steps with an opportunity? Stop adding to your buyer's plate.

Here’s what adding to their plate looks like:

"It's been a bit since we last connected. Can we find time to discuss what's changed on your end?"

This request puts all the effort on the buyer. They’d need to find time to update you on things they already know *just in case* you can help them.

Email deleted.

Here’s what removing things from their plate looks like:

"It's been a bit since we last connected. If you are anything like similar companies, you are likely working through [priority 1, 2, 3].

I've attached a hypothesis of how we could help in those areas - if I'm not completely off base, could we find some time to discuss in more depth?"

This request shows your willingness to make their job easier. You'll stand out even if your hypothesis isn’t completely accurate.

Many people treat their inbox as a “to-do” list. When a seller adds to that list, it’s the easiest email to ignore.

Turn your outreach into a “look what I did for you - imagine how much more I could help with your input,” and you’ll see higher buyer engagement.
