I remember a call with a great AE and a contact that perfectly fit our ICP (VP of Customer Experience).

The call was going great until he asked us what we do.

The rep went into what we called our “Experience Management” pitch.

The marketing-approved, persuasive, high-level overview painting an incredible picture of how we could help connect Customer, Product, Brand, and Employee Experience.

The pitch was perfect. Sounded just like the training in our LMS. Marketing would have shed a tear of pride.

Which made the customer’s response even more painful:

“Yeah, I’m mainly focused on customer experience, and it sounds like you all do way more than that. I don’t think this is the right fit.”

Oof.

We tried (and failed) to salvage the call. Once a buyer makes that initial decision, it’s tough to overcome.

The frustrating part is that the buyer did have a customer experience problem we could have solved.

But our “pitch” made him feel like we were a generalist solution and wouldn’t have the focus necessary to solve his problem.

Here’s how we should have answered his “What do you do” question:

“We help CX VPs reduce customer churn by understanding every key experience they provide their customers. We’d love to know how you are doing that today…”

I can imagine some of my former executive team yelling at me right now:

“But our ability to do all of experience management in one platform is a massive differentiator!! That should be the first thing you pitch!”

The problem is that no one cares about your differentiators until they think you can solve a problem they care about.

We could have slammed the deal home with our valuable differentiators if we nailed that.

But by leading with the “platform story,” we failed to answer the most critical question:

“How can you specifically help me?”

Forget the pitch. Solve a problem.

Then, your buyer will care about that beautiful marketing message.

content:
Ten SaaS sales realities I’ve learned the hard way:

1) If you only hear good news, you are losing the deal. All deals have risk. Champions share risk. No risk shared means no champion. No champion means you lose.

2) The longer it takes to close a deal, the longer your buyer has to realize they are ok without your solution. No velocity, no deal.

3) Solving a problem doesn’t win deals. Solving THE problem does. Every exec has hundreds of fires burning - they only pay money and spend time to stop the fires that threaten to burn the whole thing down.

4) More people constantly getting added to the evaluation committee isn’t often a good thing - it means nobody wants to take ownership of the decision.

5) Your buyers spend most of their calls with you multi-tasking. If you don’t quickly capture their attention and keep them constantly engaged, your calls are a waste of time.

6) No one believes your ROI projections. If the business case isn’t in your buyer’s language with their numbers, it’s not taken seriously.

7) Buyers are biased against sellers. Any time you sound the same as other sellers, you strengthen that bias. If you want to win, learn to sound different.

8) You can’t create compelling events (end-of-quarter discounts don’t count). The only consistent way to accelerate deals is to make the buyer’s status quo unbearable.

9) A poorly run deal with a strong executive connection beats a well-run deal with no executive connection. If you have a six or seven-figure deal, and you’re not talking to the C-Level, you’re going to get blindsided by the competitor that is.

10) There is nothing more important to cover at the end of the call than selling next steps. Much better to skip agenda items and align on next steps than to finish the agenda and take next steps “offline.”

What’d I miss?

content:
Struggling to set meetings?

Try my three-step framework to make sure you are using the right messaging, with the right contacts, within your best accounts.

Here are the questions to answer:

1) Are you calling the right accounts?

Here’s what to make sure you are focused on the right companies:

- Potential budget

Are they investing in areas tied to your solution?

For example, at MongoDB, we look for companies that are hiring developers.

Hiring developers = building applications = spending money on databases.

- Use case

Are there multiple landing spots for your product?

For example, at Qualtrics I focused on accounts that needed to understand brand, customer, and product experience. Three different use cases = three shots to win business at the account.

- Personal Familiarity

Massive budget and multiple use cases won’t help you land an account if you can’t speak their language.

Simple question to ask yourself: “If I was in a room with their executive team, could I have a conversation about their business, in their language, without being completely out of place?”

Good accounts that you understand are better targets than great accounts that you don’t understand.


2) Are you calling the right contacts?


Two questions to ask about the contacts in your sequences:

- Would this person personally benefit from our solution?

- Is this person at all responsible for solving the business pain our solution solves?

No personal benefit = no reason for them to respond.

No connection to business pain = no reason for you to want them to respond.


3) Messaging

Two points I’m looking for in effective messaging:

- Emotional relevance

What is the email/phone call your buyer never wants to get from their boss? If your email shows them a way to avoid that dreaded call, it’s emotionally relevant.

- Specificity

Could you write the same email to a different person? Or, worse, could your competitor send the same email to your buyer?

If the answer to either of those questions is “yes,” your messaging isn’t specific enough.


Meetings are tough to come by right now. But it’s hard to go wrong if you use the right messaging, with the right people, within the right accounts.

Previous customers changing jobs can be an incredible pipeline source (duh).

But I still used to screw up these opportunities by making three dangerous assumptions:

1) Assuming they were previously involved in selecting my software

Sometimes, the user was previously a champion that helped get my solution approved.

Often, they inherited my solution from someone else.

I treated all former users like former champions, and lost deals because I didn’t go through the champion building process.

2) Assuming that they understood my solution

I can see myself saying, “Well you probably don’t need to see a demo - you may know more about this product than I do!”

Facepalm.

Very few of my users were experts. I lost deals because I assumed the buyer knew we had what they needed.

While I was building proposals for my “easy win,” the competition was showing them the functionality they needed that they didn’t think we offered.

3) Assuming I could skip multithreading since you have a former user "champion"

I knew working with a former user gave me an advantage (the data shows 114% higher win rates). I thought that would offset the need to multi-thread.

I left a lot of deals on the table, because your win rate is 215% higher when you add multithreading to working with a previous user.

Here’s how you can sell much better than I did when working with previous customers:

- Find out their involvement in evaluating your software at their previous company

Adapt your motion for someone that previously made the decision vs. someone that was just along for the ride.

- Dig into their previous usage. Were they a power user? Or casual?

Instead of skipping the demo, tailor the demo based on what they had used before + their new role.

- Work with your former user to accelerate multi-threading

They have context on your product and their new organization. This can be the perfect recipe to get the right people in the room.

Former users can be a goldmine, but you still need to be relevant, personalized, and multi-threaded.

Former users can also be easily missed (job changes are happening with extreme velocity right now).

One sure way to improve your demos: bucket each feature you show into these three categories.

1) Table stakes (functionality all competitors offer):

Sounds like, “Everyone can do this - I just wanted to briefly cover because you’ll need it and didn’t want you thinking we were the odd one out.”

2) Comparative differentiators (many do this, but we do it best):

Sounds like, “You’ve likely seen something similar from our competitors. Here’s why our approach is different and why that difference matters for you.”

3) Unique differentiators (only we do this):

Sounds like, “No one else does this - here’s why we chose this approach and how it helps people like you.”

Most reps spend 80% of their demo on table stakes functionality. This drowns out the differentiators, and your buyer thinks you are the same as the competition. Lowest cost will win.

To drive more engaging demos, spend 80% of your demo on differentiators. To drive better-understood demos, help your buyer categorize what you show to make it easier to compare to the competition.


Bonus: Unique differentiators can be tricky because they often lead to buyer skepticism. “If it’s so important, why does no one else offer this?”

content:
As a new AE I'd get excited when my prospect listed their requirements and we met them all.

"We can do ALL of that!" I'd think.

I'd show them the demo, commit the deal to my manager (after all, I showed them all the things), and prepare the proposal.

Then, I lost deal after deal with my prospect saying, "Your competitor also meets our requirements and they cost 40% less."

The problem with buyer requirements is they are basic.

The problem with basic is all of your competitors offer the same.

The problem with all competitors offering the same requirements is it becomes purely about price.

So, unless you sell the cheapest product, you lose.

Everything changed when I learned a technique called "trap-setting."

In it's most basic form, trap-setting is influencing your buyer's requirements to include your product's differentiators.

Done right, it disqualifies your competition because your buyer understands their success is best met through capabilities unique to your solution.

Here's how to run this play:

1) Define your differentiators

Identify your differentiators across three types:

- Unique (features only you provide)

- Comparative (features you share with the competition that you do better)

- Holistic (company advantages, e.g., more engineers which lets you innovate faster)

2) Defend your differentiators

For unique differentiators, you’ll need to defend why your company took a different approach than the competition and the value it will bring your customer.

For comparative, you must define why it’s better and matters.

For holistic, establish why these advantages would give your customer peace of mind (think: how does this de-risk our solution?)

You should introduce unique and comparative differentiators early in the sales process.

Here’s one way to introduce on a discovery call after your customer describes one of their required capabilities:

“Many customers that require [insert customer required capability] also require [insert unique or comparative differentiator]. 

They’ve found that without that capability they [insert negative consequence].”

Holistic differentiators are best at the end of the deal cycle. Use them to give your customer confidence they are partnering with the right company, not just purchasing the right product.

Effective trap-setting takes preparation and planning, but few things in sales are more fun than disqualifying your competition from consideration.

content:
I’ve tried to accelerate deals in many ways:

- Pain amplification (dragging them through the glass)

- Proof of concepts/proof of value

- Discounts (rarely work)

Nothing I’ve tried has worked as well as having a true champion sprinting through walls to get the deal done.

Here are my top 3 recommendations for developing champions:

1) Motivate

People act in self-interest. You need to tie your solution to personal wins for your champion – not just company benefits.

2) Mitigate risk

While you excitedly talk about all the things that could go right, they are thinking about what could go wrong and how that would impact them.

3) Help remember and repackage

content:
I used to think all I needed to win deals were strong business outcomes.

If I could show ROI, I thought my champion would push the contract through for signature.

I lost deal after deal until I learned that positive business outcomes aren't enough to motivate buyers.

While positive business outcomes are necessary to get a contract signed, you need a motivated champion to get you through the process.

And people are motivated by positive personal outcomes, not positive business outcomes.

Let me explain:

Imagine you are selling to me, leading with a strong positive business outcome:

“We can help Mongo improve profitability.”

While Mongo increasing profitability benefits me, it's not a metric I'm measured by.

I'm pulled thin as it is, I can’t take time out of my week to champion a solution that isn’t making me look good based on metrics I care most about.


Now, let’s try selling to me with a positive personal outcome:

“We’ll help you earn larger commission checks by helping your AEs ramp faster.”

Ok, now you’ve got my attention. Faster ramp, more quota relief, more commission, that’s my language.


Now that I'm listening, help me sell to an economic buyer:

“While you are focused on quota relief, your executive team is thinking about profitability.

By helping you accelerate the ramp time of your new reps, we’ll increase rep productivity.

Increased rep productivity lowers your cost of sale, making Mongo more profitable.”
​

Now you’ve got a winning combination:

- A champion motivated by a positive personal outcome

- A champion enabled with a positive business outcome

You need both to win.

Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about database maintenance. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to maintain the database. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”


Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

content:
I spent my first two years as an AE making these 5 mistakes. Rarely made quota, no chance at promotion.

Learning to solve them led to becoming the #1 AE.

Teaching how to solve them helped our team finish #1 in consecutive years.

Here they are:

1) Setting an agenda instead of an objective

Earn the right to ask questions by helping your buyer understand what they will get out of the call is more impactful than a generic agenda.

Think: “What will they get out of this?” instead of “How will we spend the time?”


2) Asking, “tell me about your role”

Senior buyers don’t have time/patience to explain their job to you.

If you don’t even know the basics of their role, why would they trust your recommendations?

3) Pretending to understand

Buyers lose trust when you act like you understand and they know you don’t.

Instead of, “Yeah, that makes sense,” be willing to say, “I didn’t completely follow… can we go deeper into [reframe their words].

4) Overwhelming with irrelevant complexity

Showing unnecessary functionality makes your solution seem expensive, regardless of the price.

When planning your demos ask, “How would my customer use this?” for every feature you’ll show. If you don’t know, don’t show it.

5) Negotiating price before finalizing scope

Negotiating at the wrong time is a sure way to reduce your deal size.

If pressed, just say: “We’ll work with you to ensure a mutually beneficial agreement. To prevent unnecessary back and forth, let’s finalize exactly what we’re going to be providing your team and then we can hammer out the financial details.”

content:
Nick Sanderson hit 172% of his annual revenue target.

Here’s what worked for him:

1) Alignment / ”quarterbacking”

Winning complex deals requires aligning your champion, solution architect, business value, customer success, and sales leadership. 

You don’t have to do it all, but you do need to make sure everyone is on the same page. 


2) Obsessive territory management

Territory management is a daily activity, not monthly or quarterly. 

“80% of my revenue came from 20% of my accounts. Time spent outside of my top 20% of accounts rarely paid off.”


3) Double down on strengths 

Cold calling led to 90% of generated deals and I found that, even in deal progression situations, nothing beats picking up the phone. 

The best champions appreciate a direct line of communication. 


4) Ask the “scary” questions

Sellers often avoid the hard questions: ‘Why wouldn’t you just do this next year?” “Does anything bad really happen if we miss your goal timeline?” 

If we don’t ask the hard questions, someone else will. And then we may not have the opportunity to influence the answer. 

The best way to ensure we asked the right questions was prepping for calls with my solution architect, Clarence Ondieki, to identify gaps/risks we could run at rather than avoid. 

I’ll leave you with his key learnings:


- “Every meeting counts - do the research, prepare for every meeting, come with a point of view, listen to the customer, ask the tough questions, listen, tweak your point of view, repeat.” 

- “Be accountable - your deals, promotions, commissions, are yours… not your SA’s, not your managers, etc. It’s on me to power the boat, my ecosystem helps me steer it.”

- “Act with urgency - if a deal doesn't have urgency, it's unlikely to get done. The same goes for your operating rhythm to ensure you are having enough conversations to find and close business.”

- “All good deals die a number of times, it’s just a matter of how you respond. Sales is a game of peaks and valleys - much like my Golf Game - which is why I love it.”

content:
The most uncomfortable call of my career (35 seconds of silence felt like 5 minutes) taught me two important lessons about negotiation.

Here’s the story:

I had a great relationship with my main contacts at an account. We had worked together for over a year, and they were planning on significantly expanding their agreement with us.

Because the license was expanding, they looped in a new stakeholder that I had never met.

This individual’s only goal was to get the lowest cost possible.

We got on a call, and the tone was completely different. The new contact went on the offensive and listed their demands.

The requests were unreasonable. Since I was confident in our solution and the value of our partnership, my response was:

“We’ve been working closely with the team for several months to right-size the agreement and to ensure that the value warrants the investment. While I appreciate your goal is to get the lowest price possible, your requests aren’t reasonable, and we cannot consider them.”

Then, I shut up.

There was silence for what felt like forever (the call recording showed it was only about 35 seconds), and the contact finally said, “Ok. We’ll need to discuss internally.”

The call ended, and we received a signed contract for the proposed amount a few days later.

While uncomfortable in the moment, I learned two essential negotiation lessons:

1) Silence is ok

Be confident, communicate clearly and don’t over-explain. Then, shut up.

2) Saying “no” is ok

When you are close to a deal, it’s tempting to remove all friction by accepting all requests thrown your way.

Don’t. Be confident in your value, and say “no” when a request isn’t reasonable.

Any other tips for negotiation?

Here are the five superpowers I wish I would have developed earlier:

Decisions are made emotionally and validated with logic. Deliver critical facts with emotion to ensure they stick.

content:
Saying, “yep, that makes sense,” is killing your discovery.

Here’s my favorite coaching method to help reps fix:

When reviewing calls, if I hear a rep say, “that makes sense,” I’ll pause the recording and ask, “did that actually make sense to you?”

9 times out of 10 they’ll laugh and say “no.” It was just more comfortable to move on rather than admitting confusion.

Think about how this feels as a buyer:

1) They just walked you through a complicated problem.

2) They know they didn’t explain it clearly because it’s difficult to put into words.

And they get hit with a, “yep - that makes sense!” in response?

How are they going to believe you have a solution for them if they can’t even believe you understand their problem?

Good sellers have no problem asking for clarification.

Great sellers refuse to move on in a conversation until they are on the same page as their buyer.

Next time you are tempted to say, “that makes sense,” try, “I’m not sure I’m following. Can you explain…” and you’ll have a more meaningful conversation.

content:
Last week, we brought all of North America acquisition to Miami for a Command of the Message training. 

As these poor souls listened to me for one and a half days, I tried to hammer home three main points:

1) If you are still going “wide” in your second discovery call, you’ve lost. 

Great initial discovery uncovers the biggest problems your buyer needs to solve, and why they haven’t yet been solved.

If your second discovery is still “searching for pain” you aren’t going to get a third call. 


2) Negative consequences are not a description of what’s going wrong. They are a definition of why what’s going wrong matters. 

- “We are spending too much money” 
- “Employees are wasting their time”
- “We have data silos” 

So what? 

Every company has areas where they spend too much money, employees waste time, and have data silos. 

Keep asking, “so what?” until everyone agrees the problem is big enough to solve now. 


3) When required capabilities are only defined by the customer, the lowest cost solution will win. 

When customers form their shopping list, they default to widely available capabilities. 

Widely available capabilities are met by all of your competitors. 

Either influence the required capabilities in your favor, or make sure you are the cheapest proposal. 

Otherwise, closed/lost. 

Which of these lessons resonate with you?

Max Tierney joined MongoDB for three reasons:

1) To improve his sales skills

2) Work for a company that truly has a differentiated product and massive market opportunity

3) Lay the foundation for becoming an effective sales leader at MongoDB

I’m thrilled to celebrate his promotion into leadership after a great final year as an AE. 

Here’s what worked for him:

1) Operating Rhythm

Time is one of your most valuable assets in sales. You can easily get overwhelmed when you are sourcing new opportunities, running multiple deals, working through POCs, and still contributing to internal meetings. 

Being able to prioritize your “big rocks” is critical to having success in a competitive selling environment.

2) Authenticity

Be authentic! It sounds silly but show your buyer that you are a human and get to know them personally.

3) Champion building

Champions have professional aspirations and one way to achieve those aspirations is to solve significant business challenges (or implement a net-new project) for their company.

 After you’ve successfully tested that this individual is indeed a champion and you’ve earned the right to be a trusted business advisor, they will sell internally on your behalf.


I’ll leave you with his key learnings:

- Have intention behind what you do

- Why you do something is just as important as what you are doing. 

- Be truly open to feedback - even when it’s hard to hear. 

- It’s ok to be vulnerable and address your development gaps, not hide them. Your sales leaders aren’t mind readers and are there to help you reach your goals. We all want to be perfect but there’s always room to improve.

Congrats on the leadership promotion, Max! Excited for you and your next chapter.

content:
I managed an AE that was considered an excellent pipeline generator. They set tons of meetings.

However, they closed no deals.

Few of the meetings they set even turned into opportunities.

They had been previously diagnosed as "high skill" in prospecting but "low skill" in discovery.

Makes sense, right? Setting meetings = good prospecting. No quality opportunities resulting from those meetings = bad discovery.

Logical but wrong.

Digging deeper, I found that this rep was "high skill" at cold-calling the wrong people. The meetings they set weren't converting, not because of bad discovery, but because of the wrong persona.

So we went a level deeper in our diagnosis of prospecting:

Cold call messaging: High Skill

Identifying the right personas: Low Skill

Armed with a more specific diagnosis, we focused on finding the right people to improve their "personas" skill.

Then, they leveraged their strong cold-calling ability and became one of the most successful reps I've managed.

It’s dangerous to think you are “good” at a broad skill like prospecting or discovery. Instead, break the broader skill into smaller segments you can evaluate and improve.

You’ll master the broad skill when you understand and improve the underlying competencies.

content:
7 things I wish I could tell myself on my first day of sales: 

1) The success of your career isn’t determined in the first few years. Calm down, deep breaths, get good. 

2) You’ll hear “Ok, we’ll sign today” many times. Don’t panic when they don’t. “We’ll sign today” is buyer code for “We’ll sign in 3 weeks when you’ve lost your mind from anxiety and have given up hope.”

3) You’ll win deals you should’ve lost and lose deals you should’ve won. Sometimes it just be like that though. 

4) The nicer the procurement person is when you first meet them, the more brutal they will be in negotiations. Don’t fall for it - buckle up.

5) “You are such a good sales rep” is not a real compliment unless it comes with a signed agreement. It’s just a nice buyer that wants to let you down easy. 

6) Your potential for success is not limited by others having success, so cheer others on. 

7) Join MongoDB pre-IPO and hold onto your shares please please please trust me on this one.

content:
“People hate being sold, but... please follow a rigid sales process that makes people feel like they are being sold."

Yikes.

IMO, this is the biggest misalignment in sales.

Look, I get it. I empathize with companies trying to build sales orgs. Process scales and scale is necessary.

Unfortunately, most scalable processes are built for the lowest common denominator.

And top performers don't excel by following those processes better than their peers.

The good news is that you can take the sales process you are taught and adapt it to become a top performer.

Here's one simple tweak to get you started:

Stop thinking, "How do I get my buyer to the next step in the sales process?"

Start thinking, "What does my buyer need from me to get to the next stage in their buying process?"

Sure, this may mean you give pricing before discovery. Could mean you show a bit of a demo on the first call.

Supporting your buyer on their journey may lead to "breaking" all sorts of rules.

But I'd rather break some rules and win instead of following the rules and lose.

Great AEs and sales leaders can get an instant promotion anytime with a job move.

Be careful. Here’s what that promotion can cost you:

1) Current pipeline

If your new company doesn’t pay out a new hire bonus, you aren’t hitting your OTE in your first several months while you rebuild the pipeline coverage you left at your prior role.

2) Product mastery

If you move to a company with a complex product, you won’t effectively sell it for several months.

3) Ecosystem navigation

Half the battle in sales is knowing how to work with supporting teams for everything from support escalation to contract creation and distribution. New company means all new processes to learn.

Please note: this is not a “you need to be loyal to your company” post. We’ve all seen how that plays out. Always do what’s best for you and those you support.

It’s also not a “don’t take an external promotion” post. While you lose the above, you may be getting:

- More pay
- Better leadership
- Improved product to sell

Which makes leaving a no-brainer.

However, the shortcut may not always lead to the right destination. It’s often worth spending an extra few months to earn the promo at your current company rather than leaving for a “fast track.”

I’ve tried to accelerate deals in many ways:

- Pain amplification (dragging them through the glass)

- Proof of concepts/proof of value

- Discounts (rarely work)

Nothing I’ve tried has ever worked as well as having a true champion sprinting through walls to get the deal done.

Here are my top 3 recommendations for developing champions:

1) Motivate

People act in self-interest. You need to tie your solution to personal wins for your champion – not just company benefits.

2) Mitigate risk

While you excitedly talk about all the things that could go right, they are thinking about what could go wrong and how that would impact them.

3) Help remember and repackage

Even your strongest champions will forget most of what you discuss. Helping them remember key points and package them for other audiences will make it easier for them to champion your solution.

One of the first things I was taught as an AE was the importance of multi-threading.

But I wasn’t taught how. So when I tried to do it I failed. 

I got frustrated: why would my champion block me?

This post will teach you what took me lots of failure to learn. 

First, understand when you ask for introductions, you aren’t just asking them to send a quick email. 

You are asking them to bet their credibility on you.

If they connect you with a coworker that doesn’t end up finding value in meeting with you, it reflects poorly on them. 

This is magnified at the executive level: no one wants an executive annoyed at them because they wasted their time with a poor sales call!

Here’s my framework for successfully multi-threading with your champion:

1) Build their confidence by always adding value when you meet with them

2) Have a valid and specific reason for your request to meet with new stakeholders

3) Detail what will be expected from all attendees (not just an agenda - specifically what role each attendee will play)

4) Share your plan to make sure it’s a successful meeting


Here’s what the request could look like:

“Linda, it’s been great working with you to identify how MongoDB could help your dev team improve efficiency.

Last thing we’d want to do is begin a migration without a really clear picture of how our work would impact the broader engineering org - we want to optimize for the long-term.

Typically the CTO is the best person to speak to long-term architecture goals. We’d love to bring Angela onto the next call to bring her up to speed on our goals and planned implementation to see where she would recommend adjustments.

We don't want to waste her time: we’ll prepare an executive summary she can review before the call so we can make the most of the conversation.

The main feedback we’ll want from her is related to the milestones we’ve discussed - now is the right time to change those definitions or timing.

To ensure the call is successful, we’ll also include an executive from our solution architect team - that way, any questions she has can be addressed during the call.”

Following this approach will increase your champion’s confidence in you, earn an audience with others, and ensure you are ready to make those conversations effective.

Soft costs (e.g. ‘our solution will save your team five hours a week!) aren’t nearly as persuasive as you think.

An executive will think:

“I’m paying them to spend their time working on that problem whether it’s there or not.”

For soft costs to be convincing, you need to have validated a better way for those employees to spend their time.

Weak example:

“We can save your engineers five hours a week if they no longer need to worry about database maintenance. That’s $500k a year of savings, which is 2.5x more than our solution costs.”

The executive will think: “Part of my fixed cost (salary) is to pay them to maintain the database. I pay them the same, even if they aren’t working on that anymore. I still pay that $500k of salary, and now I’m adding $200k more for a new product.”

Better example:

“We learned from your VP of Eng that if your engineering team had an extra five hours per week to focus on [new product], you’d be able to launch one month early. Your VP of Product estimates the revenue impact of the early launch to be $2 million.”

Take your business case from, “we’ll save your team time” to “you’ll accomplish x and generate $$$ with the time saved” and watch your win rate increase.

content:
My career lowlight was being suspended for a day without pay (was close to being fired).

Here's the story:

The company was growing rapidly and we needed a new territory model. The decision was made to deploy territories based on zip codes.

I got a patch of zip codes in suburban Grand Rapids, MI.

In other words, I owned any account in the Grand Rapids area that wasn’t in the city. Nothing against the fine people of suburban Grand Rapids, but my territory sucked. To make matters worse, my friend that sat next to me was assigned to Metro New York.

I spent my days trying to get contact information for companies not even on LinkedIn.

My friend often had multiple inbounds in a single day.

Frustrated, I threw a fit about how the zip code territory was flawed to senior leaders and my peers.

Leadership didn’t love that. Some wanted to fire me.

Fortunately, my boss fought for me. Instead of termination, I was suspended for a day without pay so I could fix my attitude (bless up).

Eventually, the territory model was adjusted, and everyone lived happily ever after.

Here are a few lessons:

1) When things go wrong, be patient and propose solutions instead of throwing a fit.

2) If you want to recommend organizational changes then bring data, not emotion.

3) Vent up - not across. If you are frustrated, talk to your manager. Don’t bring negativity to your peers.

4) Everyone at your company is doing the best they can. Be forgiving of others' errors, and you’ll find people being more forgiving of yours.

p.s. I still haven’t been to Grand Rapids but I absolutely love Michigan now so I think we are on good terms.

One sure way to improve your demos: bucket each feature you show into these three categories.

1) Table stakes (functionality all competitors offer):

Sounds like, “Everyone can do this - I just wanted to briefly cover because you’ll need it and didn’t want you thinking we were the odd one out.”

Most reps spend 80% of their demo on table stakes functionality.

content:
Sellers are taught to "quantify" the problem or pain as a way to increase urgency early in the deal cycle.

A few problems with this:

1) Your buyer determines urgency - you don't

Try as we might, we aren't changing our buyer's priorities. Instead, we should map to them.

2) "How much is this problem costing you?" sounds incredibly salesy

Your buyer knows you just want this number to convince them your solution is cheap in comparison to their pain.

3) The numbers are all made up

Early in the deal cycle, quantification is inaccurate. You'll struggle to build a real ROI-based business case until you are deeper in the sales cycle.


Instead of asking your buyer to quantify the problem, ask, “How else have you tried to solve this problem?”

If they haven’t been actively trying to solve the problem, you haven’t identified a real pain. You are on the right track if they have been trying (and failing) to solve the problem.

Save quantifying pain for when you are building a business case with your champion.

Use the “How else have you tried to solve this problem?” question to see if building a business case is worth your time.

content:
A decade into my sales career, and I still get just as nervous for big presentations as I did as a new AE.

The difference is now I have a proven preparation method that guarantees a smooth, confident delivery.

Here’s how I prepare to ensure I perform at my best:
​
​Two days before:​
​
- Review prep materials/research to determine what is top of mind for attendees

The goal is to identify the top outcome they want to drive and the biggest pain they want to solve.

​​
- Identify my one takeaway that ties back to my audience’s “top of mind"

If the audience only remembers one point, what do I need it to be?
​
​

- Build talk track to emphasize my primary takeaway

They'll forget what they hear while remembering what they feel. I build my talk track around the concept of, "what do I want them to feel that is associated with my main takeaway?"

​​
​One day before:​
​
- Practice until mostly smooth, with minimal reliance on notes

The timing here is extremely intentional: sleep reinforces learning. One night’s rest between practice and presentation allows my brain to cement the flow.


If I'm 80% polished the day before, simply sleeping and waking up gets me to 95%. 

Brain science is cool.


Day of:​
​
- One more walkthrough, with emphasis on tonality (where I want to pause for emphasis, etc.)

At this point I've mastered the material. I know what I want to say, I just polish how I want to say it.

Then, I enter the call with the confidence that stems from preparation.

​
Regardless of your experience or comfort presenting, you should never outgrow the need to practice and prepare.

Next time you have a big presentation, give this framework a try and I bet you'll deliver a more confident and impactful message.

I get the approach: The idea is to “trap” the prospect into a question they can’t say no to.

“What sales leader wouldn’t want more deals, faster?”

Here’s the problem: I’m not objecting to the proposed outcome. Closing more deals faster is ALWAYS a priority for me.

I’m just already working on my top priorities to help my teams close more deals faster. We’ve identified tools supporting those priorities and are in execution mode.

My objection wasn’t to the outcome. It was the approach this solution takes to drive that outcome. The problems they solve to drive that outcome are not painful for me.

When you get a no, don’t fall back to the high-level outcome:

- “Oh, you don’t want to save money on your HR solutions?”

- “Really, you don’t want to reduce the risk of getting hacked?”

- “Huh, you don’t want your developers to be happy and productive?”

Of course your buyers want those outcomes. If they are objecting, they likely either:

- Don’t believe you can drive that outcome

- Believe a different approach will work better

Find out which of those your objection falls under and address that for better success.

If you can answer this one question, you’ll meaningfully improve every stage of the deal cycle:

“What’s the #1 email/call your buyer does not want to receive?”

Examples:

VP Sales - “how did you miss forecast this badly?”

VP Marketing - “there’s no evidence that marketing spending is leading to revenue”

VP Engineering - “we’re down, and we’ve lost client data”

VP HR - “we are being fined millions for non-compliance”

Take 30 minutes this week to write the emails you think your buyers would hate to receive.

Then, show how you can help them avoid this email in your sales cycle, and you’ll win more deals faster by successfully leveraging “emotional relevance.”
